entries: The National Security Act creates the CIA (and a National Security Council to advise the President on intelligence), with a director free of control by the Joint Chiefs. Its first leaders come largely from the wartime OSS.
Fulgencio Batista's troops seize Havana's Columbia army camp at dawn and oust President Carlos Prío.
Dwight Eisenhower, having left his post as NATO commander, is elected president.
Castro leads a failed assault on the Moncada barracks in Santiago and is captured; at trial he declares that history will absolve him. The date names his movement.
Eisenhower's National Security Council has CIA Director Allen Dulles plan for Indochina contingencies; the CIA then sets up the Saigon Military Mission to expand covert operations in Vietnam.

The CIA overthrows Guatemala's elected president Jacobo Árbenz, protecting United Fruit. David Atlee Phillips and E. Howard Hunt run the psychological warfare; David Sánchez Morales is one of Phillips's operatives.

Oswald, 15, joins the New Orleans Civil Air Patrol unit led by David Ferrie, a pilot later arrested twice (1961) on morals charges and later an investigator for ex-FBI agent Guy Banister at 544 Camp Street.
Morales goes undercover as a State Department political officer at the U.S. embassy in Caracas.
Oswald reports to the Marine Corps Recruit Depot in San Diego.
Oswald arrives at Atsugi, Japan, home of the U-2 spy plane, as a radar operator.
Phillips opens a public-relations business in Havana as a CIA front.
Morales is posted to the Havana embassy; USIA officer Paul Bethel later says he ran the CIA's "dirty tricks."
After 13 months in Japan, Oswald is reassigned to Marine Air Control Squadron Nine in Santa Ana, California.
Batista flees as Castro's 26th of July Movement sweeps into Havana.
Marita Lorenz, 19, meets Castro when her father's cruise ship docks in Havana; she becomes his mistress and is later recruited by Frank Sturgis for a plot to poison him.
Oswald takes a Marine Russian-language exam and does well enough to suggest study since Japan, though no fellow Marine saw him learning it.
Nearing discharge, Oswald applies to Albert Schweitzer College in Switzerland, claiming proficiency in Russian.
Oswald leaves the Marines on a hardship discharge, saying his mother needs support.
Having left New Orleans on September 20 and traveled via London, Le Havre and Helsinki, Oswald reaches Moscow and tells his Intourist guide he wants Soviet citizenship.
Manuel Artime's Movement of Recovery (MRR) becomes the first anti-Castro group organized widely inside Cuba.
Allen Dulles approves giving "thorough consideration" to eliminating Castro.
Richard Bissell, CIA Deputy Director for Plans, tells colleagues Dulles has put him in charge of a Guatemala-style upheaval in Cuba; he picks Hunt and Phillips as key field officers.
Eisenhower authorizes the CIA to train and equip Cuban exiles to overthrow Castro.
Francis Gary Powers's U-2 is shot down over the USSR, wrecking Eisenhower's planned summit with Khrushchev. Some speculate Oswald helped the Soviets.
Hoover memo to the State Department warns that an impostor may be using Oswald's birth certificate.
Havana banker Antonio Veciana is recruited for anti-Castro work by a CIA officer calling himself "Maurice Bishop."

CIA support chief James O'Connell meets Robert Maheu (ex-FBI, working for Howard Hughes) and mobster John Roselli about using the Mafia to kill Castro; Sam Giancana and Santo Trafficante later recruit Miami Cubans for it.
The State Department sends the CIA a list of defectors, including Oswald, asking for information.
The CIA opens a 201 personality file on Oswald, later telling the Warren Commission it was prompted by the State Department request.
The U.S. embassy in Havana closes.
George de Mohrenschildt, a Dallas petroleum engineer the chronology calls a CIA asset, spends four months in Guatemala with his wife while the CIA trains exiles there for the Bay of Pigs.
Congolese leader Patrice Lumumba is killed in Katanga with Belgian involvement and CIA complicity. Same day: Eisenhower's farewell address warns against the "military-industrial complex."
In his transition briefing, Eisenhower tells Kennedy that military intervention in Laos is better than a coalition with Communists.
Kennedy's inaugural address pairs Cold War resolve with a call for both sides to "begin anew the quest for peace."
Oswald writes to Richard Snyder at the U.S. embassy in Moscow asking to come home.
CIA Technical Services records show poisoned cigars delivered to an unidentified asset; no record of an attempt.
O'Connell gives Roselli poison pills, which Roselli says went to a Cuban official close to Castro; they were reportedly returned when the official lost his post.

On Kennedy's order, the CIA-organized exile front run by Hunt is replaced by a broader Cuban Revolutionary Council including Manolo Ray, whose politics Hunt derides as "Fidelism without Fidel." Amador Odio, Sylvia Odio's father, backs Ray. Hunt leaves the Bay of Pigs political job.
Overriding the Joint Chiefs and CIA, Kennedy drops support for General Phoumi in Laos and backs a neutral, independent Laos.
The Bay of Pigs invasion fails within two days: Brigade 2506 loses 114 men and 1,189 are captured, ransomed in December 1962 for $53 million in food and medicine.
Kennedy refuses to send U.S. forces as the brigade is surrounded. The chronology says he saw a CIA trap meant to force an invasion and reportedly vowed to splinter the agency "in a thousand pieces."
At the Vienna summit, Kennedy and Khrushchev agree only on a neutral Laos; Khrushchev's indifference to nuclear risk shocks Kennedy.
At an NSC meeting the Joint Chiefs and Dulles present a plan for a preemptive nuclear strike on the USSR in late 1963; Kennedy walks out in disgust.
Phillips becomes chief of covert action in Mexico City, serving until October 1963, when he is promoted to chief of Cuban operations.
The USSR resumes atmospheric hydrogen-bomb tests.
The U.S. cuts aid to any country that assists Cuba.
After more Soviet tests, Kennedy orders U.S. testing resumed.
At the UN, Kennedy calls for a "peace race" toward general and complete disarmament.
Khrushchev's first secret letter to Kennedy, smuggled via a Soviet agent to press secretary Pierre Salinger, likens their shared stake in peace to Noah's Ark.
A Castro assassination attempt organized by "Bishop" fails and Veciana flees Cuba. A co-conspirator, Reynol González, is caught hiding on Amador Odio's estate; Odio and his wife are arrested.
Kennedy replies privately, embracing the Noah's Ark image and calling their cooperation for peace urgent.
After the Berlin Wall goes up, General Lucius Clay provokes a 16-hour U.S.–Soviet tank standoff; a back-channel appeal from Kennedy leads Khrushchev to start a mutual pullback.
"Bishop" tells Veciana in Miami to form an anti-Castro group, later named Alpha 66.
Richard Goodwin and Edward Lansdale recommend Operation Mongoose to topple Castro.
Bissell has William Harvey apply the ZR/RIFLE assassination program to Cuba; Harvey renews contact with Roselli.
Kennedy rejects combat troops for Vietnam but sends advisers and support units, beginning a steady buildup.
Kennedy replaces Dulles and Bissell after the Bay of Pigs, naming John McCone, an industrialist and former AEC chairman, as CIA director.

Kennedy's memo starts Mongoose under the Special Group (Augmented) chaired by Robert Kennedy. The CIA's part, Task Force W, is run by Harvey; the Miami JM/WAVE station (chief Ted Shackley, operations chief Morales) has 300+ staff and 54 front companies.
Kennedy authorizes Mongoose "to help Cuba overthrow the communist regime," with Lansdale as chief of operations.
Richard Helms succeeds Bissell as head of CIA covert operations.
Kennedy forces the steel industry to roll back a price increase, making enemies among business and defense interests.
The U.S. begins a series of 24 nuclear tests in the Pacific.
McNamara orders General Paul Harkins to plan the handover of the war to South Vietnam and a reduction of the U.S. command.
Harvey receives poison pills for Roselli to pass to the same Cuban contact as before; the contact later says no chance to use them arose.

The Oswalds land at Hoboken and are met by Spas Raikin of Travelers Aid, also active in an anti-Bolshevik group. The CIA says it took no interest; Edward Jay Epstein reports a CIA psychologist interviewed a defector resembling Oswald in Washington that evening.

Oswald returns with Marina and baby June on a State Department loan. In Fort Worth he is soon befriended by George de Mohrenschildt, at the instigation, the chronology says, of Dallas CIA officer J. Walton Moore.

Peter Paul Gregory, who teaches Russian in Fort Worth, introduces the Oswalds to the Dallas White Russian community. De Mohrenschildt later says Moore told him of Oswald in late 1961 and that the CIA had an interest in him.
Oswald starts at Leslie Welding in Fort Worth assembling doors and windows at $1.25 an hour.
The U.S. signs the Geneva declaration on Laotian neutrality; CIA and Pentagon opponents undermine it. McNamara finds his May order ignored and repeats Kennedy's call for a phase-out plan in Vietnam.
As the missile crisis brews, "Bishop" has Veciana's Alpha 66 raid a British ship and two Cuban freighters; Veciana announces more raids and a $100,000 war chest.
De Mohrenschildt and White Russian friends gather at the Oswalds' apartment; Marguerite Oswald later thinks he had already lined up a Dallas job for her son.
Directed by "Bishop," Veciana orders Alpha 66 commandos to attack Soviet merchant ships in Havana harbor.
Oswald is hired by Jaggars-Chiles-Stovall, a Dallas graphic-arts firm with an Army Map Service contract involving U-2 imagery.
Kennedy learns U-2 photos show Soviet missiles in Cuba and convenes the ExComm. As advisers debate a surprise attack, Robert Kennedy passes a note comparing it to Tojo planning Pearl Harbor.
Kennedy settles on a blockade; the Joint Chiefs press for immediate strikes, and General Curtis LeMay likens the blockade to appeasement at Munich.
In a televised address Kennedy reveals the missiles, announces a quarantine of offensive weapons shipments and demands their withdrawal.

A U-2 is shot down over Cuba and the pilot killed; the Chiefs urge retaliation. Kennedy accepts Khrushchev's offer to remove the missiles for a no-invasion pledge, and Robert Kennedy secretly promises Ambassador Dobrynin that U.S. missiles in Turkey will go too, warning that generals are pushing for war. The Chiefs are outraged.

Khrushchev announces the missiles will be dismantled; Kennedy praises his contribution to peace and agrees to halt Mongoose raids. Kennedy later reflects that we all inhabit one small planet and breathe the same air.

Customs officers seize twelve CIA-trained anti-Castro raiders, mostly American mercenaries, at No Name Key in the Florida Keys, including Gerry Patrick Hemming, co-founder with Frank Sturgis of the International Anti-Communist Brigade.
After a Vietnam trip for Kennedy, Senator Mike Mansfield warns against sliding into France's former position there.
Task Force W becomes the Special Affairs Staff; Desmond FitzGerald replaces William Harvey and continues smaller raids despite Kennedy's orders to halt.

The CIA creates a Domestic Operations Division under Tracy Barnes (Bay of Pigs paramilitary and propaganda chief). Hunt becomes a deputy there; on FitzGerald's orders Phillips takes over Cuban operations.
The de Mohrenschildts bring the Oswalds to a party at Everett Glover's home, where they meet Ruth Paine, who will later take in Marina and her daughter.

At a Washington press conference arranged by "Bishop," Veciana says Alpha 66 raided a Soviet "fortress" and ship in Cuba, causing a dozen casualties, as psychological warfare. The New York Times reports the administration is embarrassed.
The chronology says the raid's secret purpose, according to Alpha 66's CIA adviser Phillips, was to embarrass Kennedy into moving against Castro.
Kennedy cracks down on CIA-backed exile gunboats in Miami: the Justice Department confines raid leaders to the Miami area and the Coast Guard seizes boats and crews.

British forces seize 17 armed exiles on a Bahamas islet as they plan to attack a Soviet tanker, the first result of a new U.S.–British agreement; the party was led by Jerry Buchanan of Sturgis's brigade.
The administration adds Navy and Customs craft to stop raids from Florida.

Pope John XXIII issues Pacem in Terris; Norman Cousins brings Khrushchev an advance copy, and its ideas inform the Kennedy–Khrushchev dialogue. Kennedy privately tells Khrushchev he is acting to stop raids on Soviet ships. The chronology says the CIA tried, through negotiator James Donovan, to give Castro a contaminated diving suit.
Oswald writes V.T. Lee of the Fair Play for Cuba Committee that he leafleted in Dallas and wants more literature; the FBI steps up surveillance of the FPCC.
Alpha 66, with branches in Miami, New York, Chicago and Dallas, announces a Los Angeles chapter.
José Miró Cardona resigns as head of the CIA-funded Cuban Revolutionary Council, saying Washington is liquidating the struggle for Cuba.
Miró Cardona charges that Kennedy has given Castro "absolute immunity" under the missile-crisis deal.
Laid off in Dallas, Oswald goes to New Orleans to find work, staying with his uncle Charles "Dutz" Murret, a small-time bookmaker the chronology ties to the Marcello organization.

At a Hawaii conference McNamara rejects the military's slow withdrawal timetable and orders plans to bring home 1,000 troops by year's end. Kennedy's NSAM 239 directs pursuit of a test ban and general disarmament.

Through Army Colonel Sam Kail (whom "Bishop" had given Veciana as a contact in Havana), de Mohrenschildt takes his Haitian partner Clémard Charles to meet a CIA officer in Washington; Charles is believed to be a conduit for CIA money via Duvalier.

Explosions at a Buddhist protest in Huế kill eight. The government blames the Viet Cong; the chronology cites a later inquiry naming a U.S. officer using CIA plastic explosive. The Buddhist crisis threatens Diem and any Diem–Kennedy withdrawal deal.
Oswald is hired at William Reily's coffee company in New Orleans; Reily backs anti-Castro causes.
Oswald asks the FPCC for a charter to open a New Orleans branch (and a framed picture of Fidel).
Oswald orders 1,000 "Hands Off Cuba" handbills; some are stamped with 544 Camp Street, the building housing anti-Castro ex-FBI agent Guy Banister's office.

Operation Tilt (the Bayo–Pawley mission): exiles, JM/WAVE personnel, financier William Pawley and two Life magazine journalists (including Richard Billings) go to Cuba to bring out Soviet officers said to know of remaining missiles. The officers aren't found; the infiltration team is lost, and Eddie Bayo is rumored executed. Others reported aboard include Rip Robertson, Virgilio González, Eugenio Martínez and John Martino.
Kennedy's American University commencement address rejects a Pax Americana, asks Americans to rethink the Cold War and the Soviet people's war losses, and announces a halt to U.S. atmospheric tests.
Oswald gets the passport within 24 hours, listing the Soviet Union among destinations, a year after returning from defection.
Reily fires Oswald. Garage manager Adrian Alba says Oswald was cheerful and talked of finding his "pot of gold."

Anti-Castro Cubans from Miami join a training camp near Lake Pontchartrain linked to the Sturgis–Hemming brigade. Explosives for it came via Victor Espinosa Hernández from Minuteman co-founder Richard Lauchli. Garrison later received reports that Oswald and Ferrie were seen at the camp.
Averell Harriman concludes the Limited Test Ban Treaty in Moscow, banning tests in the atmosphere, space and underwater.
Kennedy asks the nation to back the treaty, quoting Khrushchev that in nuclear war "the survivors would envy the dead."
The FBI seizes over a ton of dynamite, bomb casings and napalm material at a Lake Pontchartrain house owned by William McLaney, a Havana gambling figure.
HUAC lists Oswald as secretary of the New Orleans FPCC chapter.

Oswald is arrested on Canal Street after a scuffle with exiles including Carlos Bringuier of the CIA-backed DRE. The chronology calls it staged. An FBI agent interviews him in jail, but he is not added to the Security Index.

Oswald and three exiles are charged with disturbing the peace; after a night in jail he meets FBI agent John Quigley. The chronology argues the episode discredited the FPCC and set up his later portrayal as a pro-Castro assassin.

Oswald debates Bringuier on New Orleans radio, then drinks with host Bill Stuckey, who had been briefed by Ed Butler of the right-wing Information Council of the Americas. The HSCA found no corroborated whereabouts from August 22 to September 17 but concluded he was seen with Ferrie, and likely Banister, at a voter-registration drive in Clinton, Louisiana.
Silvia Durán starts as a secretary at the Cuban consulate in Mexico City.
Hilsman, Harriman and Forrestal draft a cable to Ambassador Lodge conditionally backing a coup in Saigon; Kennedy, at Hyannis Port, approves and soon regrets it.
In late August, Veciana, though restricted to Dade County, meets "Bishop" in Dallas and sees him in the Southland Building lobby with a young man he later identifies as Oswald.
William Attwood of the U.S. UN delegation begins talks with Cuba's ambassador, encouraged by Robert Kennedy.
CIA officers meet AM/LASH (Rolando Cubela) in Castro's circle, who wants to try to kill Castro and awaits a U.S. plan.
The Joint Chiefs again present a nuclear first-strike assessment; Kennedy concludes preemption is not possible.

At the UN Kennedy hopes the test ban leads to lasting peace and approves Attwood contacting Cuban UN ambassador Carlos Lechuga. In El Paso, Army counterintelligence agent Richard Case Nagell fires two shots into a bank wall to get arrested, telling the FBI he would rather be arrested than commit murder and treason.
At a party hosted by newscaster Lisa Howard, Attwood meets Lechuga and raises a secret meeting with Castro; Lechuga is very interested.
The Senate ratifies the test ban 80–19. Robert Kennedy tells Attwood to pursue a Castro meeting outside Cuba.
Per the Warren Commission, Oswald leaves New Orleans by bus for Mexico City.
Sylvia Odio is visited in Dallas by two Latin men and Oswald (dates in the record vary).
John Martino tours New Orleans and Dallas giving speeches. (Dated 1963 in the source, though listed among 1961 entries.)
Per the Warren Commission, Oswald reaches Mexico City at 10 a.m., checks into the Hotel Comercio and applies at the Cuban embassy for a transit visa to the USSR.
Odio reports three men sought her help for anti-Castro work, one introduced as "Leon Oswald."
Attwood tells Lechuga he may meet Castro outside Cuba. In Mexico City a man calling himself Oswald seeks immediate visas at the Cuban and Soviet consulates and makes angry scenes when put off.

The CIA says Oswald visited the Cuban embassy several times and phoned the Soviet consulate three times, yet it produced no photo of him at either facility from September 27 to October 1 despite camera surveillance.
The man calling himself Oswald returns to the Soviet embassy, grows agitated, puts a revolver on the table and is shown out.
Oswald and a woman said to be Durán call the Soviet consulate from the Cuban embassy.
Kennedy reopens a private channel to Khrushchev through Salinger and a Soviet agent in Washington, bypassing the State Department.
Phillips, newly chief of Cuban operations, travels to Washington.

Arthur Krock highlights Richard Starnes's report that the CIA twice defied Ambassador Lodge, quoting a senior official who likened the agency to a malignancy and said any coup attempt in the U.S. would come from the CIA.
The CIA reports a source saw "Lee Oswald" contact the Soviet embassy; it later sends the Warren Commission a photo of a man who is not Oswald, calling it a mistake.
Per the Warren Commission, Oswald returns to the U.S.
Helms gives the Commission an affidavit dating the mystery-man photo to this day, after Oswald had left Mexico.
Phillips testified he signed off on the station's cable about Oswald's Soviet embassy visit, but records place him in Miami until October 9.
The Mexico City station reports Oswald's Cuban and Soviet contacts to headquarters, including apparent contact with Vice-Consul Valeriy Kostikov.
At a Dallas employment agency Oswald lists de Mohrenschildt as his closest friend.
CIA headquarters notifies State, the FBI and the Navy of Oswald's October 1 Soviet embassy contact.
The CIA's memo on Oswald's Mexico City activities omits the Kostikov contact.
NSAM 263 says the South Vietnamese should take over essential functions of U.S. forces by the end of 1965.
NSAM 263 makes withdrawal official: 1,000 troops by the end of 1963 and most U.S. personnel by the end of 1965.
Oswald starts at the Texas School Book Depository, a job found through Ruth Paine's contact. Paine later turns over much incriminating evidence to the FBI.
Oswald begins work at the Depository on Ruth Paine's referral.
The FBI's Mexico City legal attaché cables Hoover that, per the CIA, Oswald contacted Kostikov on September 28 and October 1, and is probably the Marine who defected in 1959.

During the missile crisis, after Robert Kennedy orders McCone to halt all operations against Cuba, William Harvey sends two raiding parties in anyway, one led by Eugenio Martínez; Kennedy removes Harvey, who is sent to Rome. (The source dates this October 1963, but the missile crisis was October 1962.)

FBI Dallas sends Hoover a registered airtel (copied to Mexico City, New Orleans and Little Rock) reporting INS word that Oswald contacted the Soviets in Mexico City, and that a postal informant says Robert Oswald moved to Little Rock. The syllabus notes the FBI had doubled an agent reporting on Kostikov, a suspected officer of the KGB department for sabotage and assassination, yet Oswald was never questioned about the contact.
Kennedy meets French journalist Jean Daniel, bound for Cuba, and asks him to sound out Castro on restoring relations and report back.
In the interview Kennedy speaks warmly of the Cuban revolution but asks whether Castro knows he nearly caused nuclear war in 1962.
Desmond FitzGerald meets AM/LASH, says a coup would have U.S. support and later agrees to supply rifles, scopes and explosives, presenting himself as Robert Kennedy's personal representative.
Castro aide René Vallejo tells Lisa Howard that Castro will fly Attwood from Mexico to a private Cuban airstrip for a confidential meeting; Attwood alerts the White House.
A CIA-backed coup kills South Vietnam's President Diem.

Rebel units attack Diem's palace; Diem and his brother Nhu flee to Cholon. In Chicago, the Secret Service reportedly arrests two of a four-man sniper team suspected of planning to shoot Kennedy during his visit the next day; police watch Thomas Arthur Vallee, a troubled ex-Marine working above the motorcade route.
At a White House staff meeting, McGeorge Bundy says he spent the night watching Vietnam cables; Michael Forrestal calls the coup well executed; Diem is still holding out in the palace.

General Duong Van Minh leads the coup against Diem and has loyalist commanders executed. Ambassador Lodge uses CIA officer Lucien Conein as his go-between with the generals; Conein also cables Bundy directly. That morning Diem shrugs off coup rumors to Lodge.
Kennedy attends All Saints' Day mass at Holy Trinity in Georgetown. Christmas cards designed by Mrs. Kennedy go on sale.

Abraham Bolden, the first Black Secret Service agent on the White House detail, later says Chicago received an FBI teletype about four men planning to shoot Kennedy there with rifles; no record survives. Chicago chief Maurice Martineau reportedly tells agents, on Rowley's orders, to file nothing in writing, and shows them photos of suspects; Bolden recalls the names Gonzales and Rodriguez.

George Senator moves in with Jack Ruby. FBI agent James Hosty gets an airtel on John Thomas Masen (internal security, Cuba) and visits Ruth Paine's home, speaking briefly with Marina Oswald and Paine. Oswald is later irritated by the FBI's attention; Hosty's name, plate and phone number end up in Oswald's address book, which the FBI at first withholds from the Warren Commission. Hosty is later censured.

On his lunch break Oswald rents P.O. Box 6225 at the Dallas terminal annex, listing a nonexistent North Beckley address and the FPCC and ACLU, and mails a change of address to the Soviet embassy, an ACLU application and a note to the Communist Party. He cashes a $33 unemployment check in Irving. (Ruby rents Box 5475 there on November 7.)
The chronology notes the box application's home address does not exist and Oswald was living as "O.H. Lee," so the usual address check could not have worked (citing Oswald Talked).

A rude young man who boasts of Marine service buys rifle ammunition at Morgan's Gun Shop in Fort Worth; three witnesses think he looked like Oswald, who was collecting his first paycheck in Dallas. The chronology notes no Oswald "doubles" are reported after November 22.

At Parrot Jungle in Miami an employee overhears a man, later identified as Cuban exile Jorge Soto Martínez, describe a Russian-speaking Marxist friend named Lee, a crack shot now in Texas or Mexico, and talk of shooting Kennedy between the eyes.

Irving grocer Leonard Hutchison later says a man he identifies as Oswald tried to cash a $189 two-party check made out to "Harvey Oswald," and came in with a woman speaking a foreign language; a nearby barber says the same man got haircuts there.
The Warren Commission concludes Oswald likely was never in Hutchison's store (as quoted in Crossfire).
Carlos Marcello's federal deportation-related trial opens in New Orleans to a packed courtroom; David Ferrie is with him.
The Secret Service investigates the alleged Chicago plot.

Diem surrenders on a promise of safe conduct; he and Nhu are killed in an armored carrier. Kennedy is visibly shaken by the news. His Chicago trip is cancelled; Vallee is arrested, and only he is ever publicly identified.

Some researchers say Kennedy was to be killed in Chicago this day: two of four suspects, with Hispanic names (Rodriguez, Gonzales; names a Tampa reporter says recur in a Tampa plot), are detained, and a Chicago Daily News editor recalls a disassembled rifle. The motorcade is cancelled at the last minute; Bolden says Martineau ordered no written reports.
The alleged Chicago patsy, Thomas Arthur Vallee, an ex-Marine who served in Japan and worked as a photo-lithographer above the motorcade route, takes the day off. He dies in 1988.
After the assassination, Bolden says, Martineau had every Chicago agent initial a Washington memo barring discussion of the case with other agencies.
About 8:30 a.m. Chicago time Diem's death is on the news; Pierre Salinger says the trip is still on, with a communications post under Soldier Field.
Kennedy is due in Chicago around 11; at 9:15 Salinger calls reporters in Washington.
Salinger announces the President will not go to the game; the Chicago trip is cancelled.

The planned 11-mile route from O'Hare to Soldier Field (Army–Air Force game with Mayor Daley) required a slow 90-degree turn off the expressway at Jackson Street and passed warehouses that advance agents considered especially dangerous, features the chronology compares to Dallas.

Diem and Nhu are killed after surrendering: shot in an armored carrier, bodies mutilated, hands tied, though the generals call it suicide. When Forrestal brings the cable to a 9:35 a.m. meeting, Kennedy rushes out, visibly shocked (Maxwell Taylor); Schlesinger says he had not seen him so low since the Bay of Pigs.

Kennedy and advisers meet again at 4:30. Bundy praises Salinger's noncommittal statement. Craig Roberts (The Kill Zone) claims three Corsican hitmen cross into Texas at Brownsville, are met by Chicago mobsters and lodged in a CIA safe house arranged by Roscoe White, and study Dealey Plaza. Eisenhower writes Nixon that no American could approve Diem's cold-blooded killing.
Galbraith congratulates Harriman on the coup and asks for a list of those who said there was no alternative to Diem; Harriman files it unanswered.

Whether Kennedy bore responsibility for Diem's murder remains disputed; the Church Committee studied the coup in 1975. The generals gave the U.S. embassy four minutes' warning and cut the advisory group's phones.

Washington's information stayed partial through Diem's death (John Prados). In 1971 Hunt would propose to Charles Colson doctoring White House cables to show Kennedy ordered Diem's murder. Kennedy spends the weekend at Wexford, the family's new home in Atoka, Virginia.

L. Fletcher Prouty later argues that on November 22 a power group seeking escalation in Indochina took over the government, and that Johnson's administration began reversing Kennedy's policies within days.
That night three men held in Chicago on suspicion of plotting against Kennedy are handed to police and released. In the week of November 3, Ruby's out-of-state calls jump to 25 times his usual rate.

The Kennedys attend mass in Middleburg, Virginia. Oswald sends change-of-address cards for Box 6225 to the FPCC, The Militant and The Worker. That day or the next, shopping in Irving with his family, he reportedly asks a store where to get a rifle firing pin fixed and is sent to the Irving Sports Shop.
Hosty calls the Book Depository to confirm Oswald works there and tells New Orleans that Dallas is now the office of origin.

Texas Democratic committeeman Byron Skelton writes Robert Kennedy urging that Dallas be dropped from the trip, citing a prominent Dallasite calling Kennedy a liability to the free world, and flies to Washington to press the point.

Secret Service agents Winston Lawson (advance man) and Forrest Sorrels (Dallas chief) are notified of the trip. They weigh luncheon sites: Market Hall (unavailable), the Women's Building at Fair Park (easy to secure but poor facilities) and the Trade Mart (well equipped but many entrances, balconies and catwalks).

A Western Union night manager says he saw Oswald collect money orders while Oswald was with his family in Irving. At a hearing in El Paso, Richard Case Nagell says he won't reveal his motive, but it wasn't robbery, and tells an officer he wouldn't want to be in Dallas.
Marcello's trial on conspiracy over an allegedly falsified Guatemalan birth certificate begins; he is acquitted on November 22, minutes after the assassination.
David Halberstam's New York Times analysis reports Americans in Saigon hopeful after the coup.

Private Eugene Dinkin, who had written Robert Kennedy from France warning of an assassination plot, goes AWOL before a psychiatric exam and enters Switzerland on forged papers. Between November 4 and 8 a customer named "Oswald" has three scope-mount holes drilled at the Irving Sports Shop, though the Carcano had two and came with a scope mounted. Sightings of "Oswald" around Dallas pick up from November 9.
Attwood briefs McGeorge Bundy on Castro's offer; Kennedy suggests Attwood leave government so he can meet Castro under journalist cover.
Hosty visits Ruth Paine, who tells him Oswald is illogical and calls himself a Trotskyist.
Mrs. Kennedy and the children return to the White House.

Kennedy addresses an industry committee in the Rose Garden. Colonel William Bishop claims Jimmy Hoffa gave Rolando Masferrer $500,000 this day. Gerry Patrick Hemming says Masferrer, under CIA orders, promised weapons, including Carcano rifles, for a raid involving Loran Hall, Larry Howard and Bill Seymour.

At Ruby's Carousel Club, Wilbur Waldon Litchfield sees a sloppily dressed man go into Ruby's office; after the assassination he identifies him as Oswald, but police conclude Litchfield was untruthful.

Lodge sends Kennedy his last private Vietnam cable, calling the coup a Vietnamese affair the U.S. could neither manage nor stop. Exile Felipe Vidal Santiago is in Dallas through November 11 meeting wealthy oilmen; some researchers link him to the Walker shooting.

Dinkin tells reporters at the UN office in Geneva he is being persecuted; the CIA later confirms this to the Warren Commission, but the letter is not in the Report. He returns to his unit around November 11 and is arrested.
Oswald borrows Juan José Arévalo's The Shark and the Sardines, a critique of U.S. policy in Latin America, from the library.
In early 1964 someone anonymously returns the book.

At the Revolution anniversary Khrushchev warns that an attack on Cuba would bring an attack on U.S. allies near the USSR. A Cuban diplomat in The Hague, asked about exile raids, says "just wait" and see what Cuba can do.
A man leaves a rifle for repair at a Dallas gun and furniture shop under the name Oswald.
Ruby makes the first of two calls (today and tomorrow) to top Hoffa associates and rents P.O. Box 5475 at the terminal annex.

Around this time Oswald leaves a note for Hosty at the Dallas FBI office. The receptionist recalls a threat to blow up the FBI and police if they kept bothering his wife; Hosty recalls a milder demand to come to him directly. (The source also mentions a letter from former congressman Charles Kersten warning of Soviet assassins.)

Newsweek's Charles Roberts writes that a rifleman could kill Kennedy at any of hundreds of venues and the Secret Service can only deter. Kennedy's meetings cover wheat sales to the USSR, defense contracts and the 1964 convention.
Oswald writes a note to a "Mr. Hunt" asking for "information."
The U.S. recognizes South Vietnam's new government under General Minh. Cambodia's Prince Sihanouk fears the U.S. could do to him what it did to Diem.

Lawson finds no Protective Research Section listings of dangerous persons for the Dallas area. Governor Connally confirms the Texas schedule: San Antonio, Houston, Fort Worth, Dallas and Austin, November 21–22. Kennedy speaks in Washington and accepts the Protestant Council's award in New York.
Per Ruth Paine, Oswald arrives at her Irving home for the weekend around dinnertime.
Saturday the household drives to get Oswald a learner's permit but finds the office closed for an election; they stay home except for a Sunday driving lesson.
Monday (Veterans Day) they mostly stay home.
A man calling himself Oswald cashes a check at Hutchison's grocery in Irving; the chronology notes the real Oswald never cashed such checks and was not there.

Ruby calls Teamster leader Murray "Dusty" Miller at Miami's Eden Roc, then Barney Baker in Chicago. Life runs "The Bobby Baker Bombshell." Heroin trafficker Christian David later claims Corsican Lucien Sarti flew to Mexico about now, was driven via Brownsville to a Dallas house by Chicago mobsters, and fired once from behind the fence.

FBI surveillance records a Cuban exile saying "we're going to give him the works when he gets to Dallas." Elisabeth Cole later says she overheard a Cuban student at Rutgers describe a plot with a "nest" in a book building and an untraceable patsy, and reported it to the FBI; she was not contacted until 1978.

A man calling himself Lee Oswald test-drives a car at high speed at a Dallas dealership, saying he'll soon have money; salesman Albert Bogard later says it was not the Oswald in the photos. (The chronology adds that Bogard was later found dead of exhaust fumes.)

An Oswald look-alike draws attention at a rifle range by firing at others' targets. Barber Clifton Shasteen says he saw "Oswald" with two women at Hutchison's market; Hutchison says Oswald was a regular customer.
Ruth Paine testifies Oswald spent November 9–11 at her home; she takes him to the license office, which is closed.

Oswald writes the Soviet embassy that he left Mexico because he couldn't renew his visa without using his "real name," a phrase researchers puzzle over (Hosty later feared it would be read as evidence of an international plot). He carries a fake "Alek J. Hidell" Selective Service card. Kennedy spends his last weekend at Wexford with the Bradlees.
At Wexford, Jackie rides while Kennedy relaxes with the children.

Miami police informant William Somersett tapes his friend Joseph Milteer, of the National States Rights Party and other hate groups, saying Kennedy could be shot from an office building with a high-powered rifle, that it is "in the working," and that someone would be picked up afterwards to throw the public off.
Senate investigators plan to call Billie Sol Estes. Ferrie spends the weekend with Marcello at Churchill Farms.
Ecuadorian student Cristóbal Espinosa says a man introducing himself as Lee Oswald near the Baker Hotel wrote his name in Espinosa's notebook and pointed out the best Dallas nightclubs.

The chronology reproduces the CIA's October 10 teletype to the FBI, State and Navy: an American calling himself Lee Oswald contacted the Soviet embassy, described as about 35, athletic, six feet, with a receding hairline, probably the defector "Lee Henry Oswald," a description unlike Oswald.
The FBI updates its Milteer file noting the threat and that the Secret Service was told.
CIA contract agent Robert Morrow later claims Eladio del Valle told him the three Carcano rifles he passed to Ferrie were for "the big one" in Dallas.
The Kennedys attend mass in Middleburg.
A CIA report notes a Cuban exile's meeting with DIA chief General Joseph Carroll, who complained the CIA was interfering with "Plan Judas," exiles' name for a coup planned in Cuba for December 1.
Al Burt's front-page Miami Herald story says a secret war against Castro is undeniable, mostly hidden like an iceberg, and has stepped up in the past three months.
The Bradlees' last weekend with the Kennedys at Wexford. Lawson asks the FBI about active subjects in the Dallas area and is told there are none.

Lawson had trained as an Army counterintelligence agent at Fort Holabird, as did Richard Case Nagell around the same time. On Veterans Day at Arlington, Kennedy tells McNamara the hillside is one of the beautiful places on earth and he might like to be buried there; that night he tells Charlie Bartlett he expects Boston.
Oswald spends the holiday in Irving with Marina and, she recalls, types a letter to the Soviet embassy. Ruth Paine sees a divorce lawyer in Dallas. Ruby's doctor prescribes him a sedative.
Billie Sol Estes says he won't testify before the McClellan committee.
The chronology cites a purported Kennedy memo of this date requesting a classification review of the CIA's UFO files (its authenticity is disputed).
Miami police intelligence give the Secret Service the transcript of Milteer's taped threat; they don't know of the Chicago episode.
Atlanta FBI agent Don Adams later says he was assigned to background Milteer on a presidential plot and passed his report to the office and the Secret Service; it vanished.

The Soviets arrest Yale scholar Frederick Barghoorn as a spy, apparently in retaliation for the FBI's arrest of Igor Ivanov; Kennedy is furious and Helms confirms Barghoorn has no CIA ties. This is also suggested as the day Oswald left his note for Hosty; the La Fontaines (Oswald Talked) speculate it warned of the plot.

After the assassination, Dallas FBI chief Gordon Shanklin has Hosty destroy the note, which Shanklin later denies knowing about; the HSCA called it a serious blow to both men's credibility. William Sullivan later says he believes Hoover ordered it. Oswald rides to work with Wesley Frazier and mails his Soviet embassy letter.

Marcello's trial resumes through November 22. A Cuba contingency status report for the interagency coordinating committee (chaired by Cyrus Vance) again lists possible Castro actions including assassination of American officials.

Lawson evaluates Trade Mart security with Sorrels. In Metz, Private Dinkin is taken into custody and held nearly incommunicado in a psychiatric ward, later at Walter Reed for four months; he says his diagnosis covered up the military plot he tried to expose. The chronology says the White House, CIA and Justice Department had his warning beforehand.

Dinkin's code work involved French OAS traffic. The chronology claims OAS figure Jean Souètre (or Michel Mertz using his name) was in Dallas on November 22, and that Harvey's European assassins had OAS ties.
Cuba announces a three-year military draft for men 17 to 45.

Kennedy holds the first 1964 campaign meeting (Robert Kennedy, Sorensen, O'Donnell, O'Brien, Bailey, Scammon, Stephen Smith), setting "peace and prosperity" as the theme and joking that against Goldwater he wouldn't need to leave the Oval Office. The Black Watch pipers perform on the South Lawn; Mrs. Kennedy later asks them back for the funeral.
A White House dinner honors Greta Garbo. On November 14 Kennedy says the first 1,000 of 16,000 troops will be home from Vietnam by Christmas, and defends Barghoorn.
At his 64th and last press conference (November 14) Kennedy predicts passage of civil rights and tax bills by summer 1964.

Lawson and Sorrels drive the proposed route and meet Chief Curry. Curry testified that Lawson cut his plan of eight motorcycles flanking the car to four, kept back at the rear fenders, and vetoed a car of homicide detectives under Captain Will Fritz right behind the limousine; Fritz later told Curry they might have caught or fired on the shooter.

Accounts of the luncheon-site fight: Connally insisted on the Trade Mart (perhaps to limit Yarborough supporters) over the Women's Building favored by Kennedy, O'Donnell and the Secret Service, and threatened to pull support; a Women's Building route would have passed Dealey Plaza at speed on Main Street. Advance man Jerry Bruno's diary records his anger at Connally.
O'Donnell confirms the Trade Mart; Behn notifies Lawson.
A Klansman tells the FBI of a right-wing plan to kill the President and other officials.

The National Guard armory at Terrell, Texas, is burglarized in an apparent inside job; the guns were on loan from Fort Hood ordnance officer George Nonte, whom Nancy Perrin named as supplier to a Ruby gun-running ring. The La Fontaines suggest Oswald's note to Hosty tipped this burglary.

The chronology alleges a meeting at the Carousel Club of Ruby, Bernard Weissman and Officer J.D. Tippit. Ruby's sister says Tippit frequented the clubs; Ruby denied knowing Weissman, whose committee placed the anti-Kennedy newspaper ad on November 22.
Kennedy goes to New York without a motorcade or the usual escort at his own request, with police posted at the Carlyle.
In his evening call, Marina asks Oswald not to come out this weekend.

An FBI report says a British sailor heard an American sailor in a Southampton bar say Kennedy would be shot soon. FBI agent Don Adams questions Milteer, who denies any plot; Adams wasn't told of the tape and is stunned after the assassination.

A Secret Service report records an FBI tip from a Klansman jailed in Mexico for car theft: a militant National States Rights Party group plans to kill the President, though not soon. The FBI saw it as bargaining and found no danger for the Texas trip.
At a White House meeting on Cuba, Helms urges slowing the Attwood initiative and "war-gaming" it first.

Marita Lorenz later testified she rode from Miami to Dallas in a two-car caravan with Orlando Bosch, Sturgis, Díaz Lanz, Hemming, the Novo brothers and Oswald, with rifles in their motel rooms and a visit from Ruby, returning around November 19–20.
The Dallas Times Herald first reports the Trade Mart as the likely luncheon site.

Bruno notes that O'Donnell and Moyers gave in to Connally, who was threatening to cancel. Curry says Lawson emerged as the primary planner of security. The route turns right on Houston and left on Elm past the Depository; Penn Jones blames advance man Jack Puterbaugh for the Trade Mart and the Dealey Plaza detour. The HSCA later called the security uniquely insecure.
Ruby starts using a safe and talks of setting it in concrete, as if expecting money, and refills his sedative prescription.

A Morales informant reports a Cuban, Miguel Casas Saez, in the U.S. on sabotage. Jim Bishop recounts Johnson angrily answering "never" when a restaurateur asks when his portrait will join the presidents'.
Entertainer Bill DeMar says Oswald was a patron of the Carousel; dancer Karen Carlin vaguely recalls him.
At Marina's request Oswald stays in Dallas; his whereabouts through Monday morning aren't fully established.

Senate investigators hint the Murchison brothers may be called in the Bobby Baker inquiry. A week before the assassination, a bullet reportedly hits a car near the triple underpass. Later finds in Dealey Plaza (a 1974 fragment and a 1967 rooftop bullet) were examined by the FBI and HSCA and found not fired from Oswald's rifle.
In 1975 a worker finds a 1953 .30-06 shell on the County Records Building roof facing the plaza, long weathered; the HSCA did not mention it.

Hemming says Felipe Vidal Santiago was invited to a big meeting in Dallas that week and was warned off; he describes exile circles where talk turned to hitting Kennedy instead of Castro, reporting variously to Harvey's people, Hoover or the DIA.
Dallas papers confirm the motorcade and publish the route.
The published route does not mention the turn in front of the Depository.

At the Sports Drome range, witnesses see "Oswald" fire a 6.5mm Italian rifle with a 4-power scope with great accuracy, pocketing his shells; they say he returns November 20 and 21. Oswald reportedly tries again for a driver's license.
A parking-lot manager at the Southland Hotel says a man giving the name Oswald asked about a job and about the building's height and view; Oswald was reportedly in Irving.
Ferrie spends the weekend with Marcello at Churchill Farms and reportedly deposits over $7,000 in the three weeks before the assassination. Oswald's whereabouts that weekend are unknown.
Kennedy, on a Florida swing, watches a Polaris launch at Cape Canaveral with Johnson and Torbert Macdonald, then a Bears–Packers game and the film Tom Jones in Palm Beach.

On Air Force One, Kennedy tells George Smathers he hates to go to Texas and wishes he could get out of it, and dismisses talk of dropping Johnson from the ticket because Johnson helps him in the South.

The La Fontaines claim Oswald gave the FBI a last informant report this day, citing a November 24 Dallas Morning News story that the FBI interviewed him six days before the assassination without telling the Secret Service or police; the reporter later named Chief Curry's intelligence unit as his source.
Dallas papers say Kennedy should pass downtown around noon.

New Orleans FBI night clerk William Walter later swore he received a teletype from headquarters warning that a militant revolutionary group might try to kill Kennedy in Dallas November 22–23, and called agents with informants; all copies disappeared and the story surfaced only five years later. The La Fontaines tie it to Oswald's FBI interview.
The chronology gives the teletype's header: urgent, to all special agents in charge, from the Director.

Its text, as reproduced: the Bureau has learned a militant revolutionary group may attempt to assassinate the President in Dallas November 22–23; offices should contact race and hate-group informants and report.
The Dallas Chamber of Commerce president promises a warm welcome. The Shriners' circus comes to New Orleans; a man named José Rivera had reportedly said Kennedy would be killed after it came to town.
Ruby is reportedly seen in Las Vegas meeting Lewis McWillie at the Thunderbird.
Dallas leaders ask for no demonstrations; 100 extra police will be on duty.
FBI headquarters has learned of Oswald's November letter to the Soviet embassy.
Kennedy spends his last weekend in Palm Beach working on his speeches, seeing the danger in Dallas as coming from the far right such as General Walker.
Bay of Pigs veteran Albert Fowler, renting next door, plays loud Cuban music all weekend; he later works for Garrison.

Robert Kennedy meets exile leaders Harry Williams and Manuel Artime and asks Williams's help with security in Miami; Williams says he took three or four "hotheads" to Marathon Key until the trip was over.

At the Sports Drome, a man taken for Oswald, with a heavyset companion, rapid-fires at another shooter's target; Garland Slack complains and later says the rifle wasn't the one found in the Depository.
The companion, reportedly Henry Chenyworth, tells a co-worker on November 22 he'd know who did it by morning and might be in jail, then leaves town.
The man is then reportedly at Jack's Bar on Exposition Street, where Ruby comes in; he may then have gone to Abilene.

Marina can't reach Oswald by phone because he is registered as O.H. Lee. In Abilene, Harold Reynolds finds a note signed "Lee Oswald" asking anti-Castro leader Pedro González to call Dallas; González, an associate of Tony Varona known for anti-Kennedy talk, grows nervous, calls from a pay phone, and later leaves for Venezuela.
Gilberto Policarpo López attends a Tampa Fair Play for Cuba meeting; the chronology suggests Oswald may have too.
Toronto journalist Norman Similas attends a bottlers' convention at the Trade Mart through November 21.

With Castro listening, Vallejo agrees with Attwood that Lechuga will set an agenda. In Miami Kennedy tells Cuba that if it stops serving outside powers, "everything is possible." The Soviet embassy in Washington receives a crude letter signed "Lee H. Oswald" that seems to implicate it in a plot; the Soviets treat it as a forgery or provocation and the FBI had already copied it.
Dallas papers repeat the route; the city council passes an anti-harassment ordinance after the recent attack on Adlai Stevenson.
Oswald arrives at the Depository and fills orders.
Bertha Cheek, sister of Oswald's landlady, visits Ruby at his club. Oswald apparently phones the Soviet embassy about visas.

In Tampa, police chief J.P. Mullins later confirms a plot: Secret Service memos describe a mobile rifleman who might shoot from a tall building. The chronology identifies a suspect as Gilberto Policarpo López, a former defector who went to Mexico City trying to reach Cuba, and calls him a possible patsy; it says records released in 1994 show him in a still-classified CIA operation.
On December 4 Helms will cable Mexico City that the station has evidently not told another agency of López's November 27 trip to Cuba to protect an operation.
The Tampa motorcade is Kennedy's longest U.S. exposure, guarded by about 600 officers; the Secret Service worried about a bridge and the Floridian Hotel, where the car would make a hard left turn.

An exile ad condemns Kennedy. The Secret Service has Somersett phone Milteer to confirm he is home in Georgia. A Florida official says Trafficante had a man in a key law-enforcement post helping with motorcade security.
In Miami, Kennedy tells the Inter-American Press Association that Cuba's support for subversion is the only barrier: without it, everything is possible.
Bay of Pigs veteran Angelo Murgado, alarmed at exile talk against Kennedy, had offered Robert Kennedy through Artime to watch the dangerous element; he says Bobby told them to make a plan.

Kennedy addresses the Steelworkers at the International Inn in Tampa, having stood in his car for parts of the motorcade. In the 1990s the Secret Service destroyed records of the pre-Dallas motorcades instead of giving them to the Review Board. A Tucson police employee later says he heard a shortwave report that Oswald crossed into Mexico; the FBI never followed up.
Connally later explains he preferred the Trade Mart as a finer, more accessible venue for 2,000 people, and that he wasn't aware of a big argument over it.

O'Donnell tells Bruno to let Connally have the Trade Mart. Bruno notes the Women's Building route would have passed two blocks farther from the Depository at higher speed. Sorrels's route requires two slow, sharp turns (Main to Houston, Houston to Elm) beneath tall buildings, which he called the most direct way to the Trade Mart; Lawson keeps a police car out of the motorcade.
Hoover will report Oswald phoned the Soviet embassy, perhaps following up his letter.
In Paris, Cubela (AM/LASH) waits for Desmond FitzGerald's officer to bring a poison pen for use against Castro.
McNamara tells the Economic Club of New York a major, lasting defense cut is coming, unwelcome to the arms industry, which is large in Texas.

Kennedy's Miami speech calls Castro's government a small band of conspirators; one paper headlines it as a call to overthrow Castro, but Sorensen says it opened a door. Journalist Hal Hendrix suggests it was aimed at dissidents in Castro's forces.
Castro will discuss the speech with Jean Daniel the next day.

Some researchers say Kennedy's Miami motorcade was cancelled in favor of a helicopter because of Milteer's taped threat, and that this was never passed to Dallas; Gordon Winslow says advance documents predating the tape show a helicopter was always planned.
CIA officer Seymour Bolton reportedly brings the White House a paragraph for the Miami speech meant as a signal to an official in Castro's government planning a coup.
Marina phones Oswald's rooming house asking for him by his real name; he is angry that she didn't use "O.H. Lee," she hangs up, and he doesn't call back.
Back from Las Vegas, Ruby has his lawyer draw up a power of attorney for his sister Eva Grant.

Ironworker William Hannie says a Juárez bartender asked him to give a young man named Oswald a ride to Fort Worth; the man made long-distance calls at every stop and was dropped near a theater on Camp Bowie Boulevard on November 19.

Felipe Vidal Santiago drives from Miami toward Dallas. Cuban consul Eusebio Azcue is recalled from Mexico City (Cuba says it was planned for months). The Review Board reports the Secret Service destroyed Tampa threat records in 1995.
Castro spends six hours with Jean Daniel, explains the missiles as deterrence against invasion, and says he hopes Kennedy wins reelection and becomes a great president by accepting coexistence.

Michel Roux, a French deserter, enters the U.S. bound for Fort Worth. The chronology says OAS figure Jean Souètre used the names Roux and Michel Mertz, and that a CIA document places Souètre in Fort Worth on November 22 and then Dallas.
The real Michel Mertz, a French agent credited with foiling an OAS plot against de Gaulle, was involved in narcotics; the chronology says this was kept from the Warren Commission.
Johnson is in Dallas, reportedly for the Pepsi-Cola bottlers' convention.

Madeleine Duncan Brown, who said she was Johnson's mistress, claims he met Nixon in Dallas. The Dallas Morning News prints the full route: Main to Houston, Houston to Elm, under the triple underpass to Stemmons Freeway.

FBI New Orleans tells headquarters Oswald works at the Depository, 411 Elm. From Lisa Howard's apartment Attwood talks with Vallejo while Castro listens; Castro wants a U.S. envoy to come to Cuba and promises Che won't be involved. Attwood briefs Bundy.
A Lawson memo gives few motorcade specifics but notes agents will wear their red and white lapel pins, information the chronology says could aid impersonators.
An FBI report says Samuel Baker, a soldier from Terrell, paid Ruby in traveler's checks at the Carousel; three were on Ruby when arrested.
Secretary Evelyn Lincoln says Kennedy told her he was thinking of Governor Terry Sanford as his 1964 running mate, not Johnson.
Robert Kennedy and Richard Helms bring the President a submachine gun bearing Cuba's seal, said to be from an arms cache in Venezuela.
Bundy says goodbye before flying with McNamara to Honolulu; John Jr. serves him imaginary pie.
A UPI story in the Dallas Times Herald is headlined "Kennedy virtually invites Cuban coup."

Kennedy tells aides he will decide next steps once he gets the proposed agenda for talks with Castro. Cubela warns his CIA case officer ("Nicolas Sanson," Néstor Sánchez) he'll break off unless Washington assures backup.
Castro spends six hours with Jean Daniel discussing Kennedy and asks him to stay on in Cuba.
Exile Erneido Oliva calls Tony Varona at Fort Holabird to come to Washington to meet Robert Kennedy; Ted Shackley says Oliva used Bobby's private number regularly.
Texas Attorney General Waggoner Carr drops efforts to extradite a New York executive in the Billie Sol Estes case.

The Warren Commission says Oswald made a paper bag from Depository wrapping paper and tape to carry the rifle, presumably after the route was published. Look runs a feature on the film Seven Days in May, about a military coup; Paramount pulls a planned November 22 ad quoting a fictional plotter.
Director John Frankenheimer, who rejected the lone-gunman finding, later said there really had been people in the military who would have liked to take over.

At Red Bird Air Field, Wayne January turns down a couple seeking a Friday charter, fearing a hijacking to Cuba; he later says the man waiting in their car was Oswald. In Eunice, Louisiana, Rose Cheramie tells State Police Lt. Francis Fruge that two men she traveled with plan to kill Kennedy in Dallas.
At a breakfast with congressional leaders Kennedy remarks that things look better away from Washington.
Mrs. Kennedy returns to the White House.
The Fort Worth Press runs a front-page photo of Allen Dulles at the LBJ Ranch.

Officer Frank Ellsworth arrests gun dealer John Masen, who points out "George Perrel" (Fermín de Goicochea Sánchez); the FBI, seeking Perrel since November 1, doesn't interview him until September 1964. Gilberto Policarpo López gets a tourist card in Tampa for travel to Mexico and Cuba; a 1964 source tells the CIA he was involved in the assassination.
Two people think they see an Oswald look-alike firing a similar rifle at a range near Irving while Oswald is at work.

State police files place General Walker in New Orleans for two days of secret meetings, including with Judge Leander Perez and Citizens Council director George Singelmann; he is flying back to Dallas during the assassination. Oswald takes the bus to work.
Dobbs House waitresses say Oswald complained about his eggs at breakfast while Officer Tippit, a regular, was there and glanced at him; they saw no sign the men knew each other.

Ralph Leon Yates says a hitchhiker with a long package of "curtain rods" asked whether the route had changed and whether someone could shoot the President from a building, and was dropped at Elm and Houston; Yates told a co-worker. Two officers see men aiming rifles over the knoll fence who drive off before they arrive; their FBI report of November 26 surfaced only in 1978.
Warren Caster of Southwestern Publishing, with offices in the Depository, buys a .22 and a .30-06 Mauser at lunch.

Caster shows the rifles to Roy Truly, William Shelley and other employees. A Beckley Street tenant recalls Oswald boarding the bus with a newspaper-wrapped package about two feet long on Wednesday or Thursday. At Red Bird Airport, Wayne January turns away two men and a woman who want a plane to Mexico on the 22nd and later says one looked like Oswald.

The FBI dates January's encounter to July. January also tells Matthew Smith of a Cuban-born ex-Castro pilot, once flying for the CIA, preparing a DC-3 sold to a phone buyer to leave Red Bird on November 22. Nixon is in Dallas on Pepsi business (he later says he heard the news in a New York cab). Robert Kennedy celebrates his 38th birthday, tells Ramsey Clark he doesn't want his brother to go to Dallas, and has an anonymous warning letter, now lost.
A Dallas woman tells Salinger not to let the President come because something terrible will happen.
The chronology says Kennedy approves an accelerated withdrawal program for Vietnam.

Times stories have linked Bobby Baker to lobbyist I. Irving Davidson and Clint Murchison; Lincoln says Robert Kennedy was investigating Baker. Davidson, close to Marcello and Murchison, has become Hoffa's go-between with both parties.
At Camp Smith in Honolulu, Rusk, McNamara, Lodge, Taylor, Felt and Harkins open a Vietnam conference; part of it is unrecorded, followed by country-team briefings.

A second restricted session with Bundy, McCone and David Bell also goes unrecorded. Fletcher Prouty argues the conference agenda anticipated NSAM 273 (November 26), reversing NSAM 263's withdrawal plan, and asks who knew beforehand that a non-Kennedy agenda would be needed.
Kent Whatley of Garland offers pilots Leroy Wheat and Billy Kemp $25,000 to fly two passengers to South America on November 22; they decline.

The Paines' mail includes a package for Oswald that the Warren Report doesn't mention; John Armstrong suggests its wrapping could have carried his prints to the sixth floor. Lt. Francis Fruge picks up Rose Cheramie, injured and drugged, who tells hospital doctors Kennedy will be killed in Dallas and that she worked for Ruby.
Cubela's case officer tells him the meeting he wants, seeking Kennedy's express approval for killing Castro, will be November 22.
Boarders recall Oswald absorbed in a TV report on the route, though on the 22nd he would ask a co-worker what the crowd was about. The Supreme Court reception is held at the White House.

Ruby attends an all-night party in Dallas with Joe Frederica, a Genovese relative, and a Carousel dancer. About 11 p.m. Oswald reads magazines at a laundromat near his rooming house until midnight. In Kiev, the Danish foreign minister gives Khrushchev a rocking chair, hoping he'll rock in rhythm with Kennedy.
Shown new Vietnam casualty figures, Kennedy reportedly tells Malcolm Kilduff that will change after Texas: Vietnam is not worth another American life.
The Dallas Times Herald front-pages a map of the route.

Kennedy meets the ambassadors to Upper Volta and Gabon. Dallas police dispatcher Margie Barnes finds an unexpected invitation to the Trade Mart luncheon and is there, away from the radio, when the shots are fired.
Hairdresser Kenneth Battelle arrives to do Mrs. Kennedy's hair and recalls the couple looking relaxed and happy. Kennedy spends an hour in the Oval Office.
Ruby tells the FBI he drove a young friend, Connie Trammel, to Lamar Hunt's office building and visited an attorney there.
Oswald asks Buell Wesley Frazier for a ride to Irving that afternoon to get curtain rods for an apartment.
They drive to Irving with little talk; Frazier tells his sister Linnie Mae Randle it's for curtain rods. Rain is forecast for Friday.
A U-2 piloted by Captain Joe Hyde vanishes from radar after a Cuba mission and crashes in the Gulf; the wreck is found but pilot and seat are gone.
Kennedy gets an updated Texas weather report.
Kennedy says goodbye to John Jr.
Air Force One leaves Andrews. Kennedy tells Congressman Henry González, worried about Dallas, that the Secret Service says everything is taken care of.
Officer W.F. Dyson sees Ruby hand out Carousel cards in the District Attorney's office, telling Assistant DA Ben Ellis he'll know him soon.

Wayne January says the Cuban pilot, uneasy during preflight work on the DC-3, told him "they are going to kill your president," said he was a CIA mercenary pilot, and that Robert Kennedy and other Kennedys would be targets too.

Matthew Smith believes the DC-3 flew assassins out the next day; he says it wasn't logged out, its registration (N17888) was later reassigned, and its buyer, the Houston Air Center, was a CIA front per a former agent.
Nixon addresses the Pepsi meeting at the Trade Mart. Lodge flies toward Washington to tell Kennedy the war is much worse than thought.

Before leaving, Kennedy asks Forrestal for an in-depth study after New Year of every Vietnam option, including getting out. In Texas he dedicates the Aerospace Medical Center in San Antonio and speaks at a Houston dinner for Rep. Albert Thomas, then goes to Fort Worth's Hotel Texas, Suite 850, hung with borrowed art.
A claim (attributed to an author abbreviated B&JE) that Roselli, visiting the Desert Inn, left Banister the FBI's surveillance roster for the past nine days.

Jim Braden (Eugene Hale Brading), with a long criminal record, tells his parole officer and comes to Dallas with Morgan Brown, checking into the Cabana Hotel; he'll be detained near the Dal-Tex Building on the 22nd.
In prior weeks Braden used Room 1701 of New Orleans's Pere Marquette Building, down the hall from where Ferrie worked for Marcello's lawyer.

Braden visits H.L. Hunt's offices about when Ruby is there; Ruby later visits the Cabana, where Ruby's friend Lawrence Meyers is staying. Vidal Santiago probably reaches Dallas. Kennedy jokes he won't be left alone in a cowboy hat at Johnson's ranch. Big crowds greet him in San Antonio and Houston. Ruby is said to be in Houston.
Ruth Paine finds Oswald on her lawn playing with June; he promises Marina a washing machine. Later Paine finds the garage light left on.
Ruby drives Larry Crafard to the Vegas Club, then returns to the Carousel and reportedly talks with Lawrence Meyers.
McNamara and Bundy fly back from Hawaii; Rusk and others wait to leave for Tokyo.

A Chicago Secret Service informant hears Cuban exile Homer Echeverría of the 30th of November Movement say an arms deal will go ahead "as soon as we take care of Kennedy"; it's never fully investigated. The Dallas Secret Service enlists thirty Fort Worth Chamber of Commerce volunteers for the next morning's breakfast.

The Secret Service reportedly declines FBI help with staffing. A month earlier Adlai Stevenson was struck and spat on in Dallas and doubted the President should go; O'Donnell says he can't skip Dallas. A draft NSAM 273, prepared by William Bundy for Johnson's signature, is dated this day (found in 1991).
The Dallas Morning News headline: "Nixon Predicts Kennedy May Drop Johnson."
Five witnesses place Ruby near the President's route and the Rice Hotel in Houston between 2:30 and 7:15 p.m.
The cabinet plane leaves California for Hawaii. Kennedy had told Douglas Dillon he wished they could change places.
Air Force One leaves San Antonio. Connally recalls swapping seats with Nellie in the windy San Antonio motorcade.

Oswald arrives at the Paine house unannounced, his first Thursday visit. Marina rebuffs his kiss; he asks four times that she move with him to a better Dallas apartment and plays with June until dark.
Some suggest he came for the rifle in the garage, but Frazier said in 1987 the package he carried the next morning seemed too small for it (perhaps brought earlier or in pieces).
After the assassination, Commission counsel and a Secret Service agent find two 27½-inch curtain rods in the Paine garage; Ruth Paine says those were the only ones, so Oswald took none.

Barber Clifton Shasteen testified Oswald came in about six times, sometimes with a politically talkative boy of about 14; the chronology notes that would mean a haircut every six days after Oswald's October return.
Air Force One lands in Houston.

A cargo plane brings the presidential limousine, SS-100-X (a 1961 Lincoln Continental convertible built up by Hess & Eisenhardt, then dark blue), and a follow-up car to Love Field. After Dallas it was armored and repainted black; it is now in the Henry Ford Museum.
A Lincoln convertible on loan for Mrs. Kennedy's own use is now in a Las Vegas car collection.
Ruby reportedly dines at the Egyptian Lounge with his backer Ralph Paul. Its owner Joseph Campisi was close to Marcello, sending him sausage each Christmas and calling New Orleans often.
Secret Service agents Kinney and Hickey help Sorrels and Lawson recheck the Trade Mart's speaker's stand, seating, kitchen and exits.
The cabinet plane lands in Honolulu.
Marina says Oswald goes to bed after watching TV. Yet Helen McIntosh says a young man she later recognized as Oswald knocked at an apartment at 223 South Ewing asking for Ruby, who lived next door.
Kennedy is at the Houston Coliseum.
Air Force Two lands at Carswell AFB; Johnson reaches the hotel around midnight.
Johnson's agent Rufus Youngblood testifies that earlier that week they flew to Dallas for the bottlers' convention, then stayed at the ranch until joining the party in San Antonio.
Madeleine Brown claims Johnson arrived at Clint Murchison's Dallas home around 11 p.m.
Connally recalls arriving in Fort Worth in a drizzle around 11 and having a late snack in the hotel coffee shop, relieved; Brown claims he was at Murchison's.
Connally first hears then of the Houston flap over Senator Yarborough refusing to ride with Johnson.

Hotel staff reportedly overhear an argument in Kennedy's suite: Johnson wants Connally in his car and Yarborough with the President, Kennedy refuses, and Johnson storms out; Johnson later denied it. Connally describes the suite decorated with borrowed Picasso, Monet and Van Gogh paintings, for which Kennedy phoned thanks the next morning.

Marina goes to bed. A disputed story (first told by Penn Jones, rejected by Gary Mack): Nixon, Hoover, H.L. Hunt, George Brown, John McCloy and others gather at Clint Murchison's home; Madeleine Brown says Johnson emerged from a closed-door meeting saying the Kennedys would never embarrass him again after tomorrow.
Joachim Joesten reports witnesses heard H.L. Hunt say shooting was the only way left to get "those traitors" out of government; Hunt had called the administration communist in a Houston speech.

The chronology reprints one list of reputed attendees at the Murchison gathering, ranging from oilmen and officials to Marcello, Ruby and reporters, and says Nixon dined with Joan Crawford of Pepsi before going there. None of it is corroborated.
A Times Herald column reports Nixon and Joan Crawford at the Empire Room nightclub that night. Johnson is photographed with Kennedy at the Houston Coliseum; they land at Carswell at 11:07.
Johnson is photographed arriving at the hotel and stays up late in the Will Rogers suite (Manchester).
Researcher Jack White speculates Johnson could have slipped out through the hotel's service routes for a 45-minute drive to North Dallas.

By now Dinkin, Nagell, Gilberto Alvarado, Milteer, Cheramie and Bolden have all spoken of a coming assassination. Several are labeled unstable; Bolden is later imprisoned on a bribery charge he says was a frame-up to silence him.
Mrs. Kennedy sleeps in a separate small bedroom of the suite, a choice she later regretted.

Kennedy is killed in Dallas at 12:30 p.m. Per the Warren Commission, police are alerted at 1:45 to a man entering the Texas Theatre after Officer Tippit's shooting and arrest Oswald; he is charged with Tippit's murder at 7:10 p.m. and later with the President's.
In Paris, a CIA officer for FitzGerald offers AM/LASH a poison pen to kill Castro; he refuses it. As they part they learn of the assassination. FitzGerald later has the pen left out of the report.
The CIA sends Dallas police the Mexico City photos of the man misidentified as Oswald.

At the midnight press conference at police headquarters, Jack Ruby speaks up to correct the name of Oswald's group to the Fair Play for Cuba Committee. (The syllabus says he interrupted Chief Curry; the film shows District Attorney Henry Wade speaking.)

The day as Douglass's chronology tells it (contested claims, in its words as summarized): security stripped, crossfire in Dealey Plaza; Castro, lunching with Jean Daniel, says everything will change; 21 Parkland witnesses describe a rear head wound; Dr. Perry calls the throat wound an entrance; a second man resembling Oswald arrested at the theater, and a double flown out on a CIA plane; at Bethesda, doctors told not to probe the throat, and X-rays it calls fraudulent; and Ruby, armed, at the midnight press conference without shooting Oswald.

Nine Secret Service agents are drinking at Pat Kirkwood's Cellar in Fort Worth, where some waitresses are Carousel dancers. Kirkwood, a pilot, flies to Mexico hours after the assassination. Reporter Bob Schieffer recalls the waitresses in underwear and patrons on cushions.
The Carousel Club sits across from the Adolphus Hotel. In Madrid, the CIA hears from a Cuban journalist claiming a letter said Kennedy would be killed today.
Aristotle Onassis is in Germany christening a ship.
Clay Shaw is in San Francisco.

Shaw was a CIA Domestic Contact Division source, and a document released in 1992 shows he received a covert security approval in 1962 for project QKENCHANT, as did Hunt. Hemming is reportedly in Miami; Hunt is reportedly in Dallas.
Ruby meets a Meyers of Brooklyn for five minutes at the Cabana.
Life names Murchison lawyers Bedford Wynne and Thomas Webb in the "Bobby Baker set"; Wynne is under investigation over federal money routed through a Murchison company.
Marina notices Oswald is still awake.
Kennedy arrives at the Hotel Texas (as the chronology times it).
Seven agents are still at the Cellar.
Mary Lawrence, head waitress at Lucas B&B, says Oswald came in saying he was waiting for Ruby and the two talked for half an hour; she later gets a threatening call.
Agents at the Cellar joke that firemen are guarding the President.
One agent is still there, three hours before all must report at 8:00. Schieffer recalls agents who came along off duty and, he says, weren't drinking.
Oswald, awake most of the night, finally dozes; Marina had avoided him with an hour-long bath.

Officer J.D. Tippit leaves home after breakfast. His wife Marie babysits for extra money; they have three children and like to dance to Bob Wills's "Faded Love." He has been stabbed on duty and once had a suspect's gun misfire.
Marina gets up to feed baby Rachel.

Seventeen officers are briefed to seal the Trade Mart for a 2,500-person luncheon at 12:30. Tippit reports for duty; one source says he had asked his wife for a divorce. Some researchers note his resemblance to Kennedy and theorize his body or X-rays were substituted, a fringe claim.
Air Force Sgt. Robert Vinson hitches a ride from Andrews on an unmarked C-54 bound for Denver (his story continues later). Two agents inspect rented limousines at Fort Worth police headquarters.
Valet George Thomas wakes the President.
On local TV Chief Curry asks citizens to report anyone who has voiced violent opinions about the President.
Marina wakes Oswald, who overslept; he tells her to buy June new shoes.
Kennedy leaves his St. Jude and St. Christopher medals on the showerhead; an agent pockets them to return later.
Kennedy puts on his back brace and an elastic bandage wrapped in a figure eight that holds his torso rigid; the Warren Commission says the brace was six inches wide and waist high.
Oswald leaves his wedding ring (and by some accounts his wallet) on the dresser, a detail some take as a sign of intent, though police later say he had a wallet; inventories list no wedding ring.

Oswald goes to Linnie Mae Randle's house for his ride. Randle and Frazier see him put a package in the back seat, which both insist was too short for the disassembled rifle; their mother tells the FBI he carried nothing.

Marina later said the Secret Service advised her to cut contact with Ruth Paine, whom she believed sympathized with the CIA; the chronology notes Paine's sister worked for the CIA and her father was said to be an informant.

Frazier drives Oswald to work; asked about the package, Oswald says curtain rods. Frazier testified Oswald carried it cupped in his hand and under his arm, which the chronology says couldn't hold the rifle. No one saw it enter the building, the Commission never explained when he made the bag, and his fingerprints aren't on it (as the chronology states).

The curtain-rod question: police photographed rods dusted for prints without noting where they were found; the two rods in the Paine garage remained; Oswald's room already had rods. The Warren Commission concluded the rods were not the purpose of his trip.
Frazier recalls a gray flannel jacket; Randle recalls a tan shirt and gray jacket.
Record store owner Dub Stark claims Oswald was waiting at his Oak Cliff shop and bought a Dick Clark show ticket, then came back for another while Tippit was in the store.

Oswald and Frazier arrive in the rain; Oswald walks ahead. Others who see him enter say he carried no package. (The chronology claims a voice-stress test indicated Frazier lied about it.) A crew is laying a new floor on the sixth floor, moving book cartons toward the front windows; Oswald fills Scott, Foresman orders. Coworker Billy Lovelady resembles him.
Tippit leaves the station in car No. 10. Frazier, Bonnie Ray Williams, Danny Arce, Roy Truly and Jack Dougherty see Oswald at work.
At his dress company, Abraham Zapruder's staff urge him to fetch his 8mm camera.
Kennedy asks Times Herald president James Chambers for half a dozen Macanudo cigars. An officer reportedly sees Ruby outside City Hall where police get their assignments.
Sorrels, Kinney and Hickey drive to Love Field.
A Jiffy Store clerk tells the FBI a man showed a Texas driver's license reading Lee or H. Lee Oswald, born October 1939, to buy beer (Oswald had no license).
In light rain Kennedy crosses to greet a crowd in the hotel parking lot.

Kennedy grumbles that Mrs. Kennedy's assistant isn't keeping up and tells the crowd Jackie is "organizing herself." In Paris, FitzGerald's officer meets Cubela, promises U.S. support for overthrowing Castro, and offers the poison pen; Walt Elder later recalls FitzGerald being unusually distraught that weekend.
Marcello's trial enters its last day. At Love Field the agents take over the motorcade cars from police and have them washed and checked.
The Jiffy clerk says the same man returned for peanut brittle and paced nervously.
Zapruder goes home for his new camera.
Kennedy enters the Fort Worth ballroom through the kitchen for the Chamber of Commerce breakfast and sends for Mrs. Kennedy.
Kennedy talks with Connally about Yarborough's refusal to ride with Johnson. The chronology notes Connally had postponed the visit and saw political risk in being seen with Kennedy.
Per Manchester, Nixon leaves Dallas on American flight 82. (The chronology repeats a 1976 claim that a Pepsi plant in Laos processed heroin.)
Kennedy is at the Chamber of Commerce breakfast.
Ruth Paine takes her daughter to the dentist; Marina watches TV all morning.
Agent Clint Hill tells Mrs. Kennedy the President wants her downstairs.
Mrs. Kennedy arrives in her pink suit and pillbox hat to a warm welcome.
Back in Suite 850 the Kennedys have an hour before leaving at 10:40; she says campaigning is easy when you're President.
From about 10 to noon, Michel Roux attends classes in Fort Worth with many witnesses.
Depository worker Harold Norman testified that around 10, Oswald asked him and James Jarman what everyone was waiting for, laughed and walked off when told.
Police reportedly close traffic into Dealey Plaza and the rail yard. The Commission found Oswald brought no lunch, though he later said he had.
Two agents drive ahead to set up the seal, flags and the President's chair at the Trade Mart.
Three dispatchers report for duty at Dallas police headquarters, two on Channel 1 and one on Channel 2.
The White House switchboard is set up at the Sheraton in downtown Dallas.

The official White House record notes the flight to Love Field, the 10-mile route to the Trade Mart, two bullets at about 12:30 and death at 1 p.m. at Parkland. George H.W. Bush, a Houston oilman and Republican official, phones the FBI that afternoon to report a James Parrott had talked of killing Kennedy. An FBI memo the next day mentions briefing "Mr. George Bush of the Central Intelligence Agency" (identity disputed).
