The chronology's commentary: Texas Democrats are bitterly split, the Morning News headlines political controversy around the visit, Johnson may be a liability in 1964, and Dallas is becoming a conservative Republican stronghold.

Somersett says Milteer phoned him from Dallas saying Kennedy was there and wouldn't be visiting Miami again; some claim Milteer is in a Dealey Plaza photo. Tippit and a fellow officer take a coffee break.
Jean Hill and Mary Moorman arrive and choose a spot on Elm Street where the crowd is thinner.
In the hotel suite Kennedy remarks that last night, in the rain and dark and jostling, would have been a hell of a night to assassinate a president: suppose a man had a pistol in a briefcase.
He sees the Morning News's black-bordered "Welcome Mr. Kennedy" ad accusing him of selling out to communism and tells his wife they're heading into "nut country."

The chronology says the 112th Military Intelligence Group was told to stand down instead of helping in Dallas, over its commander's protest, yet Army reserve intelligence officer Lt. Col. George Whitmeyer rode in the pilot car and an Army officer was with Hosty on Main Street before the parade.

The 112th's Dallas office had a file on "Harvey Lee Oswald" as a pro-communist ex-defector active for Castro in New Orleans, giving the same wrong address (605 Elsbeth) as a police list; it reached Dallas police quickly.

Lt. Col. Robert Jones of the 112th told the HSCA his Dallas agents reported that afternoon an arrest of "A.J. Hidell," whose file cross-referenced Oswald's. The HSCA said this suggested a military file and possible intelligence ties; the Warren Commission never saw it, and in 1978 the Army said it was routinely destroyed in 1973.
Since Oswald used "Hidell" mainly for the rifle and pistol orders and FPCC literature, the chronology asks whether the military knew of the weapons purchases (citing Crossfire).
Johnson introduces his sister to Kennedy in the suite.
Morning News photographer Jack Beers at Love Field sees hostile and friendly placards and is told the bubble top is in the trunk and must be assembled by hand.
The Morning News front page: political controversy swirls around the visit.
The party leaves the hotel for Carswell and the 13-minute flight to Dallas on Air Force One (tail 26000, code name Angel), with 36 passengers.

Julia Ann Mercer, stuck behind a green pickup parked on the curb on Elm past the underpass, sees a man take out what looks like a wrapped rifle and walk up the knoll. Patrolmen saw a stalled pickup with three construction workers whom they helped get moving.

Mercer mentions it at lunch; police later pick her up for questioning by Dallas police and the FBI. Years later she says the statements attributed to her aren't hers, and that on November 23 she picked Ruby's photo as the driver.
Mercer says she recognized Ruby on television shooting Oswald as the man in the truck.
Gerald Posner says the Mercer story was discredited by December 9: the truck belonged to a construction company, its three men took tools to fix it, and three police watched them.
NBC's Robert MacNeil recalls the press plane leaving seven minutes late on an eight-minute flight.
Julius Hardee tells the Morning News he saw three men with long guns atop the triple underpass that morning and reported it to the FBI; no report has surfaced.
Ruby says he picked up a brochure at columnist Tony Zoppi's office. The agents bring the motorcade cars to the arrival area at Love Field.
Six cabinet members leave Honolulu for Japan; the chronology calls it unusual for so many to be away at once.
Ruby says he is talking to a salesman about the owner of another club.
AP photographer James Altgens is told by officers on the triple underpass that it is railroad property and only railroad personnel may stay.
Tippit may go home for lunch about now.
Air Force One leaves Fort Worth. Kennedy reads the intelligence checklist, which includes a bullfighter verse he had recited during the missile crisis.
Another account says the verse was in Johnson's first CIA briefing as president.
Morning News employees Jerry Coley and Charlie Mulkey take a spot near the old county jail on Houston Street.
His son is home sick; Marie makes him a sandwich and they turn on TV for the visit. In Miami Beach, John Martino's wife says he told her "they're going to kill him" when Kennedy gets to Dallas.
Ninth-grader Amos Euins leaves school to see the motorcade.
Zapruder returns to his office with his camera.
Air Force Two lands at Love Field; the Johnsons wait to greet the President.
Eisenhower phones Hoover that CBS's Fred Friendly warned a campaign to undermine the FBI is forming; Hoover offers an interview.
Air Force One lands at Love Field, completing 75,682 miles that year. The Secret Service has had over 400 threats in nine months.
Nellie Connally recalls the roar of the crowd as the Kennedys step out.
Chief Curry greets Kennedy, who remarks this doesn't look like an anti-Kennedy crowd.
Curry is told on Channel 2 the weather should be fair.
Large crowds are reported along the route.

Motorcycle officer Marrion Baker is told five minutes before departure that no one will ride beside the President's car; officer B.J. Martin testified the Secret Service wanted no one riding past the car and told them to stay to the rear.
Jean Hill says Martin told her Johnson's agents ordered an unusual formation with no forward escorts, so crowds would have an unrestricted view.
Bonnie Ray Williams and Billy Lovelady testify Oswald was on the fifth floor calling for an elevator as workers raced down for lunch.
Charles Givens sees Oswald at the fifth-floor elevator gate. Altgens moves to Main and Houston.
Givens testifies he went back up for his cigarettes and saw Oswald with a clipboard walking from the sixth floor's southeast corner toward the elevator.
The chronology argues Givens couldn't have seen this from where he was, and suggests police pressured him; Givens too was missing from the building afterwards.
A Secret Service document records John Lawrence's report of a very large, crew-cut man in a business suit carrying a rifle on Akard Street.
Someone has written "Hemming's" at the bottom; Hemming said he refused offers to kill Kennedy and had nothing to do with it.
Givens reportedly first told police he saw Oswald reading a paper in the first-floor domino room (later denied); William Shelley testifies he saw Oswald on the first floor around 11:50.
He radios he is back in service and heads to his district.
The motorcade leaves Love Field. Advance man Marty Underwood says Mrs. Kennedy, O'Donnell and Connally wanted the bubble top on but Kennedy insisted it stay off so people could see Jackie.
Agent Sam Kinney told researcher Vince Palamara the decision to remove the top was his; agents say it wasn't bulletproof but might have deflected a bullet or hindered a gunman with glare.
WFAA film shows agent Henry Rybka recalled by shift leader Emory Roberts as the motorcade leaves, throwing up his arms in apparent confusion.

In 1991 Underwood told Palamara that the CIA, FBI and Mafia knew Kennedy would be hit, citing Mexico City station chief Win Scott, and that rumors were rife 18 hours before; Kennedy told him he worried too much.

Motorcade order: Deputy Chief Lumpkin's pilot car; the lead car with Curry, Sheriff Decker, Sorrels and Lawson; then the limousine (Greer driving, Kellerman beside him, the Connallys on jump seats, the Kennedys in back), with four motorcycles behind told not to pull alongside unless the President is endangered.

Next, the Secret Service follow-up car (Kinney driving, Roberts on the radio, Clint Hill and John Ready on the front running boards, McIntyre and Landis behind, Bennett and Hickey in back, with O'Donnell and Powers).

Agent Glen Bennett's notes on the flight home say he saw a bullet hit about four inches below the right shoulder, matching the clothing holes; Lifton doubts it, citing photos showing Bennett looking to the right.
Then the Johnsons and Senator Yarborough in a rented Lincoln, with agent Rufus Youngblood and driver Hurchel Jacks.
Then the vice-presidential follow-up car, Mayor and Mrs. Cabell, and the press pool car.
Youngblood says Johnson kept asking if they were on time and how much farther.
Local TV covers little of the motorcade; the camera stays inside the Trade Mart.
Military aides usually sat in the limousine's front seat; General Godfrey McHugh was, unusually, placed farther back. Overpasses are cleared except in Dealey Plaza.
Curry testifies the Secret Service cut the motorcycles he wanted. Time's Hugh Sidey found it just another motorcade. Connally recalls a lone "Kennedy go home" sign that Kennedy saw and joked about.
Motorcycle officer Bobby Hargis recalls Kennedy jumping out on Cedar Springs to shake hands, sending agents into a frenzy.
Bonnie Ray Williams eats his chicken lunch on the sixth floor and sees no one.

Parkland nurse Jane Wester gets a call from Pathology asking whether the President is in surgery yet, saying a Secret Service agent was waiting; the chronology notes no agent is recorded there and suggests Army intelligence.
Eddie Piper says Oswald told him on the first floor he was going up to eat. Steelworker Richard Carr sees a man in a brown sport coat in an upper window.
Roux and Gachman lunch in a Fort Worth café, where they'll hear the news. In Washington, Kennedy friend Edwin Guthman lunches on Capitol Hill.
An anonymous caller tells a Cambridge, England, newspaper to phone the U.S. embassy for big news.
Shelley and Piper see Oswald on the first floor shortly after noon.
In Oxnard, California, phone supervisors overhear a woman whisper that the President is going to be killed; it's reported to the FBI only after the shooting.
Curry radios the motorcade is turning onto Turtle Creek at 12 mph; officers report good crowds.
Bystander Arnold Rowland sees a man holding a rifle back from a window in the sixth floor's west end, assumes he's security, and also notices a dark-complexioned man at the southeast window.
No order is given to watch windows along the route, though Lawson said that was usual.

The triple underpass isn't cleared (Lawson says he tried to wave people off). Driver Aubrey Rike recalls false ambulance calls to the area in prior weeks. The FBI says the rifle takes six minutes to assemble with a dime. Secretary Carolyn Arnold says she saw Oswald alone in the second-floor lunchroom about 12:15; the chronology says the FBI changed her account to a glimpse in a hallway.
Inmate John Powell says he and others in the county jail across the street watched two men in a sixth-floor window fiddling with a rifle scope.
Carolyn Walther sees two men with a gun in an upper window at the building's east end, one in a brown coat. Ruby Henderson sees two men, one darker.
Rail towerman Lee Bowers sees a 1957 Ford circle the lot behind the fence, the driver seemingly holding a microphone; it leaves around 12:20.

Photographer Tom Dillard sees two men in sixth-floor windows. The chronology tallies witnesses: several describe a man in a light shirt, several see two men, one in darker clothing; Oswald wore a brown shirt when Officer Baker confronted him. Soldier Gordon Arnold says a man claiming to be CIA turned him away from the overpass, so he filmed from near the knoll, while 13 railroad workers were allowed up.
Officers White and Foster guard the ends of the overpass.

Roy Truly and O.V. Campbell delay lunch to watch. Deputy Roger Craig, posted at the courthouse with orders to observe only, notes no officers guarding intersections; a fellow deputy mutters that maybe somebody will shoot him.
Tippit radios he'll be out of the car briefly at Bonnie View and Kiest.
The motorcade passes Cedar Springs Road.

A man in fatigues (later named Jerry Belknap) has a seizure near the Depository door; an ambulance is called at 12:19 and traffic cleared toward Parkland, which never records him. Rike, who drove it, wondered later if it was a diversion. Altgens sees the seizure and a dozen people on the railroad bridge where he had been barred.
As the ambulance clears the underpass, the motorcade's red lights appear turning onto Main.
Clint Hill moves four times between the follow-up car and the limousine's rear step as crowds surge.
The Connallys recall Mrs. Kennedy relaxed and smiling; when she puts on sunglasses, the President tells her to take them off.
Connally: she took them off for a while, then unconsciously put them back on.
It happened a third time before she left them off.
Bonnie Ray Williams leaves the sixth floor, which seemed empty to him; the Warren Commission places Oswald there from 11:55 to 12:30.

The chronology argues that in the 10 to 15 minutes left, a lone Oswald would have had to stack some two dozen 50-pound cartons into a nest, assemble the rifle with a dime, and leave just one palm print.
Pauline Sanders, in the second-floor lunchroom until about now, doesn't recall seeing Oswald.
Carolyn Arnold will say she saw him there five minutes later.

Bowers sees a 1961 Chevrolet circle the lot and leave about 12:25, and notices two men behind the fence who stay until after the shots. An older man with "kidney trouble" asks Danny Arce for a restroom in the Depository and later drives off in a black car.
Don Campbell of the Morning News last sees Ruby in the paper's offices about now.
Campbell next sees him at 12:45, leaving a 25-minute gap when some witnesses place Ruby in Dealey Plaza.
Channel 2 reports crowds spilling into the street from Harwood to Ross.
The motorcade pauses at Ervay Street.

Bowers sees a third car, a muddy white Chevrolet Impala with out-of-state plates and one man, probe the lot and pause above the later assassination site. He also sees two men by the fence toward the underpass: one heavyset and middle-aged in a white shirt, one younger in plaid.
Claims (including the Torbitt Document) that H.L. Hunt watched from his office, left Dallas under escort and went to Mexico, or was kept by FBI agents in New York.
Other reports place Hunt in Washington afterwards.
The motorcade passes FBI agent Hosty.
Carolyn Arnold says she glimpsed Oswald on the first floor near the front door.

The pilot car carries Deputy Chief Lumpkin (an Army reserve intelligence officer), Lt. Col. Whitmeyer and advance man Jack Puterbaugh. Its only recorded stop is at Houston and Elm, where Lumpkin briefly talks to the traffic officer; none of the officers there mention it in affidavits.
Channel 2: the rear car reports all is well.

Channel 1 is blocked for at least four minutes by a stuck-open microphone, long attributed to motorcycle officer H.B. McLain; later analysis suggests it may have been elsewhere and that several mikes were keyed. (This recording was the basis of the HSCA acoustics.)
Channel 1 carried routine police business, Channel 2 the visit. County clerks Ronald Fischer and Robert Edwards see a man in an upper Depository window.
They describe him as staring at the knoll area rather than the motorcade, looking uncomfortable, in a light open-necked shirt; one says he had light-colored hair and wasn't Oswald.
Connally recalls dense crowds on Main Street, at least a quarter million along the route, and a good reception everywhere.
The motorcade turns from Main onto Houston, five minutes behind schedule.

Dealey Plaza, named for Morning News founder George Dealey, is a 3-acre park at the city's birthplace, bounded by Houston Street (with the courthouses, jail, Records Building and Dal-Tex Building), with Elm, Main and Commerce converging at the triple underpass and a wooden fence atop the north slope.
The chronology includes occult and Masonic numerology about the plaza (33rd parallel, threes, the Trinity River), offered by a fringe of researchers.
More of the same: James Shelby Downard's ritual reading of the killing and Kennedy heraldry.
And wordplay on "Dealey" and Johnson's middle name.
The motorcade heads straight toward the red-brick Depository before turning left onto Elm.
The chronology notes that a sixth-floor gunman would have had his best shot as the car approached head-on down Houston; it estimates 20,000 open windows and 250,000 spectators along the route.
No precautions are taken for windows, and no report mentions the man holding an open umbrella in the sun.

Only 33 of the building's 69 workers are company employees. The old warehouse is being remodeled; the new passenger elevator stops at the fourth floor and the northwest stairway is closed for repairs, effectively limiting the upper floors to warehouse workers.

Four warehousemen are on the fifth floor at the time of the shots; six had spent the morning laying plywood on the sixth. Warehousemen were paid in cash, and the chronology claims some of the day's time records in the Commission exhibits look fabricated.
Lawson told the HSCA he had nothing to do with choosing the Houston–Elm turn before November 14 and couldn't explain who removed the police homicide car Curry expected.

Sorrels says he glanced at the building from the closed lead car and saw nothing unusual. Some claim Milteer is visible on Houston Street, and that a man in Altgens's photo resembles CIA officer Lucien Conein. Ruby is said to be in the Morning News office nearby, though some witnesses place him in the plaza.

About twenty sheriff's deputies at Main and Houston watch the car pass; of those who gave statements, sixteen later thought the shots came from the knoll area, three had no opinion, and one said the Depository.
Senator Yarborough later describes Johnson listening to a small walkie-talkie held low over the seat.
Manchester portrays Johnson slumped at a low ebb in his career sixty seconds before he becomes President.
Photos show the rear door of Johnson's follow-up car already held open, though some say it was open throughout.
Local reporters had joked all morning about when the shooting would start.

Geneva Hine, alone in the second-floor offices, says the power and phones went dead; the Commission never asked about it. Just after the shots she hears a woman on the phone behind a locked office door.
Bonnie Ray Williams, James Jarman, Harold Norman and Jack Dougherty are on the fifth floor.
Nellie Connally turns and says, "Mr. President, you can't say Dallas doesn't love you."
Kellerman glances at the building without being alerted.

The motorcade turns onto Elm; Zapruder films from the President's right. The Commission computes an average speed of 11.2 mph over the 8.3 seconds before the head shot, assuming 18.3 frames per second. Greer nearly clips a curb on the tight turn, slows, and faces an underpass full of people. David Mantik argues the film lacks the overexposure expected if the camera had been stopped, suggesting frames were removed.
A north wind gust nearly unseats Officer Marrion Baker as he turns onto Houston behind the last press car. Zapruder keeps filming.

Harrison Livingstone describes copies of the Zapruder film going to the FBI, Wade, police, the lab owners, the Secret Service and supposedly H.L. Hunt, and notes a missing processing number (0184) that critics suggest was a Hunt copy.

Homer McMahon of the National Photographic Interpretation Center told the Review Board a Secret Service agent brought the film the weekend after the assassination; from repeated viewing he thought Kennedy was hit six to eight times from three directions, but was told there were three shots from the Depository and to keep the work secret.

French journalist William Reymond says he saw a different version of the film in France. The chronology asks whether a copy was switched for the original, a question it concedes the records cannot settle.
An FBI memo says Kodak in Dallas developed the original and three copies for Zapruder, and the lab asked to copy it.

White House photographer Thomas Atkins films from six cars back with a 16mm camera; his film "The Last Two Days" is called damaging to the lone-gunman finding but was never studied by either federal panel.
In the lead car near the underpass, Sorrels tells Curry five more minutes; Lawson gives the Trade Mart a five-minute warning.
Rose Cheramie, in a Louisiana hospital, says when the motorcade appears on TV that this is when it will happen; she had told an intern a "Jack Rubinstein" was involved.

Justice Department investigator Walter Sheridan is in a Nashville courthouse where Hoffa awaits trial. In the Depository doorway are Frazier, Arce and Lovelady; Roy Truly and O.V. Campbell stand near the oak.
Agent Emory Roberts's shift report records the President arriving at the Trade Mart at 12:35. One writer notes eight agents were assigned to the Trade Mart and none to Dealey Plaza.

The detail's chief, Jerry Behn, stayed in Washington; critics say his stand-in Kellerman was overwhelmed at Parkland, where agents took orders from Emory Roberts, and argue the detail had lost its reflexes.
The chronology contrasts de Gaulle's escorts of up to 47 motorcycles with Kennedy's four at the rear.
The Protective Research Section has 50,000 threat files; it investigated 34 Texans in two years and spent ten minutes on Dallas on November 8.
Army intelligence officer James Powell is in the Dal-Tex Building, which Jim Braden will soon be found leaving.
Deputy Harry Weatherford, a marksman, is on the county jail roof with a rifle.

Altgens, across Elm from the Depository, takes his famous photo about two seconds before the head shot. A man in the doorway resembling Oswald would place Oswald downstairs; the Commission identified him as Billy Lovelady, though the shirt is debated.

Altgens says officers ran up the knoll with guns drawn and that tissue flew from the head toward his side, which critics cite for a frontal shot. The chronology lists security lapses: open car, slow turns, unwatched windows, missing units, unwelded sewer covers.
The chronology says the "barricade" the Commission cited west of the underpass was only a low curb. 178 officers line the route; reserves were told to act only on threats of harm.
Lawson waves at onlookers on the underpass to clear; the officer there doesn't notice. He later asks how 20,000 windows could have been checked.
Rowland notices an officer in front of the Depository. Curry radios the lead car has reached the underpass.
Eight seconds later the dispatcher's time stamp reads 12:30:18. Victoria Adams, on the fourth floor, sees the Kennedys turn toward the building when someone calls out.
Mary Moorman says Jean Hill shouted for the President to look their way as Moorman stepped into the street to take her picture.

In the Zapruder film Moorman appears on the grass, while photo alignment tests suggest she must have been in the street, which alteration theorists cite. Dan Rather, after seeing the film on November 25, describes Kennedy's hand going to his face just before he lurches. Embalmer Thomas Robison described a large hole in the back of the head and small wounds on the right temple and face; some attribute these to pavement debris from a missed shot.
The limousine passes the Stemmons Freeway sign. Groundskeeper Emmett Hudson said the sign was moved soon afterwards and gone by early 1965.
Sylvia Meagher notes no one knows whether it was moved before or after the reenactments, and the Commission never asked.
John Costella argues the sign in the extant film lacks the lens distortion of its surroundings and was inserted; lampposts along the curb were also later moved and shortened.
Hugh Betzner's photo may show another movie camera near Zapruder.
Freshly painted yellow curb stripes appear in the film; some researchers think they were marks for the shooters.
Beverly Oliver, filming near the south curb, later finds yellow paint on her shoes.
A man by the sign opens an umbrella and pumps it as the car passes, then sits beside a dark-complexioned man who appears in photos to hold something like a radio; they leave in different directions.

Penn Jones is tipped that the "Umbrella Man" is insurance salesman Louie Steven Witt, who refuses to talk but says he'll appear before the House committee (he testified in 1978 that it was a protest gesture).

Shots: around Zapruder frame 200 Kennedy's wave freezes and his head turns toward his wife, a reaction the HSCA noted before he goes behind the sign. Hemming claims multiple teams with silencers bought through Mitchell WerBell.
Sheriff Decker and motorcycle officer Stavis Ellis both think they see a bullet hit the pavement; neither is asked by the Warren Commission.
Officer James Chaney tells reporters the first shot missed. James Tague stands near the underpass, about 450 feet from the Depository.
Bowers notices a commotion of some kind behind the fence where the two men stood, which he can't describe.
Mrs. Donald Baker sees a shot strike the pavement near the sign, sparking like a firecracker.
Connally recognizes a rifle shot from over his right shoulder and turns right.
Nellie Connally turns and sees the President clutch his neck and slump without a word; her husband cries out "No, no, no."

James Tague, by the underpass on the Main Street curb, is nicked on the cheek by concrete from a bullet strike more than a block from the car. The Commission didn't question him at first, and he isn't publicly known for seven months.

The chronology says a line from the curb mark back through the President's position points to the Dal-Tex second floor, while the sixth-floor window lies well to the side. Tague later said Hoover didn't want him to exist because he proved there were more shots.
Officer Baker, recovering from the wind gust, hears the shots.
Mrs. Cabell tells the mayor, "Earle, it is a shot."

Kellerman testifies he heard the President say "My God, I'm hit"; no one else in the car recalls it. Kennedy clutches at his throat. The Warren Report said it wasn't necessary to determine which shot hit Connally.
Dr. David Mantik argues witnesses saw Kennedy slump forward twice, and that Jackie lifting him upright, sped up by removed frames, became the "head snap."

Mantik also entertains a frontal shot through the windshield, citing embalmer Tom Robinson's three tiny holes in the right cheek and a Ford employee's claim that the windshield had a through-and-through hole; he suggests a shooter in a storm drain on the overpass.

Clint Hill, the only agent looking at the President in Altgens's photo, jumps from the follow-up car and runs to the limousine. Moorman thought the first sounds were firecrackers and stepped back onto the grass as people fell around her.
Johnson says Youngblood shouted "Get down!" and pushed him to the floor.
Johnson's account has Youngblood sitting on him; Yarborough said both just ducked and Youngblood stayed in front. Johnson's car is the only one without a Secret Service driver.

Officer Baker sees pigeons fly from the Depository roof, runs inside with manager Roy Truly, finds the elevators stuck on the fifth floor and takes the stairs. Through a second-floor door window he sees a man and confronts him at gunpoint; Truly vouches for him as an employee. Baker's next-day statement said the man was drinking a Coke, words later struck; critics argue Oswald couldn't have shot, hidden the rifle, descended and bought a Coke in time. Oswald told police he was in the lunchroom drinking a Coke.
Jack Dougherty on the fifth floor hears what sounds like a backfire and takes the elevator down.

Directly under the sixth-floor window, Harold Norman hears the shots and the bolt and shells (he later disavowed parts of his testimony). Others give their sense of direction: William Newman, Zapruder and Roy Truly toward the knoll or railroad; O.V. Campbell behind and above; Agent Bennett sees a shot hit four inches below the right shoulder.
Yarborough cries that they've shot the President; Lady Bird says it can't be.
Dave Powers and Kenneth O'Donnell later say (Powers in his account, O'Donnell reportedly in private) that the shots came from the knoll and it felt like riding into an ambush.
Kellerman testifies he heard Mrs. Kennedy ask, "What are they doing to you?"

Some think the first shot struck the street behind the car and debris grazed Kennedy. The chronology notes Kellerman never moved back to shield him as the manual required, and asks whether he saw danger ahead.
Chuck Marler (The Fourth Decade) finds it incredible that driver Greer, after two shots and cries from the back seat, turned to look, slowed, and didn't accelerate until after the head shot.

Kellerman tells Greer "We are hit" (he later said four wounds on Kennedy and three on Connally meant more than three shots). The car slows, brake lights on, as Greer turns to look; some researchers think the film frames of his head turn were altered.
Zapruder's film shows the Umbrella Man pumping his umbrella after the first shot.
Agent John Ready starts toward the limousine and is recalled by Emory Roberts, who orders the others to stay put. Mrs. Kennedy recalls someone yelling behind her.
Mrs. Cabell and Senator Yarborough smell gunpowder; Yarborough later says he couldn't see how he'd smell powder from a rifle high in the building.
Moorman, having taken her Polaroid, drops to the grass and pulls Jean Hill down.

Five seconds after Kennedy clutches his throat, the car is still slowed with Greer looking back (Greer's son later said his father disliked Kennedy). On the press buses someone jokes it's a 21-gun salute.
Mrs. Cabell, passing the Depository, looks up at the first shot and sees something projecting from a top window.
Connally testified to the HSCA that he heard two shots, not the one that hit him, both from behind over his right shoulder.
John S. Craig notes many witnesses described the last two shots as nearly simultaneous and sounding different from the first.
Connally's first thought was two or three shooters or an automatic rifle. Three agents, including driver Greer, describe a double report at the end.
Kellerman described the first shot as a firecracker and the last as a "flurry," a double bang like a plane breaking the sound barrier.
Agent Hickey heard two reports with practically no time between; Clint Hill said the second sounded like a revolver fired into something hard, almost a double sound.
On the overpass S.M. Holland heard four shots, the last two like a pistol beside a shotgun, some from behind the fence. Deputy Roger Craig heard a long pause after the first shot and two quick ones.
Joe Molina: a longer interval between the first and second shots than the second and third.
Seymour Weitzman: the last two seemed simultaneous. Lady Bird Johnson: one sharp shot from the right above, then two in rapid succession.
Sorrels: twice as long between the first and second as between the second and third.
Yarborough estimates three seconds, then about one and a half; Mayor Cabell also recalls the last two in rapid succession.
Agents Kinney, McIntyre and Hickey describe a pause after the first shot and two more close together; McIntyre puts all three within five seconds and saw the head struck by the last.
Agent Warren Taylor (Johnson's follow-up car) hears two more bangs as he steps out.
Young Linda Willis: one shot, a little time, then two fast together; Kennedy grabbed his throat and slumped after the first.
Youngblood, Robert Jackson, Arnold Rowland and Luke Mooney all describe a longer gap before the second shot and a shorter one before the third.
Mary Ann Mitchell: the second and third closer together.
Lee Bowers: one, a slight pause, then two very close, with reverberation.
Jean Hill: three shots, a pause, then more that sounded quicker, more automatic.

Hill hears more shots as he runs. Connally insists he wasn't hit by the first bullet, felt the second, and was in Nellie's lap at the third. Greer says he accelerated when Kellerman yelled to get out fast; Kellerman hears the flurry within five seconds of the first noise.

UPI's Merriman Smith tells ABC's Bob Clark those were gunshots. Teenager Amos Euins reportedly says he saw a colored man firing from the Depository; he later testified he couldn't tell the man's race.
James Worrell sees six inches of rifle barrel in the Depository window and hears four shots.
Billy Lovelady, on the front steps, thinks the shots came from near the concrete structure on the knoll, not the building. Maggie Brown also places them on the knoll.
Aurelia Lorenzo places them to her right rear, the knoll.

The Chisms, near the sign, look behind them toward the knoll. The Newmans, between knoll and car, say the shots came from behind them. Hugh Betzner, running with his camera, reportedly tells a deputy some shots came from the fence; Deputy Eugene Boone develops his film and returns it.
Mantik's two-slump theory again. The fatal head shot.

The right side of the President's head explodes. In the Zapruder film his head moves forward an inch or two between frames 312 and 313, then snaps violently back and to the left, a motion debated ever since; some suggest two near-simultaneous hits from behind and right front.
Others suggest the motion is an artifact of deleted frames.

Mantik argues from X-rays and witnesses that Kennedy was hit in the head first from behind while slumped, then from the front while erect, and that the visible spray belongs to the second, missing shot.
On the last two shots: AP's Jack Bell, "in quick succession."
Agent George Hickey: practically no time between.
Kellerman: a flurry, like a sonic boom; Clint Hill: a double sound.
Reporter Mary Woodward: the last two were immediate, one like an echo of the other, and she saw the head explode.
Agent Bennett: a second shot followed immediately and hit the back of the head.
Warren Taylor, Seymour Weitzman and Linda Willis describe the last two as together; Lee Bowers rapped his knuckles to show how close they were.
James Jarman: the third right behind the second; Carolyn Walther: almost at the same time.
Ruby Henderson and Lady Bird Johnson: rapid succession. Altgens recalls skull and flesh flying.
Alan Smith: when the car was ten feet away a bullet hit the President in the forehead, and the car went five feet and stopped.
Charles Brehm, behind and left of the car, sees skull blown back and left and tells reporters the shots came from in front or beside the President.
James Simmons on the overpass hears shots from the left front, toward the fence.
Richard Dodd, also on the overpass, thinks they came from the knoll.
Railroad workers Nolan Potter and Dodd see smoke near the fence.

Nellie Connally thinks her husband dead, sees him move, and tells him to be still. With his head in her lap he hears a shot hit the President and both see brain tissue spatter the car; they say Kellerman's orders and acceleration came after this shot.
Connally describes the loud impact and tissue all over them. Before the HSCA, Mrs. Connally says she heard three shots.
No fewer, and that was all she heard.
Connally says he heard two shots, not the one that hit him, and none from his right front.
He rejects any shot from the knoll.
Nellie Connally later recalls her husband crying out in his sleep for weeks that someone was after him with a gun, and that she never stopped looking over her shoulder.
Mrs. Cabell: the smell of gunpowder, and the motorcade stopped dead still.
Officers Hargis and Martin, riding left rear, are splattered with blood and tissue; Hargis is struck so hard he thinks he's been shot.

Officers on the right rear are not hit. A bone fragment found the next day by Billy Harper, later identified as occipital by a Methodist Hospital pathologist, lay behind and left of the car's position.
Hargis later suffers his own near-fatal motorcycle crash and retires in 1999.

Soldier Gordon Arnold says a man with a Secret Service badge turned him away from the overpass (no agents were posted on foot), so he filmed in front of the fence, felt a shot pass his ear and dropped; an officer took his film. Yarborough recalled seeing a uniformed figure hit the dirt there. Mrs. Kennedy recalls the red roses in Dallas and later describes seeing part of his skull detach and trying to hold his head together; some of her words were left out of the Warren record, which came to light only in 2001.
Rather's November 25 description of the film: Kennedy moves forward violently, Mrs. Kennedy stands, then crawls out onto the trunk.

Ruby reportedly invited a friend, secretly an IRS informant, to "watch the fireworks" and stood with him by the Post Office Annex. Phil Willis photographs a man resembling Ruby near the Depository minutes later. Jim Bishop writes that the President never felt the final shot.
Greer testifies the last two shots seemed simultaneous.
Agent Paul Landis believes the head shot came from the knoll but an earlier one from above and behind.
At least seven witnesses see a puff of smoke on the knoll.
Howard Brennan, the key witness to a rifle in the sixth-floor window, testifies he heard but didn't see the last shot fired; Walt Brown argues the last shot didn't come from that window.

Sorrels yells to Curry to get out of there. Tague takes cover, not yet aware his cheek is bleeding; Deputy Buddy Walthers and Officer Clyde Haygood believe a bullet marked the curb near him, and Tague thinks it was the second shot. Yarborough is amazed at the agents' slow reactions.
At 12:30:18 Curry orders men to the overpass and railroad yard, tells Parkland to stand by, and says it appears the President has been hit.

Sheriff Decker's "hold everything secure" is heard on Channel 1 at 12:31:22. Aligning the two channels on Sgt. S.Q. Bellah's transmission, heard on both, places the recorded impulses at the moment of the shooting; the chronology suggests a needle jump explains the apparent minute's offset.
Marine sniper instructor Carlos Hathcock reportedly said his team at Quantico reconstructed the shots and couldn't duplicate what Oswald was said to have done.
Former Mossad officer Victor Ostrovsky claims a Mossad simulation found experts with better equipment couldn't do it.
Some fellow Marines described Oswald as poorly coordinated, which they thought hurt his shooting and driving.
Mantik notes agents and officers describe Kennedy as erect at the head shot, unlike the Zapruder film's slumped posture, a discrepancy rarely discussed.

In the follow-up car Agent George Hickey picks up the AR-15, releases the safety and stands looking for the shooter until the car's lurch throws him back. (The book Mortal Error argues he accidentally fired the fatal shot.)
Lumpkin asks what to do with his men; Curry says go to Parkland. Officer R.L. Gross notes a stuck microphone on Channel 1. Emory Roberts radios for an escort to the nearest hospital, fast but safe.
The deputies at Main and Houston run toward the knoll. In the mayor's car, Congressman Ray Roberts says they're getting out to Love Field if all is well ahead.
NBC's Robert MacNeil yells to stop the press bus, jumps off and runs up the grassy slope after people he thinks are chasing the shooter.
From the new courthouse, Richard Carr sees two men run from behind the Depository into a waiting station wagon that speeds north on Houston.

Carr describes a heavyset man in a hat, tan sport coat and horn-rimmed glasses whom he'd seen in the Depository, getting into a Rambler station wagon at Commerce and Record; James Worrell saw a man in a coat leave the building's rear. Deputy Roger Craig later sees a Rambler stop on Elm and a man in a light shirt, whom he identifies as Oswald, run down from the building and get in; motorists Marvin Robinson and Roy Cooper also describe it. A Jim Murray photo shows Craig looking toward a man heading for a station wagon, with the Hertz clock reading 12:40.
Depository employee Avery Davis thinks the shots came from the overpass ahead of the car.
Craig runs across Houston and down to Elm amid people lying on the ground, then follows a policeman up the knoll to confusion and hysteria behind the fence.
Danny Arce thinks the shots came from the railroad tracks west of the building. Jean Hill sees a man running from the fence area.

Clint Hill, holding on as the car accelerates, sees the right rear of the President's head missing and part of the skull on the seat; he shields both Kennedys to Parkland and shakes his head at the follow-up car.
Emory Roberts tells his agents they must now take care of Johnson.
Hill reaches the car 2.6 seconds after the last shot; the shooting lasts about seven seconds. Youngblood covers Johnson within three seconds (as the chronology says).
Hill testifies that by the time he climbed on, the head shot had struck and Mrs. Kennedy had climbed onto the trunk reaching for something.
Vehicles screech and swerve in the shadow of the underpass.
Press secretary Malcolm Kilduff recalls passing Johnson's slowed car to catch up.

Youngblood testifies he switched radio channels, heard the follow-up car told to keep its man covered, followed the presidential follow-up car, and told Johnson to stay close as they went into the hospital.

Victoria Adams and Sandra Styles run down the back stairs from the fourth floor right after the last shot and don't see or hear Oswald, who by the Commission's account was coming down the same stairs (tests timed his descent to the second floor at 1 minute 14 seconds).
The Commission says Adams saw Lovelady and Shelley by the elevator; Adams and Styles deny saying so, and the chronology notes those men re-entered only minutes later, which would support her timing.

Adams thought the shots came from below and to the right, not above. Outside she and Avery Davis see a man questioning people like a policeman who she later thought resembled Ruby, though Ruby was placed at the Morning News.
Worrell sees a man in a brown coat exit the Depository's back door and walk fast south on Houston; Carr sees the same man.

Beverly Oliver says she filmed the shooting from the south side of Elm, saw smoke at the fence, and had her film taken the next day by men she later named as FBI (Regis Kennedy); some researchers dispute her claim to be the "Babushka Lady."

Deaf witness Ed Hoffman says he saw two men behind the fence, one tossing a rifle to the other, who broke it down into a toolbox; he says an FBI agent told him to keep quiet, and his account surfaced only decades later. He says the car paused at the freeway and he saw the back of the President's head gone.

J.C. Price on the Terminal Annex roof sees a young man in a white shirt and khakis run fast from behind the fence toward the rail cars with something in his hand. Off-duty detective Tom Tilson sees a man in dark clothes slide down the embankment west of the underpass and drive off.
Roberts waves Johnson's car closer, shouting "they got him," and assigns agents to Johnson when they stop.
A deputy hears a woman say the shots came from the fence. Adams and Styles go out the back door about a minute after the shots, are ordered back by a policeman, and walk around to the front.

In Washington, a closed Senate Rules Committee session hears Don Reynolds testify about the Bobby Baker affair in ways that implicate Johnson, and Billie Sol Estes rumors of payoffs to Johnson are surfacing.

Within about 90 seconds of the last shot, Baker and Truly encounter Oswald in the second-floor lunchroom, calm and not winded. The Commission says he bought his Coke after the encounter; Baker's signed 1964 statement originally said he was drinking a Coke, and the words were struck out.
Captain Fritz notes Oswald said he was on the second floor drinking a Coca-Cola when the officer came in.
Mrs. Robert Reid sees Oswald on the second floor with a Coke as she returns to her desk; he then goes down and out the front entrance before the building is sealed.
As Baker and Truly head up, power and phones return and the west elevator moves down from the fifth floor.
Postal inspector Harry Holmes, watching through binoculars, sees a man on the knoll apparently taking a gun from a woman; he later says the man was protecting her.
Howard Brennan jumps from his wall and crouches for cover.

Carr sees the brown-coat man, now with hat and glasses, walking fast south on Houston and turning onto Commerce. Some researchers speculate he was Johnson associate Mac Wallace, citing a disputed fingerprint match on a box.

He gets into a gray Nash Rambler station wagon driven by a young Black man, last seen going north on Record. Carr wasn't called by the Commission; he says the FBI pressured him and that he suffered threats and attacks, yet testified at the Shaw trial. The chronology links this to Craig's Rambler sighting about 15 minutes later.
Channel 2 asks someone to tell a motorcycle officer on Stemmons his Channel 1 mike is stuck open; Parkland has been notified.

The Umbrella Man calmly lowers his umbrella, confers with a man who seems to carry a radio, and both walk off. Witt later showed the HSCA an umbrella with a different number of ribs, and critics say photos contradict his account. Zapruder, screaming "They killed him!", is so shaken he never again watches a film about Kennedy; some later claim he didn't shoot the extant film.
Doug Mizzer points to a discrepancy between the Zapruder and Nix films.
In the Nix film Hill seems to get both feet on the car and push Mrs. Kennedy back; in Zapruder he barely touches her hand as she climbs back.

Lifton notes several differing versions of the film and the missing Kodak processing number 0184, suggesting an extra copy. Witness Jim Hicks, photographed with what looks like a radio in his pocket, later told Garrison he was a radio coordinator for the team; the chronology says he was then confined and later killed, claims it does not document.
Jerry Coley and Charlie Mulkey cross Houston toward the knoll.
They find a pool of red liquid on the steps down to Elm that Mulkey says is blood; Morning News photographer Jim Hood photographs it.

Officer Joe Marshall Smith, gun drawn, smells gunpowder behind the fence and meets a man who shows Secret Service credentials. Deputy Seymour Weitzman later identified a photo of Bernard Barker as that man. Smith checked cars but not trunks. A deputy hears from a railroad worker that smoke came from the fence. Malcolm Summers says a man with a gun under his overcoat warned him off.
Sgt. D.V. Harkness meets well-armed men in suits behind the Depository who say they are Secret Service. The chronology stresses that none of the 28 agents in Dallas were on foot in the area.
Sorrels later returns from Parkland. One agent left behind is picked up by another car.

Connally later says no leader can be spared a dedicated assassin and the Secret Service's failure wasn't one of will. Weitzman, told at the fence that the shot came from the other side, sees a young blonde woman drop a lunch sack west of the building, later noting its similarity to the sack at the window. He picks up a skull fragment on Elm and gives it to "authorities"; his Commission testimony on it goes off the record.
Craig stops a woman trying to drive a brown Chevrolet out of the lot behind the knoll and hands her to another deputy.
Craig says the lot was leased by a deputy and rented to deputies, with a locked bar at its only entrance.
Altgens runs to the AP office and phones the bureau chief, who types a bulletin; it is on the wire at 12:39.
About a dozen people are detained in the following hours; Larry Florer, apparently drunk, is held after leaving the Dal-Tex Building and released.
Former Secret Service chief U.E. Baughman says it's a basic rule to clear the upper floors of buildings on the route, that no one returned fire, and that much needs explaining.
Witnesses, including the Willis family, see police lead a young man in a black leather jacket and gloves out of the Dal-Tex Building to jeers; there is no record of the arrest.

About fifteen minutes later, an elevator operator reports a stranger in the Dal-Tex Building; he is held for hours, gives his name as Jim Braden in Dallas on oil business, says he came in after the shooting to phone his mother, and is released. He is Eugene Hale Brading, a parolee with underworld ties.

Brading had legally changed his name in September; he had a long record. His parole file mentioned meeting Lamar Hunt, and Hunt's security chief placed him at Hunt's offices the day before, when Ruby was also there. He stayed at the Cabana, which Ruby visited, and had an office down the hall from Marcello's lawyer, where Ferrie worked.
On June 4, 1968, Brading will be staying in Los Angeles near the Ambassador Hotel, where Robert Kennedy is shot; police question him.

The Commission's earliest time for Oswald to leave by the front entrance. Oswald says a man he took for a Secret Service agent asked him for a phone as he left; reporter Pierce Allman later said he may have been that man. His interrogators never asked how he left.
A KBOX news car arrives behind the Depository after a trucker moves a barrier; a man in a dark sport coat runs out the back.

Oswald told Fritz two men, one with a crew cut, stopped him at the door asking for a phone; WFAA's Pierce Allman and Terrence Ford say they asked a man for a phone. An FBI report relays secondhand gossip that girls at a sewing room saw Ruby hand Oswald a pistol outside.
Craig sees police detain a Latin man on Elm who is later released by a man claiming to be Secret Service, whom Craig later thought might be Edgar Eugene Bradley.
Roy Cooper sees a young white man wave down a light Nash Rambler wagon that pulls out fast, nearly hitting his boss's Cadillac, and heads toward Oak Cliff.

Law clerk Lillian Mooneyham sees a man in the sniper's window a few minutes after the shots, when Oswald was supposedly already downstairs; witnesses to the gunman describe a light shirt, while Oswald wore brown.
The KBOX car pulls up near the rear of the building.
The Channel 1 interference ends after about four minutes, preceded by beeps the chronology reads as Morse "V". It also says Washington phone service was disrupted for an hour.
On Air Force One, Col. Swindal hears Kellerman: "Lancer is hurt. It looks bad." The plane's Secret Service radio then goes dead and he learns of the death from TV.
After Merriman Smith gets out the first UPI flash, the pool car's radiotelephone is put out of action (Smith is said to have yanked the cord).
Early broadcasts (KRLD, ABC, AP via WFAA) wrongly report a Secret Service agent killed.
Channel 2: keep Parkland's emergency entrance clear. An officer reports a witness who saw a man with a gun in the Depository; Curry asks for the witness's details.
Hoover phones Robert Kennedy at home: the President has been shot, seriously. Robert Morgenthau sees Kennedy recoil in horror; he tries to call Dallas and prepares to fly there.
Robert Kennedy reaches someone at Parkland (he believed Clint Hill), who later calls back, about thirty minutes after Hoover, to say the President is dead.

Hoover's phone log shows that besides Kennedy and the Secret Service, he called only oilman Billy Byars that afternoon, a close friend and friend of Murchison; within days the FBI hears Murchison and his aide Tom Webb knew Ruby. David Talbot describes Kennedy taking Hoover's blunt call by the pool.

Tom Dillard photographs a Rambler station wagon in the rail yard. Off-duty Sgt. Tom Tilson and his daughter chase a man in dark clothes who came down the embankment and drove off; Tilson said he looked like Ruby.
A researcher theorizes the "Badge Man" figure in Moorman's photo is Tippit and that a patch on an officer in the tramp photos is a Klan symbol; speculative.
Of the deputies, sixteen place the shots near the underpass, three have no opinion, one implies the Depository. Of police interviewed, four say the knoll, four the Depository, four no opinion.
Of 126 witnesses the Warren Commission heard from (out of 266 known), 51 placed the shots near the knoll, 32 the Depository, and 38 gave no opinion; several thought there were two locations.
A sergeant reports a witness who says shots came from the fifth floor. S.M. Holland reaches the fence and finds police already there in the deputies' parking area.
Beverly Oliver says she met officers P.T. Dean and Roscoe White near the fence.

Jean Hill sees officers with rifles rather than the standard shotguns. The chronology lists police and purported agents seen in the plaza after and before the shots, including Deputy Harry Weatherford with a rifle on the jail roof (rumored to have had a silencer). In New Orleans, Judge Christenberry announces the shooting during Marcello's trial; Ferrie leaves, books Marcello's Houston motel for that night for himself and two friends, and calls a Houston skating rink, which he later misdescribes to the FBI.
Harkness, sealing the rear of the building, finds men who say they are Secret Service.
Smith testifies he drew his pistol behind the knoll, felt silly, put it away, and a man showed him Secret Service identification.
Police had been shown samples of the real Secret Service identification beforehand. Sylvia Meagher suggests the "agent" was an assassin with false credentials, a lead the Commission ignored.
The Warren Report: motorcade agents stayed at their posts to the hospital; none stayed at the scene or entered the Depository; Sorrels was first back, about 20–25 minutes later.

The chronology says the CIA made the agents' lapel pins and that a secret 1954–1975 agreement exempted the CIA from reporting crimes by its people. WFAA's Allman asks a man in the building for a phone (possibly Oswald). UPI's wire: three shots fired at the motorcade.

Marsalis bus No. 1213 heads west on Elm toward Oak Cliff. Witnesses describe Oswald's clothing variously: tan shirt and gray jacket (Randle), light brown jacket (Baker), brown shirt with holey elbows and gray work pants (his former landlady Mary Bledsoe).
Bledsoe, on Cecil McWatters's bus, recognizes Oswald boarding a few blocks on; he walks back past her, then gets a transfer and gets off when the bus stalls in traffic.
Bledsoe prepared notes before testifying at an agent's suggestion, a common practice.
McWatters, on schedule at St. Paul and Elm at 12:36, picks up a man who bangs on the door near Griffin, pays his fare and sits on the right.

Stuck near Poydras, a motorist says the President has been shot; a woman catching a train and the man get transfers and leave mid-block near Lamar. Oswald then walks to William Whaley's cab. Police board the bus to search passengers.
McWatters recalls work clothes and a cloth jacket and at a lineup says one man only resembles his passenger.
Passenger Roy Milton Jones, interviewed in 1964, says a dark-haired man sat behind him and left by the front door, but he couldn't identify Oswald.
Jones recalled a light blue jacket and gray khakis. McWatters may have confused passengers: he recalled a man on a later run saying the President was shot in the temple.

Later on Marsalis an older woman boards and scolds McWatters for joking about the shooting; he points to the man behind him, who had said the President was shot in the temple, and she says the man is smiling.
McWatters lets the smiling man off south of Saner Avenue; he was regular rider Roy Milton Jones, who lived just there, suggesting McWatters's "temple" passenger was Jones, not Oswald.
Baker, Truly and Mrs. Reid didn't see a jacket on Oswald, yet the bus and cab witnesses describe one; the chronology wonders whether he fetched one from the domino room.
In Georgetown, Desmond FitzGerald leaves a lunch call "white as a ghost"; aide Sam Halpern says he hopes the Cubans had nothing to do with it, and they rush to CIA headquarters.
Channel 2: keep traffic off Industrial Boulevard. ABC radio reports three shots fired at the motorcade.
Officer 260 radios a witness saying the gunfire came from the Depository's fifth floor.

Head nurse Doris Nelson at Parkland gets the police call that the President is on his way. The chronology notes no advance hospital alert, no radio link from the limousine, and that Methodist Hospital was closer.

Twelve doctors converge on the emergency area, including Perry, Baxter, McClelland, Jones, Kemp Clark, Jenkins, Giesecke, Hunt, Akin, Peters, Curtis and Bashour; Bashour, shown the official head-wound photo in 1979, reportedly asked why they covered it up.
Inspector Herbert Sawyer posts guards at the Depository's front door and loading dock: no one in or out.
Parkland prepares to admit case 24740, white male, gunshot wound.
Youngblood tells Johnson they'll move off alone on arrival; Johnson agrees.
ABC radio's Don Gardiner reads the flash; UPI says the President is wounded, perhaps fatally.

KRLD's James Underwood hears Amos Euins say the gunman was a colored man and records it; Euins's sheriff's affidavit says white. Police detain a Latin man on Elm, released when he seems not to speak English (Craig thinks he later drove the Rambler).
Channel 2: a witness hit by a ricochet; officers surrounding and searching the Depository; reports that more people may have been shot.

With Deputy Buddy Walthers at the curb mark on Elm, Craig hears a whistle, sees a man run down from the Depository and get into a light Rambler station wagon driven by a dark-complexioned man; he later identifies the runner as Oswald.

Women from a Dal-Tex sewing room reportedly said they knew Oswald and Ruby and saw Ruby hand Oswald a pistol; there's no record of follow-up. Marvin Robinson and Roy Cooper describe the Rambler pickup independently, as does Helen Forrest.
In 1989 researcher Richard Bartholomew found a Rambler wagon at the University of Texas with a 1964 Mexican tourist sticker, owned by a professor who bought it from a close Johnson friend.
Bartholomew links the car to a circle around Johnson and UT; three witnesses separately saw two men leave in a light Rambler about ten minutes after the shooting.
Harrison Livingstone repeats reports of the shooters switching cars in Temple or Paris, Texas, where someone recognized Mac Wallace.

In The Men on the Sixth Floor (1996), Loy Factor claimed he was paid to join Oswald and a "Wallace" on the sixth floor with a woman coordinating by radio; the authors think Wallace was Mac Wallace. The chronology calls the story fantastic.
Madeleine Brown told those authors she believed Wallace was involved with Johnson's knowledge, repeating her Murchison-party story and saying Johnson later blamed the CIA and "oil people."

Per the Warren Commission, Oswald boards the bus seven blocks east, heading back toward the plaza. The chronology notes the Commission relied on Mary Bledsoe (shirtsleeves, sat at the back) over McWatters and Jones (jacket, sat near the front).
Oswald leaves the bus and takes a cab, offering it first to a woman, and tells driver William Whaley "500 North Beckley."
Johnson's aides reach the Trade Mart. Aboard the unmarked C-54, Sgt. Vinson hears an intercom voice say the President was shot at 12:29; the plane banks south.
Patrolman J.W. Foster leaves the underpass and finds footprints and cigarette butts behind the fence where smoke was seen.
Groundskeeper Emmett Hudson, in front of the fence, saw no guns except police guns.
Mrs. Donald Baker reaches the knoll and sees only police and railroad workers.
Curry radios that the President's head appeared practically blown off.
On the cabinet plane to Japan, a teletype reports the shooting; officials can't immediately reach the Situation Room because the codebook is missing.

General Walker, on a Braniff flight from New Orleans, reportedly urges passengers to remember he was aboard. Toronto's Norman Similas, a witness, leaves town. Bundy mans the Situation Room; the chronology claims someone in Dallas told the Pentagon McNamara and the Joint Chiefs were now in command.
Nellie Connally recalls a silent, terrible drive, her husband alive in her lap.
The cars reach Parkland. Emory Roberts looks at the President, tells Kellerman to stay with him, and goes to Johnson.

Mrs. Kennedy won't let go until Clint Hill covers the President's head with his coat; agents lift the limp body onto a stretcher. Curry says she didn't want anyone to see the back of his head blown off.
Lawson recalls the devastating head damage and gray skin and knew it was fatal.
Merriman Smith asks Hill how badly he's hit; Hill says he's dead. Connally regains consciousness, tries to rise to make way, collapses in excruciating pain and is taken to Trauma Room 2.
Nurse Diana Bowron sees one large hole in the back of the head and helps lift him; Mrs. Kennedy walks beside the stretcher, her roses and hat on top of him.

Agents hustle Johnson into a curtained room; Roberts tells him no one knows if the plot is wider and the President likely won't survive, and Youngblood says he may need to be sworn in. Johnson asks for Congressmen Thornberry and Brooks. Officers Ellis and Courson see an agent expose a boy's film of the limousine.
Kilduff has phones moved into the hospital. Nurses undress the President except for shorts and brace.

Resident Charles Carrico finds no pulse or blood pressure but agonal breathing and occasional heartbeats. Dr. Charles Crenshaw describes the right side of the brain gone and cerebellum hanging from the back of the head. Someone orders steroids, reflecting Kennedy's Addison's disease; the chronology says it couldn't have been Dr. Burkley, who arrived around 12:53.
Burkley's late arrival is documented. Clint Hill paces the room waving a cocked revolver.
Doris Nelson tells him whoever shot the President isn't in this room; he leaves.

Crenshaw and others cut off his clothes and brace; Crenshaw notes a shoe lift for a longer right leg. Burkley supplies hydrocortisone from the President's own bag. Perry tells reporters later the bullet struck him in front. Nurse Patricia Hutton, Dr. Ronald Jones and Dr. Gene Akin describe a massive wound in the back of the head with brain extruding.
Dr. Charles Baxter describes a large gaping wound in the back of the skull and a pinpoint throat wound he took for an entrance.
The chronology says at least 30 Secret Service and FBI interviews of Parkland staff were conducted, none printed in the Warren volumes.

In 1977 Dr. Burkley's lawyer told HSCA counsel Richard Sprague that Burkley, who signed the death certificate, had information suggesting others besides Oswald were involved and would talk; the record shows no follow-up, and his daughter later declined to release the lawyer's files.
Channel 2: move officers to secure the Depository; more men needed.

Crenshaw judges the head wound unsurvivable, but the team keeps working. Burkley, under protocol, becomes Johnson's physician. Nellie Connally sits outside with Mrs. Kennedy amid armed men, peeking in to make sure her husband is being cared for.
Dr. Robert Shaw, held up in traffic by the speeding limousine, hears the news and reaches Trauma Room 2, where colleagues have sealed Connally's sucking chest wound and placed a chest tube.
About now, per the Commission, Oswald leaves the bus near the jammed plaza and walks to the Greyhound station for a cab.

The limousine is partly cleaned at Parkland and the bubble top put on; it is later flown out. Officers H.R. Freeman and Stavis Ellis and medical student Evalea Glanges say they saw a bullet hole through the windshield; Ellis says an agent insisted it was a fragment, and Glanges says the car was quickly driven away when she pointed it out.

Kellerman has Hill keep a line open to Secret Service chief Behn; Robert Kennedy cuts in and Hill says it's very serious. Kellerman then tells Hill, unofficially, the President is dead. With Behn absent, Kellerman and Youngblood act independently; Kellerman isn't told when Johnson leaves.

Greer breaks down to Mrs. Kennedy that he should have swerved. The Parkland doctors' first impression is a throat wound of entrance; Perry, a hunter, sees a small wound with a bruise ring and cuts his tracheotomy through it. About six doctors and two nurses later say they took it as an entrance.

Perry later speaks twice by phone with autopsy pathologist James Humes about the neck wound; when Humes suggests Perry's surgery bruised the lung lining, Perry is offended. In the Senate, an aide tells Mike Mansfield the President has been shot.

Police broadcast a suspect description: white male, about 30, slender, 5'10", 165 pounds, possibly with a .30-caliber rifle (a Winchester is also mentioned). Its source is unclear; the chronology notes a witness could only have seen the gunman from the chest up through dirty windows.

Channel 2: the shots came from the fourth or fifth floor. In Oak Cliff, friends and Gloco station workers see Tippit parked about ten minutes watching traffic from the Houston Street viaduct, then speed off down Lancaster.
WFAA in Dallas is the first TV station to break in with the AP bulletin, read by Jay Watson.
CBS interrupts As the World Turns; Walter Cronkite gives the first national TV report.
Police car 106 with Patrolmen B.L. Jones and M.D. Hall arrives at the Depository.
A man offers Officer Hargis $17,000 for his blood-spattered helmet; he refuses.
In Washington, Katharine Graham, Schlesinger and Galbraith are interrupted with the news at the Post.
Castro, at lunch, takes the call, says it's terrible, and turns on American radio.

Zapruder tells a reporter Kennedy is dead; he saw it through his viewfinder. At Parkland Dr. Kemp Clark finds the pupils fixed and dilated; Perry starts closed-chest massage anyway. Baxter puts the heart's stopping between 12:45 and 1:00.
Dr. Robert McClelland later says he looked into a large hole in the back of the head and that some X-rays don't match what he saw, suggesting a cover-up.

Carrico testified to finding a small wound in the lower front neck, no large back wound, a large avulsed skull wound with cerebral and cerebellar tissue, fixed pupils and no pulse, and to inserting an endotracheal tube past a ragged tracheal injury.
Dr. Shaw takes charge of Connally.

Within the hour, after Lee Bowers stops a train, police roust three "tramps" from a boxcar behind the Depository. Their records went missing until 1992, when their names were found: Harold Doyle, John Gedney and Gus Abrams.
The chronology repeats speculation that the older tramp was "Albert Osborne," alias Howard Bowen, who rode Oswald's bus to Mexico; the 1992 records name him as Gus Abrams.
Doyle later says someone told the tramps at the station they were lucky to see the President's killer in person.
Tippit is ordered to central Oak Cliff to stand by for emergencies; Officer Ronald Nelson too.
The chronology notes this order wasn't in the first transcript given to the Commission and suggests it may have been added later.
A caller complains to CBS that Cronkite shouldn't report the story because he was always out to get Kennedy; Cronkite, who answers, tells her off.
Eugene Brading is held after acting suspiciously in the Dal-Tex Building and released under the name James Braden. One theory makes him a coordinator of the shooting.
The Texas Theatre on West Jefferson opens.
Oswald is reportedly seen making a call at a laundromat at Davis and Clinton.
Amos Euins again describes the window gunman as a colored man.
Tippit is told to go to central Oak Cliff.

Per the Commission, Oswald gets into Whaley's cab at the Greyhound station; Whaley's log shows a 12:30–12:45 trip, which the Commission said reflected rounding. Oswald offered the cab to an elderly woman first. The chronology argues the Commission had to discount much of Whaley's initial account to reach its finding.
Channel 2: someone mentions the seizure in the crowd before the motorcade arrived and asks it be checked out.
Captain Talbert orders the back of the Depository sealed so no one leaves.
Sgt. S.Q. Bellah asks for rope to hold back the crowds flooding the plaza. Officers ask whether Connally was hit and what to do at the Trade Mart.
Captain Fritz, at the Trade Mart, asks what to tell the crowd; told both men were shot and the President's appearance is very doubtful.
Help is requested at Main and Houston; fire and rescue units are sent.
Connally is confirmed hit; the President's injuries unknown.

Radio says the suspect is believed still in the Depository. Oswald is often said to have drawn attention as the only missing employee (Truly says he noticed), but the chronology lists some two dozen employees who were absent or didn't return, including Carolyn Arnold, Charles Givens and Mrs. Donald Baker.
A call from a Dallas Riverside 8 number to a Pablo Brenner or Bruner in Mexico City says "he's dead," before the death is announced.
Fritz again asks if the President will come to the Trade Mart; very doubtful.
Dispatcher Murray Jackson reaches Tippit at Lancaster and Eighth in central Oak Cliff and tells him to be at large for any emergency. The suspect description has been broadcast several times.
FBI agent Robert Barrett arrives at the Depository.
A fire rescue unit with rope is sent to the plaza.
The Trauma Room 1 team has worked about twenty minutes. In Room 2, Drs. Red Duke and David Mebane stabilize Connally with a chest tube and IV before X-ray and surgery.
Johnson waits under guard behind a curtain across the hall with Mrs. Johnson, Congressmen Thornberry and Brooks, and agents Youngblood, Kivett and Taylor.
Kellerman briefs Johnson; Johnson asks for coffee.
Youngblood has agents assigned to Johnson's daughters and asks for a report on the President's condition.
Mrs. Kennedy, in shock outside Trauma Room 1, asks an aide for a cigarette.
Roberts tells Johnson the President won't make it and they should leave; Youngblood says they don't know the scope of the conspiracy and only Washington is safe.
O'Donnell tells advance man Marty Underwood they don't know if Johnson is a target and to get him back to the plane.
T.F. Bowley picks up his daughter at school and drives west on Tenth Street to fetch his wife.
Housekeeper Earlene Roberts gets a call to turn on her TV.
Jackson checks that Tippit is still in Oak Cliff; Tippit says yes, his last known transmission. Car 207, with Sgt. Gerald Hill and reporter James Ewell, arrives at the Depository.
Tippit is reported back at the Gloco station watching traffic off the viaduct; Jackson can't raise him, assumed away from his radio as was his habit.

Five witnesses put Tippit at the Gloco station from about 12:45 for ten minutes, with no dispatch sending him there; he speeds south on Lancaster, reports from Eighth and Lancaster at 12:54, then turns onto Jefferson.

At the Top Ten Record Store, owner Dub Stark and clerk Louis Cortinas see Tippit rush in, use the phone without completing a call, and speed off north, running a stop sign onto Sunset, a block from North Beckley and about two minutes from Oswald's rooming house. His next 8–10 minutes are unaccounted for.
Father Oscar Huber gives the President last rites. His clothes are folded in a corner.

Baxter testifies that after the death was pronounced the Secret Service asked them to clear the room. Oswald reaches his rooming house at 1026 North Beckley and hurries to his room; Earlene Roberts says a police car stopped outside, honked twice and drove off. An FBI document calls the reason unknown.

Investigators found that only Tippit's car was officially nearby. Some suggest Assistant DA Bill Alexander, who rode with Sgt. Gerald Hill (on hand at the Depository, the Tippit scene, the theater and Fritz's office), or Roscoe White with Tippit. One theory has White shooting Tippit as Oswald realized he was being framed. All speculative.
Captain Fritz arrives and orders the building sealed, after at least 10 and perhaps 28 minutes without effective containment. Hill arrives just behind him.
Army intelligence agent James Powell of the 112th, who had been photographing in the plaza, enters the Depository and must show ID after it's sealed; no inquiry examined his role.

William C. Bishop, who later described himself as a CIA contract agent and Army colonel, says he was checking press credentials at the Trade Mart, commandeered a police car to Parkland and was posted outside the trauma room.
Bishop told researchers in 1990 he had been assigned to kill Trujillo in 1961.
Oswald, having changed his shirt, leaves zipping a jacket and is seen at the northbound bus stop.
This is when he supposedly picks up his revolver (de Mohrenschildt later wrote Oswald owned a Beretta). Dale Myers times his exit at 12:59:30.
The Warren Commission concluded Oswald didn't actually change shirts and that fresh fibers matching his arrest shirt on the rifle's butt plate were probably caught that day.

But Officer Baker testified Oswald wore a different shirt at his arrest, and Oswald said he changed, which would undercut the FBI fiber finding. Last seen by Roberts at Zang and Beckley around 1:04, he reaches the Texas Theatre unseen; the chronology suggests he was driven.

A description later broadcast in the Tippit case: white male, 27, 5'11", 165, black wavy hair, light gray Eisenhower jacket, dark trousers, white shirt, armed with a .32 automatic. Headquarters again confirms Tippit is in Oak Cliff.

Dr. Kemp Clark tells Mrs. Kennedy her husband has a fatal wound; she says "I know." He pronounces the President dead before some 19 medical staff and others. Dr. McClelland in 1988: someone on the knoll shot him.
Four physicians present (Crenshaw, Grossman, Seldin, Zedelitz) were never called by the Warren Commission; fifteen others were.
Nurse Bowron recalls wrapping extra sheets around his head so Mrs. Kennedy could see him.

Nurse Nelson sends for a plastic mattress cover to line the casket because the head wound kept bleeding through. Ernest Mentesana's film shows police on the Depository roof area examining a rifle without a scope; a secretary told a reporter it was found on the roof, and ATF agent Frank Ellsworth thought a rifle was found on the fourth floor; there is no official record. Congressman González hears a man on a hospital phone say he saw the body. Parkland staff describe a large wound at the back of the head and a small front throat wound that don't match the Bethesda record. Hoover calls Robert Kennedy again: the President is dead.

Another account has Robert Kennedy telling Hoover his brother is dead. He tells Edwin Guthman he thought "they" would get him instead. By 1:00 p.m. Dallas time, 68 percent of American adults have heard of the shooting.

CIA Director McCone spends three hours alone with Robert Kennedy, reportedly agonizing whether the Castro plots backfired; the next day he briefs Johnson on a Mexico City cable implicating Castro. Kilduff addresses Johnson as "Mr. President," and Lady Bird cries out. FBI agent J. Doyle Williams, sent to offer help, says agents wrestled him to the floor and Kellerman asked him to leave. Youngblood: told of the death, Johnson asked about Mrs. Kennedy; O'Donnell said to take Air Force One, and Johnson agreed to wait aboard for her and the body.

Car salesman Jack Lawrence, an Air Force-qualified marksman, rushes into a nearby dealership muddy and sweating and vomits; co-workers find the car he borrowed parked behind the knoll fence. He is briefly held, then leaves Dallas; claims tying him to Marcello and Charles Harrelson are attributed to Sam Giancana.

A phone operator told the FBI that on a collect call from Michael Paine to Ruth, he said he felt sure Oswald had killed the President but didn't think him responsible, adding "we both know who is responsible." This is before the arrest.

Ruby calls his sister from the Morning News. Neighbors of Red Bird airport complain about a twin-engine plane revving at the end of the strip for an hour before it takes off. Police search the bus Oswald reportedly took.

No Depository employee says they fear going back in. Theatre employee Butch Burroughs hears someone enter shortly after 1:00 and go to the balcony; he later says Oswald bought popcorn around 1:15 and moved seat to seat beside several patrons.
Tippit has not yet been shot.

Bricklayer William Lawrence Smith sees a man he later identifies as Oswald walking west toward Tenth and Patton; Jimmy Burt and William A. Smith also see him. Some witnesses say he reversed direction as Tippit approached. Assistant DA Alexander doubted Oswald could have walked there unseen.
In 1977 Max Allen Long claimed Oswald was headed for his mother's house on Tenth as a safe house.
Mechanic Domingo Benavides is diagnosing a stalled car on Patton.

The Texas Theatre starts newsreels and cartoons before War Is Hell; Burroughs later says Oswald slipped in between 1:00 and 1:07. Deputy Luke Mooney finds the stacked cartons around the southeast sixth-floor window, almost half an hour after fifth-floor workers said they heard shells overhead.
Burt and Smith see the man walking west (the Commission says east), a block and a half east of the Tippit site.

Insurance salesman James Andrews says a patrol car forced him to the curb near the Top Ten store; the officer, nameplate Tippit, looked agitated, checked inside his car without a word, and drove off east on Tenth.
Another account has Tippit leaving the Gloco station at high speed south on Lancaster.

Helen Markham, walking to her bus, sees a police car moving slowly east on Tenth. Cabbie William Scoggins, eating lunch, sees a man walking west as Tippit passes; Jack Tatum sees the man turn toward the police car.

Tippit stops beside a man walking east on Tenth who resembles the suspect; the man leans in to talk through the passenger window. When Tippit gets out and walks around the front, the man draws a pistol and shoots him. That morning Tippit had told his son he loved him no matter what happened.
In 2004 Marie Tippit recalls 17 years of marriage and knowing she was loved.
Myers's book puts Tippit's Top Ten visit at 1:11.
Off-duty officer Harry Olsen is guarding an estate near the scene; that night he and his girlfriend, a Ruby dancer, talk with Ruby for an hour. He leaves Dallas a month later (Anthony Summers).

Theories: Tippit was set up to be killed to implicate Oswald, who was to die at the theater; Ruby was the backstop; the conspiracy was meant to look like one. Others note Tippit's resemblance to Kennedy and propose his body or X-rays were substituted. These are speculation.

More from the "Dallas underground" claims: Tippit as a "dirty cop" close to Ruby, seen with Ruby and Oswald at a restaurant, and out of his assigned district all afternoon; a mechanic says he saw Oswald in a parked car after the shooting. These rest on secondhand reports.

The chronology says Tippit seemed to be frantically searching for someone, notes Andrews's employer once employed Roscoe White (whose wedding Marie Tippit attended), Tippit's moonlighting at a theater owned by Manuel Avila with anti-Castro ties and at Austin's Barbecue, and that he last had coffee with Officer Billy Anglin around 11:30–11:45.
The Warren Commission called no Tippit relatives, associates or fellow officers.
Jack Tatum says the gunman walked around the car to the fallen officer and shot him in the head; the HSCA called that more like an execution than an escape.

Four bullets hit Tippit, the last to the head; the gunman walks toward Patton ejecting shells and reloading. Myers times the murder at 1:14:30. A previously unreported witness, Doris Holan, told researchers before her death that she saw a second police car in a driveway across the street and a man who looked at Tippit and went back up the driveway.
Sam Guinyard reportedly saw a police car in the alley. Prints on Tippit's car were not Oswald's, though accounts conflict. A police shirt not Tippit's was found on his back seat.
Witnesses describe the killer in a white shirt under a tan-gray jacket, lighter than the rust-brown shirt Oswald wore when arrested.
