Of thirteen witnesses, the chronology says only Markham and Benavides could reconstruct it. Mark Lane says Markham was pressed through several lineup attempts before identifying Oswald, and told him the killer was short and heavy; Benavides didn't identify Oswald.

Benavides watches the gunman reload and leave, then struggles with Tippit's radio. He couldn't identify Oswald and wasn't called by the Commission (he gave a deposition to counsel). A red Ford also pulls over at the corner.
T.F. Bowley stops at the scene and notes the time as 1:10, which the chronology says leaves too little time to walk from the rooming house.

Acquilla Clemons says she saw a short, heavy man with a gun wave a tall, slender man to "go on" before they left in opposite directions. Deputy Craig says the news reached the sixth floor at 1:06. KRLD's Wes Wise heard a car near the scene was traced to Carl Mather, a Tippit friend.
Mather worked for Collins Radio, had a security clearance and worked on Air Force Two; the chronology says Collins leased a boat used to run guns to anti-Castro rebels.
The Commission had the killer walking east, the same direction as Tippit's car, which the chronology says its timeline required.
Of the four bullets from Tippit's body, three are Winchester-Western and one Remington-Peters; of four shells at the scene, two are Winchester and two Remington.
Oswald's .38 had been rechambered for .38 Special; the chronology argues shells fired in it would bulge, while the Archives shells look normal.

Helen Markham reaches Tippit, who seems to try to speak and dies. The chronology argues the official walking times (13 minutes per the Warren Commission, 14½ per the HSCA, from 1:03 at Beckley and Zang) put Oswald at Tenth and Patton no earlier than 1:16, contradicting Markham (1:06), Bowley (1:10), Craig (1:06) and the police log, and that the evidence has the gunman walking west, which the Commission rejected.
Dale Myers, in With Malice, times the murder at 1:14:30.

Frank Cimino runs out and Markham tells him to call the police. Frank Wright says he saw a man in a long coat, unarmed, look down at the fallen officer, then drive off in a gray 1951 Plymouth. Mechanic T.F. White says he saw a man he later recognized as Oswald in a red Ford Falcon parked oddly in the El Chico lot, who sped off when approached; the plate traced to Carl Mather, a friend of the Tippits, whose HSCA deposition remains classified.
Used-car men Warren Reynolds and B.M. Patterson chase the gunman down Jefferson until he hides behind a Texaco station; a false alarm at a library draws police away.
Highway patrolmen south of Dallas stop a speeding car with three men in suits; one says they're Secret Service hurrying to New Orleans to investigate. No such dispatch is recorded.
Ruby leaves the Morning News building.
Police get reports of a man with a rifle near Cobb Stadium on the Trade Mart route; nothing comes of it, though some theorize a backup team.
Channel 2: the Secret Service is coming downtown; a K-9 unit is requested for the Depository search.
About an hour after the news, reporter Haynes Johnson, in exile leader Harry Williams's room at Washington's Ebbitt Hotel after Williams's meeting with CIA officials, calls Robert Kennedy.
Robert Kennedy tells him flatly, "One of your guys did it."
Channel 2: rifle hulls found on the sixth floor, a man apparently there some time; a drunk on the tracks is to be brought in; all officers on duty to be held.
In Hollywood, Andy Griffith's cast hears the news; in Atlanta, Martin Luther King tells his wife that's what will happen to him, in such a sick society.
Police seal off the Kennedy compound at Hyannis Port.

An inspector reports shells on the "fifth" floor. No one notices the long paper bag near the shells: Sgt. Hill and crime-lab man J.B. Hicks saw only a lunch bag, and the long bag isn't photographed in place (L.D. Montgomery may have picked it up, yet his prints aren't on it).
Lt. Carl Day's photo seems to show two empty shells and one live round on the floor.

No clip is photographed or mentioned until the Warren Report says the rifle contained one. With three spent shells and one live round, the chronology notes the rifle held only four rounds, and no other ammunition was ever found.

Deputies Craig and Mooney say the three hulls lay side by side, pointing the same way, unlike normal ejection. A rifle is found and first called a 7.65 Mauser. The chronology asks why the shooter hid the rifle but left shells in view, and notes Sgt. Hill, who led the search, knew Ruby.
Craig says the hulls were within an inch of each other, and one was crimped at the mouth.
Marina first told the FBI she knew of no ammunition; in February 1964 she recalled a box in New Orleans and on Neely Street.
No rifle-cleaning equipment was ever found among Oswald's things, yet the rifle was well oiled.
Mooney says Fritz was first to pick up the shells. One analysis argues the live round looks like European cupronickel rather than American gilding metal.
It also claims the spent cases' shoulder dimensions differ from Carcano specifications.
And that they better fit a 6.5×54 Mannlicher-Schoenauer, a much finer rifle.

An FBI evidence envelope signed this day holds photos showing two empty cases and one live round; an early evidence sheet lists two spent 6.5mm rounds. Hoover's report to Curry lists two cases and a live round. The chronology says Fritz produced a third case days later, marked "GD."
"GD" presumably stood for Captain George Doughty, who didn't recall handling it.

Later finds: a .30 military bullet in a roof on Stemmons Freeway (1966), a .30 soft-point on the Massey Building (1967), a 6.5mm sporting fragment in the plaza (1974) and a rusty crimped shell on the Dal-Tex roof (1977), none from Oswald's rifle. Commission photos of the sniper's nest show three different box arrangements, and Sylvia Meagher notes no one asked whose prints were on the cartons.

Testimony on the paper bag is contradictory: Mooney didn't see it; it wasn't photographed; R.L. Studebaker says he taped over a print, but no tape was on it in Washington; Montgomery's prints aren't on it; Craig, Hill and Hicks recall only a lunch sack; and it showed no oil stains.

Chicken bones, a bag and a soda bottle are attributed to Bonnie Ray Williams's lunch, but officers place them in at least three different spots, from the top of the nest boxes to the third window west; filmmaker Tom Alyea says there were none near the nest. Bowley reaches the Tippit scene at 1:10.
Inspector Sawyer radios from outside the Depository that empty hulls were found on the "third floor" and the man had been there some time.
Lt. J.C. Day arrives at the Depository.
At Parkland, Roberts tells Johnson the President is dead; Johnson checks his watch and tells his wife to note the time.
Used-car manager Ted Callaway sees the gunman cut through hedges and run toward him on Patton.
Burroughs says Oswald came down from the balcony, bought popcorn and sat by a pregnant woman who soon went upstairs and was never seen again; he says Johnny Brewer arrived about 20 minutes later.

Bowley takes the radio in car 10 from Benavides and reports an officer shot, the first report of Tippit's murder. The chronology notes the bullets couldn't be matched ballistically to Oswald's altered revolver, and no prints were on the gun.
It calls the official sequence (nearly a mile in twelve minutes, the murder and reloading) virtually impossible.
Channel 2: more officers needed at Parkland. The killer drops a light jacket a few blocks away; it bears laundry tag B 9738.

Checks of 424 Dallas-area and 293 New Orleans cleaners find no match; none of Oswald's clothes bore cleaning marks, and the jacket was a medium when his clothes were small. Anthony Summers reports researchers found Tippit had a two-year affair with a married waitress at Austin's Barbecue, who said she was pregnant by him; her estranged husband had followed them.
An ambulance from Dudley Hughes Funeral Home is dispatched (logged 1:18) and arrives within a minute.

Attendants and Bowley load Tippit before police arrive. Officer Westbrook is given a brown wallet said to be from where Tippit fell, holding Oswald's ID, which FBI agent Barrett insists was found at the scene. Department of Public Safety employees later say Oswald had a driver's license file that was pulled after the assassination.

Sgt. Gerald Hill and Assistant DA Bill Alexander are in the second car at the scene; Hill later takes custody of the revolver. Alexander tells Anthony Summers in 1978 that he still doesn't know how or why Oswald got there: to meet someone, to escape, a missed connection.
Matthew Smith theorizes Roscoe White asked Tippit to drive a CIA man to Red Bird airport, then shot him when Tippit realized he'd been set up, and Oswald fled to the nearest theater.
Dale Myers calls any Tippit-conspiracy idea ludicrous: friends and family said it was foreign to his character, and he was working three jobs.
The ambulance arrives at the Tippit scene (Myers times it at 1:18:59).
The ambulance leaves for Methodist Hospital. Tippit's sister calls Marie Tippit, who phones the station and is told he is dead.
NBC's Bill Ryan reports a neatly dressed young man, clearly not Oswald, taken into custody.
O'Donnell confirms the death to Johnson and urges him back to Washington.
Channel 2: 20 more uniformed officers to Parkland as a precaution.
Officer H.W. Summers reaches the Tippit scene. The feature War Is Hell starts at the theater.

Deputy Eugene Boone finds a rifle between boxes near the sixth floor's northwest stairs, less than an hour after the shooting. Boone and Deputy Constable Weitzman describe it as a 7.65 German Mauser in their reports, Craig says he saw "Mauser" stamped on it, and DA Wade calls it a Mauser that night. The Commission says Weitzman was mistaken and others repeated him.
Boone thought Fritz called it a Mauser. A CIA report from Italy days later says press descriptions of the model are wrong. Army testers had to shim the scope to fire accurately.
No prints are found at first; Oswald's palm print is reported later. Lt. Day said in 1993 the prints on the rifle were weeks or months old.
The chronology explains that "no prints" means no usable prints, not that the gun was wiped, and notes a third possible print under the wood that was never examined.

Hoover's August 1964 letter to the Commission describes a worn, rusty but oiled firing pin and residue showing many shots fired. The chronology says the clip first appears in the Warren Report, argues manual reloading would have been impossible in time, and lists the rifle's defects: stiff bolt, odd trigger, misaligned scope, worn firing pin.

Oswald's clipboard isn't found on the sixth floor for ten days, suggesting no thorough search. No search witness mentions a clip, though the FBI said it bore no prints. ATF agent Ellsworth told the Secret Service the rifle was found on the fourth or fifth floor by a city detective.
A report signed by Lt. Day this day lists one live round in the chamber, three spent hulls, and a clip stamped SMI 952, the clip now at the Archives.

Police broadcast a Tippit suspect last seen in the 300 block of East Jefferson: white male, about 30, 5'8", black hair, slender, white jacket and shirt, dark slacks. Officer Roy Walker arrives. In the theater, Oswald sits beside evangelist Jack Davis, odd in a near-empty house, then moves.
Cronkite repeats the false report that a Secret Service man was killed. Reporter Seth Kantor notes, "They even have to die in secret."
The chronology repeats the claim that 18 material witnesses died in the next three years by violent or sudden causes (a list Reitzes and others dispute).
In Rome, William Harvey reportedly says it was bound to happen and probably good that it did. A bystander tells police the Tippit suspect dropped his jacket behind Ballew's Texaco.
In New Orleans, Perry Russo (later Garrison's witness) recalls reacting with glee. In the Depository, Lt. Day hands the shells to Detective Richard Sims, who bags and initials them.
Sgt. Owens and others search two used-furniture stores on East Jefferson for the suspect.
Davis sees Oswald sit beside another man across the aisle, then leave again, as if looking for someone.

Justice of the Peace Theron Ward, viewing the body from the doorway, is asked by Kellerman to release it; on advice from Wade and Curry he wants the bullet first. The chronology says Texas law required a local autopsy and the Secret Service took the body without authority.

Johnson tells Kilduff to wait to announce the death until he is back at the plane, since they don't know whether it's a wider conspiracy against him or others in succession. FBI agent Vincent Drain describes the standoff with the Secret Service over the body and autopsy.
Chief Curry drives Johnson, crouching in the back seat, to Love Field without sirens; Mrs. Johnson follows in a second car. Youngblood has Johnson's luggage moved to Air Force One.
Youngblood testifies to the ride: picking up Congressman Albert Thomas, Thornberry climbing into the back, and asking Curry to cut the sirens to avoid attention.
O'Donnell later wrote he never told Johnson to take Air Force One or wait for Mrs. Kennedy, and that Commission counsel Arlen Specter asked him to change his testimony to match Johnson's.
He refused to change sworn testimony.
Connally's words "They also got the President" go out on the air, eight minutes before the networks confirm the death.
Texas has no statute of limitations on murder.
FBI agent Barrett leaves the Depository for Oak Cliff.
Tippit is pronounced dead on arrival at Methodist Hospital.
Reporter Seth Kantor says he spoke briefly with Ruby at Parkland; Wilma Tice also says she saw Ruby there. (Ruby denied it; the Warren Commission doubted Kantor, the HSCA thought him probably right.)
Reporter Harry McCormick brings Sorrels to Zapruder, who agrees to give the Secret Service a copy if it isn't given to the media.
A second search of the Depository begins after 1:30; employees are told not to discuss the case, even with family.

ATF agent Frank Ellsworth, in that search, told the Secret Service a detective found the rifle on the fourth or fifth floor, not with the shells, which with the "Mauser" description suggests to the La Fontaines a second gun. Kilduff announces the President's death; it goes out on the wires.
Time's Hugh Sidey recalls Kilduff reading that the President died at about 1 p.m., then weeping in a side office: "Oh, that man's head."
Ruth Paine tells Marina, hanging laundry in Irving, that Kennedy is dead and the shots reportedly came from the building where Lee works; Marina doesn't respond.

Johnson boards Air Force One, tells the pilot it won't leave without the President's body, and has the shades drawn and TV on. He tells O'Donnell that Robert Kennedy advised swearing in there and that Judge Sarah Hughes is coming.

Agents secure the plane. Youngblood says he'll stick to Johnson like glue; Johnson calls for Judge Hughes. FBI agent Vincent Drain says seats were removed for the casket, which had to be tilted up to get it aboard. (The chronology repeats that the Tippit gunman hid behind a Texaco station as police converged.)
Police are drawn to the Jefferson branch library by a report that the suspect is inside; some researchers think it was a diversion. Oswald is near the Texas Theatre about this time.
Police at the library report "wrong man." The chronology asks how they knew without knowing the right man, and notes the library was a block from Ruby's apartment and frequented by Oswald.
Myers says an officer mistook Adrian Hamby, running into the library, for the suspect.
FBI headquarters' Alan Belmont orders all offices to locate bombing suspects, Klan members and other extremists.

(Robert Kennedy's "one of your guys did it" to Haynes Johnson.) The book Farewell America claims Secret Service chief Rowley soon told Robert Kennedy there were three or four gunmen, and that Behn told Sorrels "It's a plot." Myers asks why Oswald risked returning to busy Jefferson Boulevard unless the theater was his destination.

A man slips into the Texas Theatre without paying. Burroughs says it couldn't have been Oswald, who'd been inside since shortly after 1:00, which would clear him of Tippit's murder. Shoe-store manager Johnny Brewer, who saw a man duck from passing police cars, tells cashier Julia Postal; only on December 6 does he mention a brown shirt. Postal didn't think she sold him a ticket and sold 24 that day.

A tip leads police to a car seen on Commerce Street; its driver, picked up in Fort Worth, says he came from Ranger to visit a friend and stayed for the parade, and is released when Oswald's arrest is announced.
Channel 2 reports the Depository is being secured, an hour and five minutes after the shots.
An officer at the Tippit scene radios an eyewitness description of the gunman, armed with a .32 dark automatic; Sgt. Hill soon says the shells indicate an automatic .38 rather than a pistol.
Tippit's autopsy report isn't in the Warren Commission volumes.
Captain W.R. Westbrook sends squads to search west of the Tippit scene.
Undertaker Vernon O'Neal brings a 400-pound bronze casket to Parkland. In Tampa, lawyer Frank Ragano says Hoffa called gloating that Bobby would now be out as attorney general.
A Hoover memo records calling Robert Kennedy with the first flash and being told to do whatever the FBI could.

In the theater, the pregnant woman who sat by Oswald goes up to the balcony and is never seen again. Westbrook and FBI agent Barrett come in the back, perhaps looking for the name in the Tippit-scene wallet.
Brewer checks the concession stand, balcony and exits with Burroughs, then has Postal call the police; she says the man ducks every time a siren goes by.

Police cars race to the theater on a report the suspect is in the balcony. Officers who enter from the front go up; Walker, McDonald and Hutson come in the back, where Hutson counts seven patrons on the main floor, including Oswald, Jack Davis, John Gibson and George Applin.
Applin told the Commission a man at the back watched the arrest calmly; in 1979 he said he later recognized him as Ruby and had been afraid to say so (Crossfire).

The chronology wonders why so many police answered a ticket-skipping call, citing Matthew Smith's story of police already waiting in an alley. A Secret Service veteran later claimed "we lost a man that day," echoing the false early reports.

Ruby arrives at the Carousel and closes the club for the night, makes calls and watches TV. Zapruder, his partner, Sorrels and McCormick go to the Morning News, then WFAA, where Zapruder is interviewed live.
Senior engineer Darrell Tomlinson finds a nearly pristine bullet on a Parkland stretcher; it becomes CE 399.

Hoover told Johnson within a week the bullet came from the President's stretcher, which would rule it out as the single bullet. Fragments found under Mrs. Connally's seat have since disappeared, and an agent finds another skull piece on the flight home. Dr. Shaw tells reporters a bullet remains in Connally's thigh. In the Senate, Don Reynolds's testimony about a $100,000 TFX payoff to Johnson via Bobby Baker (denied by Baker) is cut off by the news.
Radio Free Europe broadcasts the news to Eastern Europe.
Lt. Day leaves the Depository carrying the rifle.
Inspector Sawyer asks detectives to pick up Charles Givens, a Black porter with a police record who left the building.

Brewer opens the stage door to find police with guns drawn and leads them in. Officer Nick McDonald orders Oswald up; Oswald draws his pistol and they struggle until he is subdued (one witness said he was pistol-whipped). Officers had first questioned an unidentified young man in the balcony whom a "manager" said had been there since noon, though no manager was on duty; police reports even say Oswald was arrested in the balcony. Of 24 patrons, police recorded only two names.

Nixon cancels his afternoon and stays in watching the coverage; told jokingly that better makeup might have made him president, he says he'd be dead too. Police were looking for a man in a white shirt and jacket in the balcony but focus on a man in a brown shirt on the main floor. Officers hear the snap of the revolver misfiring; the FBI later notes a dented primer and bent firing pin. Westbrook orders him out fast, and Postal hears an officer say they have their man on both counts, calling him Oswald.
Walt Brown notes the search for other evidence or assassins stopped once Oswald became the suspect.
No report shows anyone checked his ID before an officer named him "Oswald" to Postal; WFAA film shows police looking through the wallet from the Tippit scene.
FBI agent Bardwell Odum and others describe a brown jacket; Oswald actually wore a brown shirt over a white T-shirt.

Oswald tells Fritz he changed his trousers at the rooming house, and the next day says shirt too, describing a reddish button-down shirt and gray trousers in his dresser; police inventory a brown button-down shirt and gray trousers there.
Those gray trousers match what Bledsoe, Jones and Whaley described. Police at the Depository find an unclaimed blue "Sir Jac" jacket.

Marina said Oswald had two jackets, blue and gray; she identified the blue one from the Depository and the gray one (CE 162) from the parking lot. Meagher doubts Westbrook found it, and police never showed it to Oswald.
Oswald complained he wasn't allowed a jacket for a lineup like the others; the chronology asks why police didn't put him in the gray jacket before witnesses.
CE 162 is a light gray zipper jacket; Benavides recalled light beige.
Markham: a short grayish-tan jacket, open in front; she didn't recognize CE 162.
Scoggins gave no independent description; Barbara Davis said a dark coat.
William Arthur Smith: a sport coat of some kind; Virginia Davis: light brown tan jacket.
Ted Callaway: a light tannish-gray windbreaker, same type but more tan. Earlene Roberts couldn't identify it.
Frazier couldn't recognize the gray jacket.
Only Sam Guinyard described and identified it without qualification.
The chronology tallies the rest as failing to describe or identify it, and notes the same witnesses didn't recognize the brown shirt.

In the car Oswald is calm and quiet, protesting he only carried a pistol in a movie; told he killed a policeman, he remarks you can only fry for that. Hill says he found six rounds in the revolver; five more were in Oswald's pocket. The chronology notes no box of either brand was found among his things.

Hill says Detective Bentley found a Selective Service card for "Alek J. Hidell" in his wallet, but none of the arresting officers' early December reports mention it, and early publicity was about "O.H. Lee," not Hidell. Marina first denied the alias, then said he used it; she said she signed "Hidell" on his FPCC card. Bernard Haire, behind the theater, saw a flushed young man brought out the back and put in a police car, and learned 25 years later that Oswald was taken out the front.
Captain Talbert and officers question a boy in the alley near an idling pickup; Talbert was among the few who filed no arrest report and wasn't asked about it by the Commission.
Offered a chance to hide his face, Oswald says he has nothing to be ashamed of.

The Warren Report describes reporters and cameramen crowding Oswald from the basement elevator to the homicide office, and his walking the 20-foot corridor past them at least 15 times over the weekend, cameras and microphones in his face.

Oswald is brought to Fritz's third-floor office. Meagher notes no question in his interrogations suggests the police or FBI suspected a conspiracy, and Tippit's name doesn't appear in the early questions.
Between 1:00 and 2:00, agent Richard Johnsen takes the stretcher bullet from O.P. Wright; Tomlinson later says it looked different from CE 399.

FBI examiner Robert Frazier testified the bullet was clean, without blood, tissue or fibers; Cyril Wecht calls that nearly impossible for a bullet that passed through clothing and two men. The FBI's spectrographic results were never put in evidence.

In 1993 Parkland's former nursing director Elizabeth Wright told researcher Wallace Milam her husband, security chief O.P. Wright, also found an unfired .38 Special on a gurney that day, which she had kept.
The Warren Commission ruled out the President's stretcher as the source, saying he stayed on it until placed in the casket and it was then moved to Trauma Room 2.
In 1964 none of the men in the chain of possession (Tomlinson, Wright, Johnsen, Rowley) could positively identify CE 399 as the bullet found.
The bronze casket is wheeled out to O'Neal's hearse.
The chronology claims the casket came back to O'Neal with green paint marks instead of blood, and that oxygen tanks and a body bag taken with it suggest a substitution; photos show the handles down.

From Air Force One Johnson calls Robert Kennedy, Abe Fortas (asking about Reynolds's testimony) and Dallas lawyer Waddy Bullion about his stocks. Marshals guard Hickory Hill. O'Donnell is overheard saying they'll take it back in '68. Robert Kennedy sends Jack Miller of the Criminal Division to Dallas.

Film by the Dallas Cinema Associates shows a different rifle, short-stocked and heavy-barreled, perhaps an Enfield, brought down the Depository fire escape; officials said in 1967 it was a security man's. (Weatherford's rooftop rifle is mentioned again.)

The chronology says one photo of Day dusting the rifle shows no clip while another of him carrying it shows one, and that the sling swivels appear on the side rather than the bottom as in the backyard photo.

It cites Life photos as showing the rifle is a rare Mussolini-bodyguard variant. The FBI quickly took interest in a Johnson semiautomatic .30-06 tied to anti-Castro raiders Hemming and Loran Hall, which Hall and a Hispanic man reclaimed from a California detective's office a week before the assassination.
Detective Richard Hathcock told the HSCA that Hemming and Hall pawned the rifle with him; Garrison later showed him a photo of a rifle found in Dealey Plaza that looked just like it.
FBI agent Jerry Crow questioned Hathcock and his associate Roy Payne the next day; Payne described the rifle as accurate and reclaimed 10–15 days before the assassination.

Payne said Hall told him on November 18 he was flying to Dallas, and later that he was in the Dallas Hilton lobby during the shooting (Hall told Dick Russell he was in California). Hemming claimed Hall stole rifles from him and gave a long account of Hathcock and a mob-money story.

Mechanic T.F. White sees a man in a red 1961 Falcon idling in the El Chico lot five blocks from the theater, who speeds off when approached; White later says he looked like Oswald and wore a white T-shirt.

Told Oswald was already in jail, White still says the man was possibly identical. The plate he noted belonged to a 1957 Plymouth owned by Carl Mather of Collins Radio, a friend of Tippit, who was nervous when reporters asked and talked to the HSCA only with immunity.
An FBI report confirms plate PP4537 was Mather's. The HSCA dismissed the incident; James Douglass calls the odds against coincidence astronomical.

The chronology notes Oswald once visited Collins executive Admiral Henry Bruton with de Mohrenschildt, Collins's Southeast Asia radio contract, and a boat leased to Collins, the Rex, captured by Cuba in November and said by an exile aboard to be running CIA arms.
Castro said the arms were for assassinating Cuban leaders.
Its scenario: an Oswald double in a car traced to Tippit's friend at a CIA-linked firm.
Brading is still held at the sheriff's office; his companion Morgan Brown checks out of the Cabana abruptly.
Sorrels asks Zapruder for copies; Zapruder had refused police who came brandishing shotguns and insisted on a federal representative.
The limousine leaves Parkland, driven by agent George Hickey with a police officer, and is flown to Washington on a C-130.
The New York Stock Exchange closes early after a 24-point drop; the chronology claims short sellers made huge profits.
A Hoover memo: Shanklin reports the President in very poor condition but alive, shots from a fourth floor with a Winchester; asks if Robert Kennedy is coming.

After a heated argument, the Secret Service removes the body over Dallas medical examiner Earl Rose's objection that Texas law requires a local autopsy and the chain of evidence will be broken; Kellerman says they'll take care of it in Washington.
A policeman at Rose's side says they can't go; O'Brien, O'Donnell and Burkley push through. Judge Ward hears DA Wade say he has no objection. The casket is wheeled out.
Agent Andy Berger drives the ambulance to Love Field; Kellerman and O'Donnell radio ahead to let it through and have the pilot ready.

Sorrels told the FBI he stayed at Parkland until the body left, but photos show him back at Dealey Plaza, where he finds two witnesses to shots from the "Oswald window," learns Oswald is the missing employee, and takes Zapruder to Kodak.
Lt. Jack Revill, finishing the Depository search, says Charles Givens told him he saw "Mr. Lee" by the sixth-floor window; Givens's own later account doesn't mention it.
A Hoover memo: he called Robert Kennedy about the President's condition and was told he was dead.
A Dallas police memo relays that a former Cuban employee at Parkland was overheard saying the President would be killed; one theory makes him the planter of CE 399.

The hearse reaches Air Force One and the casket is loaded. Mrs. Kennedy stops Clint Hill from going after a photographer: she wants them to see what they've done. Gary Mack says an NBC cameraman's close film of the loading was taken by police and is missing.
AP again wrongly reports a Secret Service agent and a policeman killed.
Edward Kennedy and Eunice Shriver reach the White House.
Robert Kennedy later said he asked McCone, in a way he couldn't lie, whether the CIA killed his brother, and he said no. McCone came to believe there were two shooters.
NBC reports a rifle found on the fifth floor; papers call it a Mauser and mention a chicken lunch left by the assassin.
Police take Sorrels, Zapruder and others to Kodak to process the film; Phil Willis agrees to give the Secret Service copies of his slides.
Fort Worth photographer George Smith arrives at the plaza.
Hoover memo: Shanklin reports the President dead, three or four shells found, one man picked up, and (wrongly) an agent killed.

The casket is placed aboard Air Force One; the Kennedy party is shocked to find the Johnsons aboard. Mrs. Kennedy declines to change her bloodstained clothes and walks in on Johnson in the bedroom checking the typed oath.
Photographers Smith, Beers and Allen photograph the three "tramps" being marched through the plaza. Police report a two-tone green car with a rifleman, though Oswald is in custody.

At the doctors' press conference Perry describes the throat wound as an entrance. Fritz returns, saying Oswald was the only employee unaccounted for (four others hadn't returned). FBI agent Hosty, compiling a list of right-wing suspects, learns of Oswald's arrest, finds the Oswald file missing from its place, and is sent to join the interrogation.
Hoover notes Secret Service chief Rowley is thinking of subversives in Mexico and Cuba while Hoover mentions the Klan, and that witnesses disagree whether the shooter was white or Black.

Controller Louis Gaudin sees a Comanche leave Red Bird with three men and return with two. CIA documents released in 1977 report two Cubans flying from Dallas via Tijuana to Mexico City, where one boarded a Cuban flight in the cockpit.

Judge Sarah Hughes swears in Johnson, who then orders "Let's get airborne." General McHugh says the pilot had been told to wait and claims he found Johnson hiding in the lavatory crying that it was a plot, an account others dispute.
Johnson asks Mrs. Kennedy to stand with him; he takes her hands and thanks her. Twenty-five people crowd the stateroom.
Manchester describes Johnson waiting for her as photographer Cecil Stoughton arranges the scene.
David Lifton theorizes the body was taken from the casket during this unattended period (2:18–2:32).
Only McHugh stays with the casket during the oath; the chronology notes claims linking him to the CIA.
Channel 2 relays a Secret Service teletype report (false) of an agent killed. NBC's MacNeil logs Perry's statement that a bullet struck the President in front.
Two men in police uniforms reportedly demand Zapruder's film; he refuses, and police files have no record.
John Franklin Elrod is arrested in Dallas.

Elrod later claimed his cellmate was Oswald, who talked of a gun deal, a man with a smashed face and Ruby; the chronology links this to a November 18 gun-laden Thunderbird crash tied to Ruby's mechanic and dealer John Masen. The story surfaced only in 1992.
Manchester: Johnson says "Now we're going" and orders bouillon; Mrs. Kennedy excuses herself to go back to the casket.
Sitting with O'Donnell by the casket, she weeps for the first time.
She and O'Donnell agree nothing matters but what they've lost.
Leaving the plane, Judge Hughes gives an unknown, officious man the Bible used for the oath, Kennedy's own, which was never recovered (Manchester).

Air Force One takes off. Johnson phones Rose Kennedy and Mrs. Connally and repeatedly calls Bundy in the Situation Room; the chronology traces Bundy's later hawkish role. General Clifton arranges a forklift at Andrews and an autopsy at Walter Reed.
McHugh's lavatory story is repeated. Robert Kennedy has Bundy change the combinations on the President's files.
Secret Service agent Robert Bouck begins dismantling Kennedy's secret White House taping system.
Bouck says only a few people knew of it; the tapes went to the Kennedy family and in 1976 to the Kennedy Library, which concedes some items were removed. Tapes after November 8, 1963 are missing.
A patrolman turns in a snub-nosed .38 found in a paper sack at Ross and Lamar.
Paraffin tests of Oswald are positive on the hands and negative on the cheek.
A criminal-investigation text explains the paraffin test is nonspecific and can give false positives and negatives.

Fritz, Curry, Alexander and detectives describe Oswald as unusually composed and quick in interrogation, refusing anything pertinent; Curry later said no one could put him in the building with a gun, and Wade first said more than one person may have been involved.
Hosty tells Lt. Revill a Communist killed the President and the FBI knew he was capable of it.

Revill's report records Hosty saying Oswald was a Communist Party member living in Dallas whom the FBI knew capable of the assassination; when Curry repeats this to the press, Shanklin has him retract it.
An officer tells Fritz Oswald has a room on Beckley, though Oswald gave no address and neither Marina nor Paine knew it; some suggest the officer was Roscoe White.
Four Depository employees are still out of the building. AP transmits Ferd Kaufman's photo of Oswald.
Johnson, told Oswald has a State Department file, asks whether State erred in letting him return.
Agents in Austin fly back to Washington on a KC-135 still not knowing if the President is alive.
Ruby stands in line at a bank with $7,000 in cash, then stops at a deli.
O'Donnell gives Mrs. Kennedy her first Scotch.
A dispatcher asks for an escort for Bill Moyers, coming to swear in Johnson.
George Smith enters the Depository with the press between 3 and 4.
FBI records show George H.W. Bush phoning to report hearsay that James Parrott had talked of killing the President in Houston.
A November 29 Hoover memo reports Miami exile reaction as shock and no plans for raids.
It says this was orally given to "Mr. George Bush of the Central Intelligence Agency" on November 23.
Joseph McBride published the memo in The Nation in 1988; whether it referred to the future president is disputed.
Ruby drives to his sister's and leaves to buy food.
Johnson keeps phoning Bundy from the plane.
Johnson calls Rose Kennedy; Mrs. Kennedy takes calls only from Robert Kennedy. The flight lasts 150 minutes.
Agents McIntyre, Roberts, Lawton and Ready leave on the backup plane.
Lt. Col. Robert Jones of the 112th tells the FBI in Dallas that "A.J. Hidell" is linked to Oswald.
The autopsy on Officer Tippit's body begins.

Photographer Jerry Cabluck is flown by a Bell helicopter over Dealey Plaza for aerial pictures; his brother Harry spots for him from the ground and photographs Officer J.W. Foster beside a manhole cover on Elm Street, near where a bullet is thought to have struck the curb.
In New Orleans, Carlos Marcello is acquitted and leaves the courtroom showing no emotion.

Deputies and Detective Guy Rose arrive at the Paine house in Irving; Ruth Paine lets them search without a warrant, to Marina Oswald's evident displeasure. Linnie Mae Randle tells them Oswald rode to work with her brother that morning and put a long, wrapped package on the back seat.
Hoover writes that Oswald went to Cuba several times but would not say why (as reported by Armstrong).

Air Force Sgt. Robert Vinson later claims that a C-54 he was riding landed briefly on a rough strip by the Trinity River in Dallas, picked up two men in coveralls (one of whom he later thought resembled Oswald), and flew on to Roswell. He kept silent for about thirty years.
Assistant Treasury Secretary Robert Wallace announces that no Secret Service agent was hurt in the attack.
Agents Kinney and Boring later said agent Stewart Stout died soon after Dallas, but Stout's 1963 and 1964 reports and later film of him with Johnson show the story was wrong.

Researcher Vince Palamara suggests agent Dennis Halterman, who vanishes from the shift records after November 21, as the only plausible "dead agent." Shortly before 4 PM, Mary Moorman gives one of her Polaroids to agents Howlett and Patterson.
NBC's Bill Ryan announces on national television that Oswald seems to be the prime suspect.
Aboard Air Force One, Johnson receives word from Washington that the assassination was the act of one man and that there was no conspiracy.
The message comes from the White House Situation Room (McGeorge Bundy or Cmdr. Oliver Hallet). Johnson tells Bundy he wants bipartisan meetings that night and the next morning.
Robert Kennedy telephones Bay of Pigs veteran Harry Ruiz Williams and tells him, "One of your guys did it" (per Talbot, Brothers).
Chief Curry returns to police headquarters from Love Field. At Parkland, Dr. Charles Gregory begins operating on Connally's wrist.
Jack Ruby is reportedly seen in the crowded police headquarters.
Oswald phones Ruth Paine from City Hall about finding a lawyer. His first interrogation begins at 4:20.
The afternoon Dallas Times Herald quotes witnesses who said six or seven shots were fired.

Acting Secretary of State George Ball asks legal adviser Abram Chayes to assemble the Department's Oswald files and a report by the next morning. The chronology's author asks what, two hours after the arrest, justified that effort.

The first search of the Paine garage finds no backyard photographs. Police inventory lists cards with the names G. Hall, A.J. Hidell, B. Davis and V.T. Lee; a vaccination certificate signed "Dr. A.J. Hidell" in Oswald's own handwriting is found at his Beckley Avenue room.
The alias "O.H. Lee" is publicized at once; "Hidell," said to have been found on Oswald at his arrest, is not.

Sheriff's deputies, including Harry Weatherford, leave the Paine search to Dallas police, who find little beyond a blanket. The backyard photographs will be reported found there the next day; another version later surfaces among Roscoe White's effects.

Commercial photographer Robert Hester, called in to process assassination photos, later says he saw an FBI agent with a color transparency of a backyard photo, and one print with no figure in it, before the photos were officially found. His wife corroborates him.
Arrest records are filed for the three "tramps": John Gedney, 38; Gus Abrams, 53; and Harold Doyle, 32. Officer W.E. Chambers is listed as arresting officer; they are released on November 26.
Hoover calls Robert Kennedy to say he thinks they have the man who killed the President.

After radio reports that Tippit was shot by a man in a car, police photographer W.E. Barnes photographs a knocked-down stop sign at Tenth and Patton; later evidence suggests it was down before the shooting.
Oswald is taken to his first lineup. A second search of his pockets turns up five .38 rounds and a bus transfer. Helen Markham's identification of him is shaky.

While Fritz is still questioning Oswald, Capt. Westbrook gives Sgt. Gerald Hill a biography of him (communist, ex-Marine, dishonorable discharge, Russia, New Orleans arrest), information that could not yet have come from Oswald. Westbrook later works in South Vietnam (per Armstrong).
Twenty-six Secret Service agents are reportedly at Bethesda awaiting the body; the Warren Commission mentions five.
Lt. Cmdr. William Pitzer, head of audio-visual at the Naval Medical School, takes a phone call, leaves dinner with his 35mm camera and does not return home until the next afternoon.
Dr. Robert McClelland's written report gives the cause of death as a gunshot wound of the left temple; Drs. Jenkins and Giesecke also later describe left-side head wounds.
Ruby, weeping, phones Cecil Hamlin to say he has closed his clubs for the weekend.
Agent Paul Rundle organizes three rings of security around Johnson's Washington home, the Elms: city police, the National Guard, then Secret Service agents.
Mrs. Kennedy wants the President's friends to carry the coffin from the plane, but at Andrews Gen. Godfrey McHugh's military team takes over.

Air Force One lands at Andrews. As the bronze casket is unloaded, a helicopter takes off from the far side of the plane, its purpose unknown. Johnson makes a brief statement and flies to the White House.
The flight's half-hour delay later fuels theories that the body was taken from the casket, either in flight, at Andrews, or before leaving Love Field, and altered before the autopsy.
Mrs. Kennedy refuses to change her bloodstained suit: "Let them see what they've done." It is later stored by her mother and eventually goes to the National Archives.
Mrs. Kennedy and Robert Kennedy ride with the bronze casket in a gray Navy ambulance driven by William Greer to Bethesda.

In the ambulance, Robert Kennedy speaks briefly with agent Roy Kellerman. Kellerman's widow later says he believed there was a conspiracy; one account says Secret Service chief Rowley told RFK of a crossfire, though Rowley told the Warren Commission Oswald acted alone.
Hoover tells Robert Kennedy that Oswald is a pro-Castro extremist "in the category of a nut," not a communist but with communist leanings, and that he shot at two policemen while fleeing.
The Navy Surgeon General calls Dr. James Humes and tells him to hurry to the hospital.
Johnson's helicopter lands on the White House lawn.

Deputy Roger Craig is brought to Fritz's office and identifies Oswald as the man he saw run from the Depository and get into a Rambler station wagon. Oswald says the car is Mrs. Paine's and not to involve her. Fritz uses no stenographer or tape recorder.
By one account Ruby spends two hours at his sister's home; Detective August Eberhardt says he spoke with Ruby at police headquarters between 6 and 7.
Felipe Vidal Santiago is said to arrive back in Miami from Dallas by 5:30 PM, perhaps by private or military jet.

David Atlee Phillips comes home and says nothing, his wife recalls. Gilberto Policarpo Lopez crosses into Mexico at Nuevo Laredo hours after the border reopens; the CIA later notes his name but never tells the Warren Commission.
Dennis David says a black hearse brings a plain metal casket to Bethesda's rear entrance; Paul O'Connor says the body arrived in a body bag with no brain in the skull.
The gray Navy ambulance, driven by Greer, reaches Bethesda's front entrance and Mrs. Kennedy goes inside.
The ambulance then drives off; the casket team loses it amid confusion over two ambulances. The FBI escorts the bronze casket to the morgue but is kept out of the morgue itself.
Erwin Schwartz and Zapruder reportedly have three copies of the film made at Jamison Film and further prints at Kodak, possibly accompanied by Forrest Sorrels.
Life's Richard Stolley learns of the Zapruder film from reporter Patsy Swank.
Casket-team member Sgt. James Felder later confirms to David Lifton the confusion over two ambulances and a half-hour gap in locating the coffin.

Accounts of the casket's arrival at Bethesda conflict: a decoy ambulance, a casket team that lost its way, FBI and casket-team reports that disagree by forty minutes, Dennis David's sailors unloading a coffin, and technician Jerrol Custer's claim to be carrying head X-rays when Mrs. Kennedy arrived.
Richard Lipsey, aide to Gen. Wehle, later describes a decoy hearse sent to the front while the body went to the morgue, which would require the body to have been moved before the plane left Dallas.
Lipsey also describes a third wound near the hairline; the HSCA medical panel calls that spot in the photographs a fleck of brain tissue.

Greer, Kellerman and Burkley go with the casket to the morgue; Clint Hill and Paul Landis guard Mrs. Kennedy and Robert Kennedy in the 17th-floor suite. O'Donnell and Powers go to Gawler's to choose a mahogany casket.

Bus driver Cecil McWatters is brought in and identifies transfer No. 4459 as one of two he issued on that run. Dr. Robert Livingston of NIH says he phoned Dr. Humes to stress that the small throat wound looked like an entrance wound, and that Humes broke off, saying the FBI would not let him talk.
The FBI later gives this as the time preparation for the autopsy began.
Oswald's second interrogation begins; a paraffin test is made on his hands. He asks if they are trying to prove he fired a gun.
W.E. Barnes performs the paraffin test in Fritz's office.
Oswald is taken to a second lineup. Fourteen-year-old Mike Robinson, at headquarters with a policeman's son, sees motorcycle officer Bobby Hargis return spattered with blood and break down.

Robinson later says that in a basement restroom he overheard three men saying "Lee" should have been killed instead of a cop and would have to be killed before going to Washington; he believes one was Roscoe White. He came forward in 1993.

Fritz, prosecutors Jim Allen and Bill Alexander, and Sorrels talk over the case at the Majestic Cafe. Fritz later calls Oswald intelligent and controlled. Reporter Victor Robertson sees an officer stop Ruby, by name, from entering Fritz's office.

CIA officer Gary Underhill reportedly drives to friends on Long Island, says Oswald is a patsy and that a rogue group connected to the CIA killed the President, then returns to Washington. He is found shot six months later; his death is ruled suicide.
X-ray technician Edward Reed later says he reached the morgue about 6:30, found a casket already delivered and guarded, and saw the body inside in a plastic bag, supporting earlier-arrival accounts.
The second lineup ends; Oswald is returned to Fritz's office.

Dennis David tells the Review Board (1997) that his sailors carried a gray shipping casket from a black hearse into the morgue anteroom before the Navy ambulance with the ornamental casket arrived at the front.
Oswald is formally charged with Tippit's murder; the Tippit autopsy is completed.
Ruby is seen at police headquarters, carrying a loaded gun, as he later admits.
Marina Oswald and the Paines are brought to headquarters. Shown the rifle, Marina says it is like her husband's but she is not sure.
Johnson's first meeting as President is with CIA director John McCone; its content is unknown.
Capt. Taswell Shepard, carrying the nuclear "football," recalls no atmosphere of crisis at the White House that night, contrary to Johnson's later account.
In Tampa, Santos Trafficante, in high spirits, toasts Kennedy's death at dinner with lawyer Frank Ragano, as Ragano later recounts.

In New Orleans, Guy Banister pistol-whips investigator Jack Martin after a night of drinking; Martin says it began when he asked if Banister would kill him as they killed Kennedy. Neither Banister nor Ferrie appears in the Warren Report.
Dallas FBI chief Shanklin tells New Orleans that Oswald is probably a good suspect, but the rifle has not yet been connected to him.

An FBI memo says the U.S. ambassador in Mexico City suspects more than a lone gunman; Mexico City photos believed to show Oswald are to be flown to Dallas, described as "deep snow stuff" to be kept within the FBI.
FBI agents Sibert and O'Neill, following the bronze casket, guide Greer's ambulance to the morgue entrance and help carry the casket into the anteroom at about 7:17.
Johnson phones Hoover and orders a full FBI investigation; until then the FBI had acted without clear jurisdiction.
Johnson writes letters to John and Caroline Kennedy.
Agent Richard Johnsen hands Bullet 399, carried in his pocket from Dallas, to Secret Service chief James Rowley.
Dr. Humes, summoned by senior Navy officers, takes charge of the autopsy; he later testifies he was in the morgue from 7:30 PM until 5:30 AM.
Humes orders out a man with a Speed Graphic camera; a general from the Military District of Washington says he is in charge.
Dr. Finck later testifies they were told not to trace the bullet's path through the body.
Detective Roy Standifer says he greeted Ruby at headquarters around now. At Bethesda, the room is cleared while photographs and X-rays are taken.
Agent Jerry Blaine dines at home before reporting for the midnight shift at the Elms.

Oswald's third interrogation begins, without notes, recordings or a lawyer. Six Secret Service and four FBI agents present at the interrogations are never questioned by the Warren Commission; Curry later concedes the sessions broke every rule of good practice.
The Kennedy children are brought back to the White House.
Robert Kennedy asks Julius Draznin of the NLRB in Chicago to look into possible Mafia involvement.
Oswald phones Ruth Paine again, his second call to her that day.
Marie Tippit recalls a sleepless night and the long grief that followed. She says Robert Kennedy called and all but apologized for the Texas trip; she told him both men died doing their jobs.

The presidential limousine arrives at Andrews by C-130 and is driven to the White House garage. Agent Charles Taylor notes a small hole left of center in the windshield from which fragments were removed; the FBI later reports no hole, and the windshield tested in 1964 has only surface damage. Reports that the Secret Service ordered many replacement windshields persist.

RFK's phone logs show that in February 1964 Evelyn Lincoln suggested he claim the limousine for the Kennedy Library to stop it being rebuilt for Johnson, which would erase evidence (per Talbot, Brothers).

Lt. J.C. Day says he has photographed partial prints on the rifle and lifted a palm print from under the barrel, which the FBI will not receive until November 29; when the rifle reaches the FBI, no trace of the print or the lift remains. Lt. Samuel Bird's honor guard report says it carried the bronze casket into the morgue at 8:00 PM. In Haiti, George de Mohrenschildt later writes, he learned of the killing at a Lebanese Embassy reception.

From the Bethesda suite, Robert Kennedy has the President's belongings removed from his bedroom. Dr. Burkley, sent out of the morgue early, later tells Henry Hurt (1982) that Kennedy was killed by a conspiracy but will not elaborate.

Texas Attorney General Waggoner Carr later testifies that a White House caller asked him to make sure Oswald's indictment did not allege an international conspiracy; DA Henry Wade assured him it would not. FBI agent Vincent Drain is ordered to rush the rifle, revolver and Oswald's effects to Washington and gets a Strategic Air Command tanker at Carswell for the flight.
Sibert, O'Neill and others are let back into the autopsy room. Corpsman James Metzler, sent to the anteroom, finds about ten men in civilian clothes checking identification against a roster.

Sibert and O'Neill record the first incision, and that surgery appeared to have been done on the head, though none was done at Parkland. Technician Edward Reed says the first incision was in the forehead; photographer John Stringer says the doctors had to crack the skull to remove the brain, a step not in the autopsy report.

The chronology argues that such work could have enlarged the head wound to suggest a shot from behind. Saundra Spencer of the Navy photo lab tells the Review Board (1996–97) she developed autopsy negatives on November 23 showing a thumb-sized throat wound and a blown-out wound at the back of the head, and that none of the official photographs she was shown were ones she printed.
David Lifton argues that if the film or the body was altered, Secret Service personnel were likely involved operationally.

The autopsy begins. Those known to be present include Drs. Humes, Boswell, Finck, Burkley, Ebersole, Galloway and Canada; technicians Custer, Reed, Riebe, O'Connor, Metzler and Rudnicki; Dennis David; and FBI agents Sibert and O'Neill. Researchers believe more, including civilians in the gallery, attended; a "Dr. George Bakeman" on the list has never been identified.
The three autopsy pathologists have little experience with gunshot wounds; Finck later says officials in the room hampered him.
Humes, Boswell, Karnei, Stringer and Riebe say photographs of the chest interior were taken, and Finck says he photographed beveling of the skull wound; none are in the National Archives inventory.
Review Board records show the HSCA misstated the autopsy witnesses' views: their accounts and drawings place the skull defect at the rear, as the Dallas doctors did (per Dr. Gary Aguilar).
A medical-legal journal later notes the autopsy report's silence on Kennedy's adrenal condition and questions its reliability.
Dr. Robert Karnei tells the Review Board he remembers a photograph of a probe in the body; none exists in the record.

Jerrol Custer says his neck X-rays showing many fragments are missing and that a fragment fell from the back when the body was lifted. Other technicians recall a bullet rolling from the sheets; Adm. David Osborne says he held it, though the official chain of custody never brings any bullet to Bethesda.
Mrs. Kennedy's obstetrician gives her a sedative, which has no effect.

Despite Dr. Livingston's warning that the throat wound looked like an entrance, Humes does not dissect it. Several witnesses, including Drs. McClelland, Jenkins and Giesecke, Father Huber and RFK's emissary Hugh Huggins, describe a wound at the left temple.
Gawler's embalmer Tom Robinson later describes three tiny holes in the right cheek that leaked fluid.

FBI agent Sibert later rejects the single-bullet theory outright. Radiologist John Ebersole recalls calls between Bethesda and Dallas that night; White House photographer Robert Knudsen tells the HSCA he saw photos with probes through the body, an interview later withheld.
In the White House garage, Paterni and Boring find two fragments of a bullet in the front seat area and a piece of skull on the rug (per Jim Bishop).
Agent Sam Kinney later says he found a piece of the right rear of the skull in the limousine on the flight to Washington.
The original Zapruder film and at least one copy are said to be flown from Love Field to Andrews and taken to the CIA's National Photographic Interpretation Center in Suitland, Maryland.
Secret Service chief Rowley sends Bullet 399 to the FBI laboratory.
Oswald is fingerprinted and paraffin casts are made of his hands and right cheek; hands test positive and cheek negative, consistent with firing a pistol but not a rifle.
A caller calling himself Jim Rizzuto tells a New York radio station Oswald was seen with a right-wing agitator; the FBI finds the story a hoax by Stephen Landesberg, who is later charged.
David Ferrie and two young friends drive overnight through a storm to Houston, supposedly to go skating; at the rink Ferrie never skates and waits by a pay phone for two hours for a call.
Secret Service report: the presidential cars reach the White House garage about 9 PM and are covered and guarded.

Some researchers allege the film was altered at NPIC overnight and copies returned to Zapruder by morning. Johnson tells Arthur Goldberg the world order could "deteriorate pretty quick" if extremists act on wrong assumptions.
Ruby is reported back at his apartment.

Oswald is formally told he is charged with Tippit's murder. In a call that evening, Jerry Behn of the White House detail tells Forrest Sorrels "It's a plot," and Sorrels agrees. Johnson talks with Hoover for fifteen minutes.
The afternoon Secret Service shift travels with Johnson to the Elms for a security briefing.

New Orleans FBI chief Harry Maynor asks headquarters whether to keep pursuing Klan suspects; Alan Belmont is reluctant to authorize interviews. With Hoover already settled on Oswald, contrary leads are unwelcome.
Ruby attends services at a Dallas synagogue.

Zapruder and Schwartz give a copy of the film to the Dallas Secret Service for Washington; agent Max Phillips's note says Zapruder keeps the "master." At 10:10, Paterni, Boring and White House medical staff inspect the limousine. The Kennedy children are moved back to their rooms.

A Cubana flight in Mexico City is said to have been held for hours for a passenger who boarded from a private plane without customs and rode in the cockpit, believed by some to be Cuban agent Miguel Casas Saez. The HSCA finds the flight left at 8:30 PM, before the private plane arrived, and concludes the transfer did not happen.
Ruby has a Nichols garage attendant sign a receipt for $5 given to Karen Carlin.

Switchboard operator Mrs. Troon later says officers were waiting to listen as Oswald tried a collect call to a John Hurt in Raleigh, North Carolina; operators were told to say the number did not answer. The note surfaced in a 1970 lawsuit; HSCA counsel Blakey called the outgoing call deeply troubling.
Former CIA officer Victor Marchetti suggests Oswald was trying to reach an intelligence cutout.

One of two Raleigh John Hurts, John David Hurt, a wartime Army counterintelligence officer, denied any contact with Oswald. Agent Abraham Bolden says Dallas asked Chicago for any "Hurt" or "Heard" spellings the next night.
The Warren Report lists Oswald's calls to the Paine house and his visit from the Dallas Bar Association president, but not the Raleigh call.
Johnson arrives home at the Elms, agents carrying their guns openly, and toasts a portrait of Sam Rayburn.
Ruby returns to police headquarters with sandwiches for the officers and gets in easily; Oswald passes within three feet of him on the way to the press conference.
Life's Richard Stolley reaches Zapruder, who agrees to meet at his office at 9 AM.
At the White House, Arthur Schlesinger blames the far right's preaching of hate.
Captain Fritz signs the complaint charging Oswald with the President's murder.
Dallas police release the rifle to FBI agent Vincent Drain for examination by fingerprint expert Sebastian Latona the next morning.

Chief Curry has ordered Lt. Day to stop processing the rifle. No one witnessed Day's work, and police make no mention of the palm print at press briefings. Latona later matches the lift to Oswald's inked palm; Sylvia Meagher questions how a print from a hand curled around a barrel could match a flat inked print so closely.
Drain later describes being saluted by generals at both air bases, flown by helicopter to the Justice Department, and watching the FBI's tests.
James Angleton's counterintelligence staff writes that Oswald's Soviet contacts in Mexico City might have sinister implications.
Silvia Durán, who processed "Oswald's" visa application, is arrested by Mexican police at CIA direction.

Material on Oswald is flown from Mexico City to Dallas overnight. Helms tells the Mexico City station to drop cable jargon and talk plain English. At 6 p.m. the station says the tapes from the period were already erased, though headquarters is still asking for them the next day.

In Johnson's first recorded call of the morning (10:01 a.m. on November 23), he asks Hoover about Oswald in Mexico City. Hoover says the tape and photos don't match Oswald and that someone seems to have impersonated him. (The syllabus dates this call November 24.)

Men in civilian clothes press Dr. Humes to adopt a back-to-front trajectory exiting at the throat. Corpsman Paul O'Connor says Adm. Galloway stopped the doctors from examining the throat wound, calling it just a tracheotomy.
Humes concludes two shots struck from the rear.
Most of those present at the autopsy are never shown the X-rays or photographs; the chronology says none of the doctors fully agreed with them.
Dr. Finck later concedes the autopsy was not complete by professional standards; the bullet track was not dissected. Jerrol Custer says he was told the next day to X-ray skull bones with fragments.
FBI agent O'Neill says he saw the body fully clothed in a coffin as he left; agent Clint Hill testifies that around 1 AM he was shown the unclothed body to confirm a bullet hole in the back.
Robert Bouck of the Secret Service signs a receipt for "a missile removed during the examination of the body," matching Sibert and O'Neill's report; officially no such bullet exists.

Secret Service agent Elmer Moore later tells Jim Gochenaur he handled the Dallas doctors' testimony, including persuading Dr. Perry away from calling the throat wound an entrance, and rants that Kennedy was a traitor.

Army wound-ballistics consultant Dr. Joseph Dolce later conducts tests showing that shooting a wrist badly deforms a bullet, and says CE-399 could not have caused all the wounds. He is absent from the Warren Report.
DA Henry Wade tells reporters the rifle was a Mauser, he believes, on secondhand information whose source the Warren Commission never asks.
Drain flies the rifle and evidence to Washington on an otherwise empty C-135, returning a day later on an F-104.
The limousine guard detail changes at 12:01 AM.
Three people named Mertz fly from Houston to Mexico City; it has been suggested Jean Souetre posed as John Mertz or Michel Roux.
Michel Roux takes a bus from Fort Worth to Houston, then goes to Mexico City and returns to France via Laredo on December 6.
Dr. Burkley drafts Kennedy's death certificate, a day before signing the autopsy face sheet.

The Dallas Morning News quotes witnesses describing Tippit's killer as a bushy-haired man about 30. A second search of the Paine garage finds two prints and a negative of the backyard photographs. The chronology notes that the chain of custody is broken for nearly every piece of evidence.
At the midnight press conference, Ruby corrects Wade that Oswald's group was the Fair Play for Cuba Committee.
Witnesses say no credentials were checked; reporter Seth Kantor likens the scene to the Middle Ages.

Oswald is put in a maximum-security cell. Waitress Mary Lawrence later says she saw Ruby with a man she was positive was Oswald at the B&B Restaurant after midnight, and was later told by phone to leave town.
The Warren Commission never interviews Lawrence.
Oswald is fingerprinted a second time and photographed.
The cabinet's plane lands at Andrews.
Marina and Marguerite Oswald hide from reporters at an Irving motel. In Jacksonville, Joseph Milteer, just back from Dallas, boasts to informant William Somersett that it happened as he predicted.

From 1 to 4:30 AM an FBI team examines the limousine, removing fragments from the windshield and rear floor; the Secret Service report notes a small hole left of center in the windshield and a dented chrome strip.

About 1:35 AM Oswald is woken and arraigned for the President's murder before Judge J.P. Johnson, still without a lawyer after asking for John Abt all day. Police tell the ACLU he has declined counsel.
The FBI's report of its limousine examination specifically says no bullet holes were found.
At the Elms, agent Jerry Blaine nearly fires his submachine gun at a figure in the dark, who turns out to be Johnson.
Clint Hill is summoned from the presidential suite to view the body in the autopsy room.

FBI official Cartha DeLoach later writes that he watched the film around now and that Kennedy pitched forward; the existing film shows him thrown backward. Dan Rather also reports a forward motion after viewing it.

Gawler's morticians prepare the body. They describe an orange-sized hole only at the back of the head; Tom Robinson also describes a small wound at the right temple and three small holes in the cheek.

Agent Kellerman delivers the autopsy photographs and X-rays to Robert Bouck. They pass to Robert Kennedy's control in 1965; when opened at the Archives in 1966, the brain and tissue slides are missing.
An ambulance leaves Bethesda for the White House with the President's body.

A Navy plane brings photographs from Mexico City to Dallas; former agent Eldon Rudd later says there were no tapes. The chronology notes that the man photographed is not Oswald, and asks why he was being impersonated.

Searching their records overnight, Klein's Sporting Goods finds that rifle C2766 was shipped on March 20, 1963, to A. Hidell, P.O. Box 2915, Dallas; government examiners attribute the order coupon and envelope to Oswald's handwriting.
The body arrives at the White House; Marines escort the ambulance and an honor guard carries the casket to the East Room.
Jack Ruby shoots Oswald at 11:21 a.m. as detectives lead him through the police basement.
A CIA summary says its first information came from Mexico City on October 9 and that Oswald entered Mexico "probably by car," omitting the mistaken photo and description sent October 10.
Douglass's chronology stresses Ruby's renewed access to the basement during the transfer to the county jail, before a live television audience.
President Johnson tells Ambassador Lodge he will not lose Vietnam as China was lost.
FBI headquarters asks Mexico City to send the tapes to the lab; Mexico City replies that no tapes were ever sent to Dallas.
Johnson creates the Warren Commission. Warren first declines and is pressed to accept amid rumors blaming a faction within government; Allen Dulles is named a member.
The FBI finishes its five-volume report; Deputy Attorney General Katzenbach urges the Commission to announce publicly that it shows Oswald acted alone.
The Fair Play for Cuba Committee disbands.
The CIA makes a subordinate of Angleton the point of record for all assassination and Commission matters.
"Bishop" asks Veciana to offer his cousin, a Cuban intelligence officer in Mexico City, money to say publicly he met Oswald; the cousin is recalled before contact.
KGB officer Yuri Nosenko defects, saying the KGB had no interest in Oswald as too unstable; the CIA confines and interrogates him for years before accepting him as genuine.
Ruby begs Earl Warren to take him to Washington to tell the truth; Warren declines.
Guy Banister dies of a heart attack.

Loran Hall reportedly tells the FBI that he, William Seymour and Lawrence Howard were Odio's visitors, and the Commission uses this to dismiss her account; Seymour and Howard deny it, and Hall later tells the HSCA he never said it.
The Warren Report: Oswald fired three shots from the sixth floor, killed Kennedy and wounded Connally, acted alone, and was not a government agent.
Khrushchev is ousted. On November 3 Johnson is elected president.
After Mongoose and JM/WAVE wind down, Ted Shackley and Thomas Clines go to Laos to organize Hmong forces against the Pathet Lao.
Morales goes undercover as an AID public-safety officer in Lima, Peru.
Phillips becomes station chief in the Dominican Republic after the U.S. intervention; Mitchell WerBell III, an OSS veteran and weapons supplier, advises its military.
Rolando Cubela (AM/LASH) is arrested in Havana for plotting to kill Castro.
Johnson names Richard Helms CIA director.
With his death sentence likely to be overturned on appeal, Jack Ruby dies of cancer in a Dallas jail.
New Orleans papers reveal that District Attorney Jim Garrison has been secretly investigating the assassination since November.
David Ferrie is found dead; despite notes read as suicide notes, the autopsy finds a cerebral hemorrhage. Garrison calls him one of history's most important individuals.
Garrison arrests businessman Clay Shaw, whom the chronology calls a CIA asset, for conspiring to kill Kennedy.
Morales joins Shackley on the Phoenix Program against the Viet Cong infrastructure, which the chronology says killed some 40,000 people.
Desmond FitzGerald, who organized at least three attempts on Castro, collapses and dies playing tennis.
Helms creates a Special Operations Group inside counterintelligence to monitor the domestic peace movement (later known as MHCHAOS).
Robert Kennedy is shot in Los Angeles (he dies June 6).
Veciana becomes an AID banking consultant in La Paz, Bolivia, a job he says "Bishop" arranged; the State Department confirms he never applied for it.
Richard Nixon, promising to end the war, wins narrowly.
A New Orleans jury acquits Clay Shaw.
The CIA's Santiago station is approved to recruit assets in the Chilean armed forces.

Former CIA director John McCone, now an ITT director, tells Helms ITT will spend $1 million to stop Salvador Allende. On September 15 Nixon orders Helms to block Allende; Phillips runs the coup effort, Track II.
Allende is inaugurated. A "Plan Z" document alleging a leftist plot surfaces; CIA defector Philip Agee later says a CIA officer under Phillips wrote it.
Former Mexico City station chief Winston Scott dies; Angleton flies in to retrieve his manuscript and files. Speculation persists that Scott kept an Oswald photo; Angleton denies it.
Hunt joins the Nixon White House, plans operations against Edward Kennedy and Daniel Ellsberg, and fabricates cables blaming Kennedy for Diem's murder, with help from CIA Technical Services.

On "Bishop's" instructions Veciana organizes an attempt on Castro in Chile; Veciana says Luis Posada helped plan it, and Phillips later admitted to the HSCA that Posada worked with him in Chile. (The source dates it November 31.)
The White House "Plumbers" are arrested in the Watergate offices, among them Hunt's team: Frank Sturgis and Eugenio Martínez, still on the CIA payroll.

Haldeman, for Nixon, presses Helms to block the Watergate inquiry, warning it could "blow the whole Bay of Pigs thing." Haldeman later concluded this meant the Kennedy assassination; Helms erupted that the Bay of Pigs had nothing to do with it.
Nixon is reelected in a landslide.
Nixon removes Helms and makes him ambassador to Iran; Helms blames his lack of help on Watergate.
William Colby names Phillips chief of the CIA's Western Hemisphere Division.
Veciana proposes a new Castro plot to "Bishop" at the Caracas racetrack; Bishop says the timing is wrong.
In a two-day meeting at a Dallas Ramada Inn, Bishop again rejects Veciana's push for a Castro assassination.
Veciana is charged with conspiring to import cocaine; the only witness is a former partner already charged. He calls himself innocent, first suspecting "Bishop," later Castro agents.
"Bishop" ends the relationship, paying Veciana $253,000 in cash.
Chile's military overthrows Allende, who dies in the coup; the junta kills large numbers of leftists. Philip Agee says the CIA station probably helped supply target lists.
Nixon resigns; Gerald Ford, a former Warren Commissioner, becomes president and nominates Nelson Rockefeller as vice president.
Colby fires Angleton after Seymour Hersh tells him the Times will expose CHAOS and HTLINGUAL, illegal domestic spying and mail-opening programs Angleton controlled.
Ford creates the Rockefeller Commission on CIA domestic activities, naming as executive director David Belin, a former Warren Commission counsel who had defended its report.
The Senate creates the Church Committee; after 15 months it acknowledges the CIA limited its access to the record.
Soon after receiving the Distinguished Intelligence Medal, Phillips retires to found an association of former intelligence officers and defend the agency against critics.
After Colby testifies on assassination plots, Senator Church says it is intolerable for any U.S. agency to engage in murder.

The Rockefeller report finds scores of unlawful CIA activities (break-ins, mail opening, drug testing, domestic spying) but no credible evidence of CIA involvement in Kennedy's death, after limiting itself to the tramp photos (Hunt and Sturgis claims) and the knoll. It attributes the backward head motion to a neuromuscular reaction.
A week before he is to testify about the CIA–Mafia plots, Sam Giancana is shot dead in his basement kitchen with a .22, then shot six more times around the mouth and chin.
Roselli tells the Church Committee how he linked the CIA with Giancana and Trafficante on Castro plots; he says little about Harvey and isn't asked about training teams with Morales at JM/WAVE.

Shocked that Dulles never told the Warren Commission about the Mafia plots, Senator Richard Schweiker reviews the case, sees "the fingerprints of intelligence" on Oswald, and gets a subcommittee to examine the agencies' investigation.
The Washington Post reports Hunt told associates he was ordered in 1971–72, by a senior White House official, to kill columnist Jack Anderson with poison, an order cancelled at the last minute.
Former ambassador to Chile Edward Korry tells the Church Committee the CIA is amoral and could act behind his back, an "invisible" government.
Ford replaces Colby with George H.W. Bush at the CIA.
Schweiker, seeing the staff focus on Castro, decides CIA ties to exile groups need probing and hires Gaeton Fonzi to work Miami's Little Havana.

Veciana tells Fonzi that his CIA controller "Maurice Bishop" started Alpha 66, instigated two Castro plots, staged missile-crisis raids to embarrass Kennedy, and was once seen by him with Oswald, the first evidence (the chronology says) of direct CIA contact with Oswald.
Schweiker notices that a police-artist sketch of "Bishop" closely resembles retired CIA officer David Atlee Phillips.
In a secret session, Roselli admits to Schweiker that his Castro-retaliation story given to Jack Anderson was only his opinion, with no facts behind it.
The Schweiker report finds the FBI and CIA investigations deficient and that important facts were withheld, but omits Veciana's testimony; Schweiker keeps Fonzi investigating.
Orlando Bosch convenes militant exile groups in Bonao, Dominican Republic, to form CORU, which claims over fifty bombings; members are implicated in the Letelier murder. Luis Posada attends.
Roselli's mutilated body is found in an oil drum in Biscayne Bay.
The House creates the Select Committee on Assassinations (Kennedy and King), chaired by Thomas Downing over Henry González's objection; it must be renewed by the next Congress.

Fonzi brings Veciana to a meeting of retired intelligence officers in Reston, Virginia, and introduces him to Phillips by name; flustered, Phillips says he has never heard of Veciana and won't answer more questions.

Former Chilean minister Orlando Letelier is killed by a car bomb in Washington on the junta's orders, with anti-Castro Cubans involved. The chronology links them to Phillips and says he spread disinformation afterwards.
Downing names Philadelphia prosecutor Richard Sprague, with a long record of murder convictions, as chief counsel; Sprague says he will run it as a homicide investigation.

Questioned early by the HSCA, Phillips says the Mexico City cameras weren't working when Oswald came and the tape was routinely destroyed. The CIA demands that Sprague sign a secrecy oath to see its files; he refuses because the agency is a subject of the inquiry.
Deputy counsel Bob Tanenbaum asks Fonzi to join the House inquiry.
William Pawley, backer of Operation Tilt, shoots himself at his Miami Beach home before Fonzi can question him.

The House gives the committee only two months' funding and orders it to justify itself amid press and political attacks on Sprague's methods and his $6.5 million budget request. Henry González becomes chairman after Downing retires.
González fires Sprague and orders police to remove him; the other members overrule him within hours.
González resigns as chairman, calling Sprague an "unconscionable scoundrel"; Louis Stokes takes over.
Carter names Admiral Stansfield Turner to the CIA; Turner cuts 820 positions, mostly in covert operations.
Sprague offers to resign if he is a millstone; members refuse.
George de Mohrenschildt dies of a shotgun wound hours after Fonzi tries to reach him to testify. Sprague resigns that evening; the next day the House renews the committee at $2.5 million a year.
Former Cuban president Carlos Prío, tied to the Havana casinos and to Sturgis's anti-Castro work, shoots himself before Fonzi can question him.
Sprague tells Robert Sam Anson the budget fights were a smoke screen for his conflict with the CIA, and that he would start over by probing Oswald's ties to the agency.
Blakey holds a staff conference on investigative techniques.
In a debate with Mark Lane, Phillips says Oswald had no connection to the CIA and promises to call for abolishing the agency if a cover-up is proven.
Teams are told to define their issues. Blakey agrees that staff may review CIA files but the agency will sanitize their notes, and contacts with former officers must be cleared through headquarters.
Helms pleads no contest to misleading Congress about the CIA's role in Chile.
Manuel Artime, Hunt's close associate, dies of cancer at 45 before HSCA investigators can question him. G. Robert Blakey of Cornell's organized-crime institute had become chief counsel on June 20.
Deputy chief counsel Gary Cornwell says the time for "foraging" is over: only "linchpin issues" answerable before the final report.

A former JM/WAVE officer code-named "Ron Cross" tells investigators Phillips used the name Maurice Bishop and was called "Mr. Bishop" by a deputy, "Doug Gupton"; Gupton says he doesn't recall it. Neither testifies under oath.
The CIA tells the committee several of its offices have no record of a Maurice Bishop.
Phillips swears he never used the name Bishop and was never introduced to Veciana by name; staff urge perjury charges and Blakey declines.
Morales, retired, has a sudden heart attack after returning from Washington and dies the next morning in Tucson; he had told a friend he feared his own people because he knew too much.
Blakey cites a budget crunch and dismisses two-thirds of the investigative staff.
Helms testifies that Oswald was not a CIA agent and that, to his knowledge, the agency never contacted him.
In a deposition, former director McCone says yes, he knew of Maurice Bishop and Bishop was an agency employee.

Questioned by researcher Dan Hardway, Phillips is evasive about his Mexico City role; the questioning shows most sources of disinformation stories in Mexico City and Miami were his assets, and he acknowledges working with Luis Posada in Chile.

HSCA public hearings begin (16 days through December 29), mostly on scientific evidence and organized crime; of four dozen witnesses only Helms is from intelligence, and he is asked about Nosenko and the Castro plots.
John and Nellie Connally testify that he was hit by the second shot, separately from Kennedy, contradicting the single-bullet theory.
Acoustics expert James Barger testifies, from a police motorcycle recording and Dealey Plaza tests, to a 50 percent chance a shot came from the knoll.
Time says the hearings add credence to the Warren finding that Oswald alone killed the President.
The CIA says McCone's deposition was wrong; reinterviewed by the agency, McCone says he was mistaken about knowing a Maurice Bishop.
Acoustics consultants Mark Weiss and Ernest Aschkenasy testify to a better than 95 percent probability of a shot from the knoll.
The HSCA reports that Kennedy was probably killed by Oswald in a conspiracy with unknown others; Blakey says he believes "the Mob did it."
Veciana is shot in the head by an unknown gunman and survives; the FBI investigates a possible foreign-government link.
Reagan names William Casey, an OSS veteran on the board of Phillips's former-officers association, as CIA director; Casey seeks fewer restrictions and later becomes the architect of Iran-Contra.

A Contra supply plane is shot down over Nicaragua; crewman Eugene Hasenfus names "Max Gómez" (Félix Rodríguez, who worked with Morales in capturing Che) and "Ramón Medina" (Luis Posada) as running supply at Ilopango, El Salvador.
James Angleton dies of lung cancer.
David Atlee Phillips dies of cancer; the chronology concludes that Maurice Bishop was buried with him.
